chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: Supposing that Truth is a woman — what then? Is there not ground for suspecting that all philosophers, insofar as they have been dogmatists, have failed to understand women — that the terrible seriousness and clumsy importunity with which they have usually paid their addresses to Truth have been unskilled and unseemly methods for winning a woman? Certainly she has never allowed herself to be won; and at present every kind of dogma stands with a sad and discouraged mien — if, indeed, it stands at all. There are scoffers who maintain that it has fallen, that all dogma lies on the ground — nay more, that it is at its last gasp. But to speak seriously, there are good grounds for hoping that all dogmatizing in philosophy — whatever solemn, whatever conclusive and decided airs it has assumed — may have been only a noble childishness and novice work; and probably the time is at hand when it will be understood once and again what has actually sufficed for the foundation of such imposing and absolute philosophical edifices as the dogmatists have hitherto reared. Perhaps some popular superstition of immemorial time (such as the soul-superstition, which in the form of subject- and ego-superstition has not yet ceased doing mischief); perhaps some play upon words, a deception on the part of grammar, or an audacious generalization of very restricted, very personal, very human — all-too-human — facts. The dogmatists' philosophy, it is to be hoped, was only a promise for thousands of years afterwards, as astrology was in still earlier times, in whose service probably more labor, gold, acuteness, and patience have been spent than on any actual science hitherto: we owe to it, and to its "super-terrestrial" pretensions in Asia and Egypt, the grand style of architecture. It seems that in order to inscribe themselves on the heart of humanity with everlasting claims, all great things must first wander about the earth as enormous and awe-inspiring caricatures. Dogmatic philosophy has been a caricature of this kind — for instance, the Vedanta doctrine in Asia, and Platonism in Europe. Let us not be ungrateful to it, though it must be confessed that the worst, the most tiresome, and the most dangerous of errors hitherto has been a dogmatist error — namely, Plato's invention of Pure Spirit and the Good in Itself. But now that it has been overcome, now that Europe, rid of this nightmare, can again draw breath freely and at least enjoy a healthier sleep, we whose very duty is wakefulness are the heirs of all the strength that the struggle against this error has fostered. It amounted to the very inversion of truth and the denial of perspective — the fundamental condition of life — to speak of Spirit and the Good as Plato spoke of them. One might indeed ask, like a physician: "How did such a malady attack that finest product of antiquity, Plato? Had the wicked Socrates really corrupted him? Was Socrates after all a corrupter of youths, and did he deserve his hemlock?" But the struggle against Plato — or, to speak more plainly and for "the people," the struggle against millennia of ecclesiastical oppression by Christianity (for Christianity is Platonism for "the people") — produced in Europe a magnificent tension of soul such as had not existed anywhere previously. With such a tensely strained bow one can now aim at the furthest goals. Of course the European feels this tension as a state of distress, and twice grand attempts have been made to unbend the bow: once by means of Jesuitism, the second time by means of democratic enlightenment — which, with the aid of freedom of the press and newspaper-reading, might indeed bring it about that the spirit no longer so easily finds itself in "distress." (The Germans invented gunpowder — all credit to them! but they then made things square — they invented printing.) But we, who are neither Jesuits nor democrats nor even sufficiently Germans — we good Europeans and free, very free spirits — we still have it: all the distress of spirit and all the tension of its bow. And perhaps also the arrow, the task, and — who knows? — the goal.
Sils Maria, Upper Engadine, June 1885.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — Prejudices of Philosophers
paragraphs: 1. The will to truth, which is to tempt us into many a hazardous enterprise — the famous truthfulness of which all philosophers have hitherto spoken with respect — what questions has this will to truth not laid before us! What strange, perplexing, questionable questions! It is already a long story — yet it seems as if it were hardly begun. Is it any wonder if we at last grow distrustful, lose patience, and turn impatiently away? That this Sphinx teaches us at last to ask questions ourselves? Who is it really that puts questions to us here? What really is this "will to truth" in us? In fact we made a long halt at the question of the origin of this will — until at last we came to an absolute standstill before a still more fundamental question. We inquired about the value of this will. Granted that we want truth: why not rather untruth? And uncertainty? Even ignorance? The problem of the value of truth presented itself before us — or was it we who presented ourselves before the problem? Which of us is Oedipus here? Which the Sphinx? It seems to be a rendezvous of questions and notes of interrogation. And could it be believed that at last it seems to us as if the problem had never before been raised, as if we were the first to perceive it, to catch sight of it, and risk raising it? For there is risk in raising it — perhaps there is no greater risk.

2. "How could anything originate out of its opposite? For example, truth out of error? or the will to truth out of the will to deception? or the generous deed out of selfishness? or the pure, sun-bright vision of the wise man out of covetousness? Such genesis is impossible; whoever dreams of it is a fool — nay, worse than a fool. Things of the highest value must have a different origin, an origin of their own — in this transitory, seductive, illusory, paltry world, in this turmoil of delusion and cupidity, they cannot have their source. But rather in the lap of Being, in the imperishable, in the hidden God, in the 'thing-in-itself' — there must be their source, and nowhere else!" This mode of reasoning discloses the typical prejudice by which metaphysicians of all times can be recognized; this mode of valuation stands at the back of all their logical procedure. Through this "belief" of theirs they toil for their "knowledge," for something that in the end is solemnly christened "the truth." The fundamental belief of the metaphysicians is the belief in antitheses of values. It never occurred even to the wariest of them to doubt on this very threshold (where doubt was most necessary) — though they had made a solemn vow, de omnibus dubitandum. For it may be doubted, first, whether antitheses exist at all; and second, whether the popular valuations and antitheses of value on which the metaphysicians have set their seal are not perhaps only superficial estimates, only provisional perspectives — besides being probably made from some corner, perhaps from below, "frog perspectives," to borrow an expression current among painters. In spite of all the value that may belong to the true, the positive, the unselfish, it might be possible that a higher and more fundamental value for life generally belongs to deception, to the will to illusion, to selfishness, and cupidity. It might even be possible that what constitutes the value of these good and respected things consists precisely in their being insidiously related to, knotted with, and crocheted to these evil and apparently opposed things — perhaps even essentially identical with them. Perhaps! But who is willing to concern himself with such dangerous "perhapses"? For that investigation one must wait for the advent of a new order of philosophers, such as will have tastes and inclinations the reverse of those hitherto prevailing — philosophers of the dangerous "perhaps" in every sense of the term. And to speak in all seriousness, I see such new philosophers beginning to appear.

3. Having kept a sharp eye on philosophers, and having read between their lines long enough, I now say to myself: the greater part of conscious thinking must be counted among the instinctive functions, and it is so even in the case of philosophical thinking. One has to learn anew here, as we did about heredity and "innateness." Just as little as the act of birth comes into consideration in the whole process and procedure of heredity, so little is "being-conscious" opposed to the instinctive in any decisive sense. The greater part of the conscious thinking of a philosopher is secretly influenced by his instincts, and forced into definite channels. Behind all logic and its seeming sovereignty of movement there are valuations — or, to speak more plainly, physiological demands for the maintenance of a definite mode of life. For example, that the certain is worth more than the uncertain, that illusion is less valuable than "truth": such valuations, despite their regulative importance for us, might nevertheless be only superficial valuations, a special kind of niaiserie necessary for the maintenance of beings such as ourselves. Supposing, in effect, that man is not exactly the "measure of things."

4. The falseness of an opinion is not for us an objection to it: it is here, perhaps, that our new language sounds most strange. The question is how far an opinion is life-furthering, life-preserving, species-preserving, perhaps even species-rearing. We are fundamentally inclined to maintain that the falsest opinions (to which the synthetic judgments a priori belong) are the most indispensable to us; that without a recognition of logical fictions, without a comparison of reality with the purely imagined world of the absolute and immutable, without a constant counterfeiting of the world by means of numbers, man could not live — that the renunciation of false opinions would be a renunciation of life, a negation of life. To recognize untruth as a condition of life: that is certainly to challenge traditional ideas of value in a dangerous manner, and a philosophy that ventures this has thereby alone placed itself beyond good and evil.

5. What makes philosophers regarded half-distrustfully and half-mockingly is not the oft-repeated discovery of how innocent they are — how often and easily they make mistakes and lose their way, in short, how childish and childlike they are — but that there is not enough honest dealing with them, whereas they all raise a loud and virtuous outcry whenever the problem of truthfulness is even remotely hinted at. They all pose as though their real opinions had been discovered and arrived at by the self-evolution of a cold, pure, divinely indifferent dialectic (in contrast to all sorts of mystics who, fairer and more foolish, talk of "inspiration") — whereas in fact a prejudiced proposition, idea, or "suggestion," generally their heart's desire abstracted and refined, is defended by them with arguments sought out after the event. They are all advocates who do not wish to be regarded as such — generally astute defenders, too, of their prejudices, which they dub "truths" — and very far from having the conscience that bravely admits this to itself, very far from having the good taste of courage which goes so far as to let this be understood (perhaps to warn friend or foe, or in cheerful confidence and self-ridicule). The spectacle of the tartuffery of old Kant — equally stiff and decent, with which he entices us into the dialectical byways that lead (more correctly mislead) to his "categorical imperative" — makes us fastidious ones smile, we who find no small amusement in spying out the subtle tricks of old moralists and ethical preachers. Or, still more so, the hocus-pocus in mathematical form by means of which Spinoza has, as it were, clad his philosophy in mail and mask — in fact, the "love of his wisdom," to translate the term fairly and squarely — in order thereby to strike terror into the heart of any assailant who should dare to cast a glance on that invincible maiden, that Pallas Athena: how much personal timidity and vulnerability does this masquerade of a sickly recluse betray!

6. It has gradually become clear to me what every great philosophy has so far consisted of: the confession of its originator, and a species of involuntary and unconscious autobiography; moreover, that the moral (or immoral) purpose in every philosophy has constituted the true vital germ out of which the entire plant has always grown. Indeed, to understand how the most abstruse metaphysical assertions of a philosopher have been arrived at, it is always well (and wise) to ask oneself first: "What morality is he (or are they) aiming at?" Accordingly, I do not believe that an "impulse to knowledge" is the father of philosophy; rather that another impulse has, here as elsewhere, made use of knowledge (and of mistaken knowledge!) as an instrument. Whoever considers the fundamental impulses of man with a view to determining how far they may have here acted as inspiring genii (or demons and imps) will find that all of them have practiced philosophy at some time, and that each one would have been only too glad to view itself as the ultimate end of existence and the legitimate master over all the other impulses. For every impulse is tyrannical; and as such it attempts to philosophize. To be sure, in the case of scholars, really scientific men, it may be otherwise — "better," if you will. There there may really be something like an "impulse to knowledge," some kind of small, independent clockwork that, when well wound up, works away industriously to that end without the rest of the scholarly impulses taking any material part. The actual "interests" of the scholar, therefore, are generally in quite another direction — in the family, perhaps, or in money-making, or in politics; it is almost indifferent at what point of research his little machine is placed, and whether the hopeful young worker becomes a good philologist, a mushroom specialist, or a chemist. He is not characterized by becoming this or that. In the philosopher, on the contrary, there is nothing whatever impersonal; and above all, his morality bears decided and decisive testimony as to who he is — that is, in what order the deepest impulses of his nature stand to one another.

7. How malicious philosophers can be! I know of nothing more stinging than the joke Epicurus took the liberty of making on Plato and the Platonists; he called them Dionysiokolakes. In its original sense, and on the face of it, the word means "flatterers of Dionysius" — that is, the tyrant's accessories and lickspittles. But it also means, "they are all actors; there is nothing genuine about them" (for Dionysiokolax was a popular name for an actor). This last is really the malignant reproach Epicurus cast at Plato: he was annoyed by the grandiose manner, the mise-en-scène style of which Plato and his scholars were masters — and of which Epicurus was not! He, the old schoolteacher of Samos, who sat concealed in his little garden at Athens and wrote three hundred books — perhaps out of rage and ambitious envy of Plato, who knows! It took Greece a hundred years to find out who this garden-god Epicurus really was. Did she ever find out?
8. There is a point in every philosophy at which the "conviction" of the philosopher appears on the scene; or, in the words of an ancient mystery: adventavit asinus, pulcher et fortissimus.

9. You desire to live "according to nature"? O you noble Stoics, what fraud of words! Imagine to yourselves a being like nature — boundlessly extravagant, boundlessly indifferent, without purpose or consideration, without pity or justice, at once fruitful and barren and uncertain; imagine indifference as a power: how could you live in accordance with such indifference? To live — is that not precisely an endeavor to be otherwise than this nature? Is not living valuing, preferring, being unjust, being limited, endeavoring to be different? And granted that your imperative "to live according to nature" means the same as "to live according to life" — how could you do otherwise? Why make a principle out of what you yourselves are, and must be? In reality, however, it is quite otherwise: while you pretend to read with rapture the canon of your law in nature, you want something quite the contrary, you extraordinary stage-players and self-deluders! In your pride you wish to dictate your morals and ideals to nature, to nature herself, and to incorporate them in her; you insist that she shall be nature "according to the Stoa," and you would like to have everything made in your own image, as a vast eternal glorification and generalism of Stoicism! With all your love of truth, you have for so long, so persistently, and with such hypnotic rigidity forced yourselves to see nature falsely — that is, Stoically — that you are no longer able to see her otherwise. And to crown all, some unfathomable superciliousness gives you the Bedlamite hope that because you are able to tyrannize over yourselves — Stoicism is self-tyranny — nature too will allow herself to be tyrannized over: is not the Stoic a part of nature? But this is an old and everlasting story: what happened long ago with the Stoics still happens today, as soon as any philosophy begins to believe in itself. It always creates the world in its own image; it cannot do otherwise. Philosophy is this tyrannical impulse itself, the most spiritual will to power, the will to the "creation of the world," the will to the causa prima.

10. The eagerness and subtlety — I should even say craftiness — with which the problem of "the real and the apparent world" is treated at present throughout Europe furnishes food for thought. He who hears only a "will to truth" in the background, and nothing else, certainly cannot boast of the sharpest ears. In rare and isolated cases a certain will to truth — a certain extravagant and adventurous pluck, a metaphysician's ambition of a forlorn hope — may really have taken part in it: something that in the end always prefers a handful of "certainty" to a whole cartload of beautiful possibilities. There may even be puritanical fanatics of conscience who prefer to put their last trust in a sure nothing rather than in an uncertain something. But that is nihilism, and the sign of a despairing, mortally wearied soul, despite whatever courageous bearing such a virtue may display. It seems, however, to be otherwise with stronger and livelier thinkers who are still eager for life. In that they take sides against appearance and speak superciliously of "perspective"; in that they rank the credibility of their own bodies about as low as the credibility of the ocular evidence that "the earth stands still"; in that they thus, apparently, allow their most secure possession to escape (for what do we at present believe in more firmly than in our body?) — who knows if they are not really trying to win back something which was formerly an even more secure possession, some part of the old domain of the faith of former times, perhaps the "immortal soul," perhaps "the old God" — in short, ideas by which one could live better, that is, more vigorously and more joyously, than by "modern ideas"? There is distrust of these modern ideas in this mode of looking at things, a disbelief in all that has been constructed yesterday and today; there is perhaps some admixture of satiety and scorn that can no longer bear the bric-a-brac of ideas of the most varied origin, such as so-called positivism at present throws on the market; a disgust of the more refined taste at the village-fair motleyness and patchiness of all these reality-philosophasters, in whom there is nothing new or true, except this motleyness. Here I think we should agree with these skeptical anti-realists and knowledge-microscopists of the present day: their instinct, which repels them from modern reality, is not yet refuted — what do their retrograde bypaths concern us? The main thing about them is not that they wish to go "back," but that they wish to get away from it. A little more strength, swing, courage, and artistic power, and they would be off — and not back!

11. It seems to me that there is everywhere an attempt at present to divert attention from the actual influence Kant exercised on German philosophy, and especially to ignore prudently the value he set on himself. Kant was first and foremost proud of his Table of Categories; with it in hand he said: "This is the most difficult thing that could ever be undertaken on behalf of metaphysics." Let us only understand this "could be"! He was proud of having discovered a new faculty in man, the faculty of synthetic judgment a priori. Granting he deceived himself in this matter, the development and rapid flourishing of German philosophy nevertheless depended on his pride, and on the eager rivalry of the younger generation to discover, if possible, something — at least some "new faculties" — to be still prouder of! But let us reflect for a moment — it is high time. "How are synthetic judgments a priori possible?" Kant asks himself — and what is really his answer? "By means of a means (a faculty)." But not in five words — so circumstantially, imposingly, with such display of German profundity and verbal flourishes, that one altogether loses sight of the comical niaiserie allemande involved in such an answer. People were beside themselves with delight at this new faculty, and the jubilation reached its climax when Kant further discovered a moral faculty in man — for at that time Germans were still moral, not yet dabbling in "practical politics." Then came the honeymoon of German philosophy. All the young theologians of the Tübingen institution went immediately into the bushes — all seeking for "faculties." And what did they not find — in that innocent, rich, and still youthful period of the German spirit, when Romanticism, the malicious fairy, piped and sang, when one could not yet distinguish between "finding" and "inventing"! Above all, a faculty for the "transcendental"; Schelling christened it intellectual intuition, and thereby gratified the most earnest longings of the naturally pious-inclined Germans. One can do no greater wrong to the whole of this exuberant and eccentric movement (which was really youthfulness, notwithstanding its bold disguise in hoary and senile conceptions) than to take it seriously, or even treat it with moral indignation. Enough, however — the world grew older, and the dream vanished. A time came when people rubbed their foreheads, and still rub them today. People had been dreaming, and first and foremost — old Kant. "By means of a means (a faculty)," he had said, or at least meant to say. But is that an answer? An explanation? Or is it rather merely a repetition of the question? How does opium induce sleep? "By means of a means (a faculty)," namely the virtus dormitiva, replies the doctor in Molière: quia est in eo virtus dormitiva, cujus est natura sensus assoupire. But such replies belong to comedy, and it is high time to replace the Kantian question "How are synthetic judgments a priori possible?" with another: "Why is belief in such judgments necessary?" — that is, it is high time to understand that such judgments must be believed to be true, for the preservation of creatures like ourselves; though they might still, of course, be false. Or, more plainly and roughly: synthetic judgments a priori should not "be possible" at all; we have no right to them; in our mouths they are nothing but false judgments. Only, of course, the belief in their truth is necessary, as plausible belief and ocular evidence belonging to the perspectival view of life. And finally, to recall the enormous influence "German philosophy" — I hope you understand its right to inverted commas? — has exercised throughout all Europe, there is no doubt that a certain virtus dormitiva had a share in it. Thanks to German philosophy, it was a delight to the noble idlers, the virtuous, the mystics, the artists, the three-fourths Christians, and the political obscurantists of all nations, to find an antidote to the still overwhelming sensualism that overflowed from the last century into this: in short, "sensus assoupire."

12. As for materialistic atomism, it is among the best-refuted theories that have been advanced, and in Europe there is probably no one in the learned world now so unscholarly as to attach serious significance to it, except for convenient everyday use (as an abbreviation of the means of expression) — thanks chiefly to the Pole Boscovich: he and the Pole Copernicus have been the greatest and most successful opponents of ocular evidence. For while Copernicus has persuaded us to believe, against all the senses, that the earth does not stand still, Boscovich has taught us to renounce the belief in the last thing that "stood still" of the earth — the belief in "substance," in "matter," in the earth-residuum and particle-atom; it is the greatest triumph over the senses so far achieved on earth. We must, however, go still further and declare war, relentless war to the knife, against the "atomistic requirements" which still lead a dangerous afterlife in places where no one suspects them (as do the more celebrated "metaphysical requirements"); above all, we must give the finishing stroke to that other and more portentous atomism which Christianity has taught best and longest — soul-atomism. Let me be permitted to designate by this expression the belief that regards the soul as something indestructible, eternal, indivisible, as a monad, as an atomon: this belief ought to be expelled from science! Between ourselves, it is not at all necessary to get rid of "the soul" thereby, and thus renounce one of the oldest and most venerated hypotheses — as often happens to the clumsiness of naturalists, who can hardly touch "the soul" without immediately losing it. But the way is open for new versions and refinements of the soul-hypothesis; and conceptions such as "mortal soul," "soul as subjective multiplicity," and "soul as social structure of the instincts and passions" want henceforth to have legitimate rights in science. In putting an end to the superstitions that have hitherto flourished with almost tropical luxuriance around the idea of the soul, the new psychologist is really thrusting himself into a new desert and a new distrust — the older psychologists may have had a merrier and more comfortable time of it; but eventually he finds that precisely thereby he is condemned to invent — and, who knows, perhaps to discover — the new.

13. Psychologists should bethink themselves before putting down the instinct of self-preservation as the cardinal instinct of an organic being. A living thing seeks above all to discharge its strength — life itself is will to power; self-preservation is only one of its indirect and most frequent consequences. In short, here as everywhere else, let us beware of superfluous teleological principles — one of which is the instinct of self-preservation (we owe it to Spinoza's inconsistency). This is what method ordains, which must be essentially economy of principles.

14. It is perhaps just dawning on five or six minds that physics too is only a world-interpretation and world-arrangement (according to us, if I may say so!), and not a world-explanation. But in so far as it is based on belief in the senses, it is regarded as more, and for a long time to come must be regarded as more — namely, as an explanation. It has eyes and fingers of its own, it has ocular evidence and palpableness of its own: this acts fascinatingly, persuasively, convincingly upon an age with fundamentally plebeian tastes — it in fact follows instinctively the canon of truth of eternal popular sensualism. What is clear, what is "explained"? Only what can be seen and felt — every problem must be pursued that far. Obversely, the charm of the Platonic mode of thought, which was an aristocratic mode of thought, consisted precisely in resistance to obvious sense-evidence — perhaps among men who enjoyed even stronger and more fastidious senses than our contemporaries, but who knew how to find a higher triumph in remaining masters of them, by means of pale, cold, gray conceptional networks thrown over the motley whirl of the senses — the mob of the senses, as Plato said. In this overcoming and interpreting of the world in the manner of Plato there was an enjoyment different from what the physicists of today offer us — and likewise the Darwinists and anti-teleologists among the physiological workers, with their principle of the "smallest possible effort" and the greatest possible blunder. "Where there is nothing more to see or grasp, there is also nothing more for men to do" — that is certainly a different imperative from the Platonic one, but it may nonetheless be the right imperative for a hardy, laborious race of machinists and bridge-builders of the future, who have nothing but rough work to perform.

15. To study physiology with a clear conscience, one must insist that the sense-organs are not phenomena in the sense of idealistic philosophy; as such they certainly could not be causes! Sensualism, therefore, at least as a regulative hypothesis, if not as a heuristic principle. What? And others say even that the external world is the work of our organs? But then our body, as a part of this external world, would be the work of our organs! But then our organs themselves would be the work of our organs! This seems to me a complete reductio ad absurdum, if the conception causa sui is something fundamentally absurd. Consequently, the external world is not the work of our organs?

16. There are still harmless self-observers who believe there are "immediate certainties" — for instance, "I think," or, as Schopenhauer's superstition puts it, "I will" — as though cognition here got hold of its object purely and simply as "the thing-in-itself," without any falsification on the part of either subject or object. I would repeat, however, a hundred times: that "immediate certainty," as well as "absolute knowledge" and the "thing-in-itself," involve a contradictio in adjecto; we really ought to free ourselves from the misleading significance of words! The people on their part may think that cognition is knowing all about things, but the philosopher must say to himself: "When I analyze the process expressed in the sentence 'I think,' I find a whole series of daring assertions whose proof would be difficult, perhaps impossible: for instance, that it is I who think, that there must be something at all that thinks, that thinking is an activity and operation on the part of a being thought of as a cause, that there is an 'ego,' and finally, that what is to be designated by thinking has already been determined — that I know what thinking is. For if I had not already decided within myself what thinking is, by what standard could I determine whether what is just happening is not perhaps 'willing' or 'feeling'? In short, the assertion 'I think' assumes that I compare my state at the present moment with other states of myself that I know, in order to determine what it is; on account of this retrospective connection with further 'knowledge,' it has at any rate no immediate certainty for me." In place of the "immediate certainty" in which the people may believe in the particular case, the philosopher thus finds a series of metaphysical questions presented to him, veritable conscience questions of the intellect, namely: "Where did I get the notion of 'thinking'? Why do I believe in cause and effect? What gives me the right to speak of an 'ego,' and even of an 'ego' as cause, and finally of an 'ego' as cause of thought?" He who ventures to answer these metaphysical questions at once, by appealing to a sort of intuitive perception — like the person who says, "I think, and know that this at least is true, actual, certain" — will today encounter a smile and two notes of interrogation in any philosopher. "Sir," the philosopher will perhaps give him to understand, "it is improbable that you are not mistaken, but why should it be the truth?"

17. With regard to the superstitions of logicians, I shall never tire of emphasizing a small, terse fact which these credulous minds unwillingly recognize: namely, that a thought comes when "it" wishes, and not when "I" wish — so it is a perversion of the facts to say that the subject "I" is the condition of the predicate "think." It thinks; but that this "it" is precisely the famous old "ego" is, to put it mildly, only a supposition, an assertion — and assuredly not an "immediate certainty." After all, one has gone too far with this "it thinks" — even the "it" contains an interpretation of the process, and does not belong to the process itself. One infers here according to the usual grammatical formula: "To think is an activity; every activity requires an agent; therefore—." It was pretty much on the same lines that the older atomism sought, besides the operating "power," the material particle in which it resides and out of which it operates — the atom. More rigorous minds, however, learned at last to do without this "earth-residuum," and perhaps we shall someday get used to doing without the little "it" (to which the worthy old "ego" has refined itself), even from the logician's point of view.

18. It is certainly not the least charm of a theory that it is refutable; it is precisely thereby that it attracts the more subtle minds. It seems that the hundred-times-refuted theory of "free will" owes its persistence to this charm alone: someone is always appearing who feels himself strong enough to refute it.

19. Philosophers are accustomed to speak of the will as though it were the best-known thing in the world; indeed, Schopenhauer has given us to understand that the will alone is really known to us, absolutely and completely known, without deduction or addition. But it again and again seems to me that in this case Schopenhauer only did what philosophers are in the habit of doing: he adopted a popular prejudice and exaggerated it. Willing seems to me to be above all something complicated, something that is a unity only in name — and it is precisely in a name that popular prejudice lurks, which has mastered the inadequate precautions of philosophers of every age. So let us for once be more cautious, let us be "unphilosophical": let us say that in all willing there is, first, a plurality of sensations — namely, the sensation of the state "away from which," the sensation of the state "toward which," the sensation of this "from" and "toward" itself; and then, besides, an accompanying muscular sensation, which, even without our putting arms and legs in motion, commences its action by force of habit as soon as we "will" anything. Just as sensations — indeed many kinds of sensations — must be recognized as ingredients of will, thinking is also to be recognized; in every act of will there is a ruling thought; and let us not imagine it possible to sever this thought from the "willing," as if the will would then remain over. In the third place, the will is not only a complex of sensation and thinking; it is above all an emotion, and specifically the emotion of command. What is called "freedom of the will" is essentially the emotion of supremacy in respect to him who must obey: "I am free, 'he' must obey" — this consciousness is inherent in every will; and equally so the straining of the attention, the straight look that fixes itself exclusively on one thing, the unconditional judgment that "this and nothing else is necessary now," the inward certainty that obedience will be rendered, and whatever else pertains to the position of the commander. A man who wills commands something within himself that renders obedience, or that he believes will render obedience. But now let us notice what is strangest about the will — this affair so extremely complex, for which the people have only one name. Inasmuch as in the given circumstances we are at the same time the commanding and the obeying parties, and as the obeying party we know the sensations of constraint, impulsion, pressure, resistance, and motion that usually commence immediately after the act of will; inasmuch as, on the other hand, we are accustomed to disregard this duality and deceive ourselves about it by means of the synthetic concept "I" — a whole series of erroneous conclusions, and consequently of false judgments about the will itself, has become attached to the act of willing. So much so that he who wills firmly believes that willing suffices for action. Since in most cases there has been exercise of will only where the effect of the command — consequently obedience, and therefore action — was to be expected, the appearance has translated itself into the feeling that there was a necessity of effect. In short, he who wills believes with a fair amount of certainty that will and action are somehow one; he ascribes the success, the carrying out of the willing, to the will itself, and thereby enjoys an increase of the sensation of power that accompanies all success. "Freedom of will" is the expression for the complex state of delight of the person willing, who commands and at the same time identifies himself with the executor of the order — who as such enjoys also the triumph over obstacles, but thinks within himself that it was really his own will that overcame them. The one willing adds the feelings of delight of his successful executive instruments, the useful "underwills" or under-souls — indeed, our body is but a social structure composed of many souls — to his feelings of delight as commander. L'effet c'est moi. What happens here is what happens in every well-constructed and happy commonwealth: the governing class identifies itself with the successes of the commonwealth. In all willing it is absolutely a question of commanding and obeying, on the basis of a social structure composed of many "souls" — on which account a philosopher should claim the right to include willing-as-such within the sphere of morals, regarded as the doctrine of the relations of supremacy under which the phenomenon of "life" manifests itself.

20. That individual philosophical ideas are not something optional or autonomously evolving, but grow up in connection and relationship with one another — that, however suddenly and arbitrarily they seem to appear in the history of thought, they nevertheless belong just as much to a system as the collective members of the fauna of a continent — is betrayed in the end by the circumstance that the most diverse philosophers fill in, again and again, a definite fundamental scheme of possible philosophies. Under an invisible spell, they always revolve once more in the same orbit; however independent of each other they may feel themselves with their critical or systematic wills, something within them leads them, something impels them in definite order, one after the other — namely, the innate methodology and relationship of their ideas. Their thinking is in fact far less a discovery than a recognizing, a remembering, a return and homecoming to a far-off, ancient common household of the soul out of which those ideas formerly grew: philosophizing is so far a kind of atavism of the highest order. The wonderful family resemblance of all Indian, Greek, and German philosophizing is easily enough explained. In fact, where there is affinity of language, owing to the common philosophy of grammar — I mean owing to the unconscious domination and guidance of similar grammatical functions — it cannot but be that everything is prepared at the outset for a similar development and succession of philosophical systems, just as the way seems barred against certain other possibilities of world-interpretation. It is highly probable that philosophers within the domain of the Ural-Altaic languages (where the conception of the subject is least developed) look "into the world" otherwise, and will be found on paths of thought different from those of the Indo-Germans and Muslims: the spell of certain grammatical functions is ultimately also the spell of physiological valuations and racial conditions. So much by way of rejecting Locke's superficiality concerning the origin of ideas.

21. The causa sui is the best self-contradiction yet conceived, a kind of logical violation and unnaturalness; but the extravagant pride of man has managed to entangle itself profoundly and frightfully with this very folly. The desire for "freedom of will" in the superlative, metaphysical sense, such as still holds sway, unfortunately, in the minds of the half-educated; the desire to bear the entire and ultimate responsibility for one's actions oneself, and to absolve God, the world, ancestors, chance, and society from it — involves nothing less than being precisely this causa sui, and, with more than Münchhausen's daring, pulling oneself up into existence by the hair, out of the slough of nothingness. If anyone should find out the crass stupidity of the celebrated conception of "free will" in this manner and put it out of his head altogether, I beg him to carry his "enlightenment" a step further, and also put out of his head the contrary of this monstrous conception of "free will": I mean "unfree will," which is tantamount to a misuse of cause and effect. One should not wrongly materialize "cause" and "effect," as the natural philosophers do (and whoever, like them, naturalizes in thinking at present), according to the prevailing mechanical doltishness which makes the cause press and push until it "effects" its end; one should use "cause" and "effect" only as pure concepts — that is, as conventional fictions for the purposes of designation and mutual understanding, not for explanation. In the "in-itself" there is nothing of "causal connection," of "necessity," or of "psychological unfreedom"; there the effect does not follow the cause, there no "law" obtains. It is we alone who have devised cause, sequence, reciprocity, relativity, constraint, number, law, freedom, motive, and purpose; and when we interpret and intermix this symbol-world with "being-in-itself," we act once more as we have always acted — mythologically. The "unfree will" is mythology; in real life it is only a question of strong and weak wills. It is almost always a symptom of what is lacking in himself when a thinker, in every "causal connection" and "psychological necessity," manifests something of compulsion, indigence, obsequiousness, oppression, and unfreedom; it is suspicious to have such feelings — the person betrays himself. And in general, if I have observed correctly, the "unfreedom of the will" is regarded as a problem from two entirely opposite standpoints, but always in a profoundly personal manner. Some will not give up their "responsibility," their belief in themselves, the personal right to their merits, at any price (the vain races belong to this class); others, on the contrary, do not wish to be answerable for anything, or blamed for anything, and, owing to an inward self-contempt, seek to get out of the business no matter how. The latter, when they write books, are in the habit at present of taking the side of criminals; a sort of socialistic sympathy is their favorite disguise. The fatalism of the weak-willed embellishes itself surprisingly when it can pose as "la religion de la souffrance humaine"; that is its "good taste."

22. Let me be forgiven, as an old philologist who cannot desist from the mischief of putting his finger on bad modes of interpretation, but the "conformity of nature to law," of which you physicists talk so proudly as though — why, it exists only owing to your interpretation and bad "philology." It is no matter of fact, no "text," but rather just a naively humanitarian adjustment and perversion of meaning, with which you make abundant concessions to the democratic instincts of the modern soul! "Everywhere equality before the law — nature is not different in that respect, nor better than we": a fine instance of hidden motive, in which the vulgar antagonism to everything privileged and autocratic — a second and more refined atheism — is once more disguised. "Ni dieu, ni maître" — that too is what you want; and therefore "cheers for natural law!" Is it not so? But, as has been said, that is interpretation, not text; and somebody might come along who, with opposite intentions and modes of interpretation, could read out of the same "nature," and with regard to the same phenomena, precisely the tyrannically inconsiderate and relentless enforcement of the claims of power — an interpreter who should so place before your eyes the unexceptionalness and unconditionalness of every "will to power" that almost every word, including even the word "tyranny," would eventually seem unsuitable, or like a weakening and softening metaphor, as being too human; and who nevertheless would end by asserting the same about this world as you do — namely, that it has a "necessary" and "calculable" course, not, however, because laws obtain in it, but because they are absolutely lacking, and every power effects its ultimate consequences every moment. Granted that this also is only interpretation — and you will be eager enough to make this objection? — well, so much the better.

23. All psychology hitherto has run aground on moral prejudices and timidities; it has not dared to launch out into the depths. To take it as what has been written up to now is evidence of what has up to now been kept silent, it seems as if no one had yet harbored the notion of psychology as the morphology and development-doctrine of the will to power, as I conceive of it. The power of moral prejudices has penetrated deeply into the most intellectual world, the world apparently most indifferent and unprejudiced, and has obviously operated in an injurious, obstructive, blinding, and distorting manner. A proper physio-psychology must contend with unconscious antagonism in the heart of the investigator; it has "the heart" against it: even a doctrine of the reciprocal conditionality of the "good" and the "bad" impulses causes (as refined immorality) distress and aversion in a still strong and manly conscience — still more, a doctrine of the derivation of all good impulses from bad ones. If, however, a person should regard even the emotions of hatred, envy, covetousness, and imperiousness as life-conditioning emotions — as factors that must be present, fundamentally and essentially, in the general economy of life (which must, therefore, be further developed if life is to be further developed) — he will suffer from such a view of things as from seasickness. Yet this hypothesis is far from being the strangest and most painful in this immense and almost new domain of dangerous knowledge, and there are in fact a hundred good reasons for every one to keep away from it who can. On the other hand, if one has once drifted hither with one's bark, well! very good! now let us set our teeth firmly! let us open our eyes and keep our hand fast on the helm! We sail right over morality, we crush out, perhaps destroy, the remains of our own morality by daring to make our voyage thither — but what do we matter? Never yet did a more profound world of insight reveal itself to daring travelers and adventurers; and the psychologist who thus "makes a sacrifice" — it is not the sacrifizio dell'intelletto, on the contrary! — will at least be entitled to demand in return that psychology shall once more be recognized as the queen of the sciences, for whose service and equipment the other sciences exist. For psychology is once more the path to the fundamental problems.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — The Free Spirit
paragraphs: 24. O sancta simplicitas! What extraordinary simplification and falsification human beings live within! Once our eyes have opened to this marvel, we can never stop wondering at it! How clear, free, easy, and simple we have made everything around us! How we have licensed our senses to embrace everything superficial, and given our thoughts a godlike appetite for reckless play and false conclusions! From the very beginning, how cleverly we have preserved our ignorance so as to enjoy an almost unimaginable freedom, carelessness, rashness, warmth, and cheerfulness—so as to enjoy life! Only upon this hardened, granite foundation of ignorance has knowledge so far been able to rise: the will to knowledge rests on a much stronger will, the will to ignorance, uncertainty, and untruth! It is not that will's opposite, but its refinement! Indeed, we must hope that LANGUAGE, here as elsewhere, will not overcome its clumsiness, and will go on speaking of opposites where there are only differences of degree and many subtle gradations. We must likewise hope that the incarnate Tartuffery of morality, now part of our unconquerable “flesh and blood,” will twist the words in the mouths of those of us who see through it. Here and there we grasp what is happening and laugh: precisely our best knowledge tries hardest to keep us in this SIMPLIFIED world, wholly artificial, conveniently imagined and conveniently falsified. Willing or unwilling, it loves error, because it too is alive, and therefore loves life!

25. After such a cheerful opening, a serious word asks to be heard, addressed to the most serious minds. Philosophers and friends of knowledge, take care: beware of martyrdom! Beware of suffering “for the sake of truth”! Even in your own defence! It destroys your conscience's innocence and fine impartiality; objections and red rags alike make you stubborn. Struggling against danger, slander, suspicion, expulsion, and still worse consequences of hostility, you end by playing your final card as truth's guardians on earth; and this dulls you, makes you animal, makes you brutal—as though “the Truth” were some innocent, helpless creature in need of guardians! And you, of all people, knights of the sorrowful countenance, Messrs Loafers and Cobweb-spinners of the spirit! You know perfectly well, after all, that YOUR winning an argument cannot matter very much. You know that no philosopher has yet won his argument, and that every little question mark placed after your special terms and favourite doctrines—and sometimes after yourselves—may contain more admirable honesty than all your solemn acting and trump-card playing before accusers and courts! Better step aside! Escape into hiding! Keep your masks and your tricks, so that people may mistake you for what you are, or fear you a little! And please remember the garden, the garden with its golden trellises! Surround yourselves with people who are like a garden—or like music drifting over water at evening, when the day has already become a memory. Choose the GOOD solitude: free, playful, light-footed solitude, which also leaves you the right to remain good in whatever sense you choose! How poisonous, cunning, and wicked every prolonged war makes us when we cannot wage it openly by force! How PERSONAL we become through prolonged fear, through endlessly watching enemies and possible enemies! These outcasts, these people hunted for years and cruelly persecuted—including the unwilling recluses, the Spinozas and Giordano Brunos—always end, even behind the most intellectual disguise, and perhaps without knowing it, as subtle seekers of revenge and brewers of poison (just expose the foundations of Spinoza's ethics and theology!). That is to say nothing of the stupidity of moral indignation, the infallible sign that a philosopher has lost his philosophical sense of humour. The philosopher's martyrdom, his “sacrifice for truth,” brings into daylight whatever agitator and actor have been lurking within him. If we have previously studied him with an artist's curiosity alone, it is easy to understand, in the case of many a philosopher, the dangerous wish to watch his decline as well—his decline into a “martyr,” a ranter on stage and platform. Anyone with that wish must, however, understand WHAT spectacle awaits: merely a satyr play, merely a farcical afterpiece, merely further proof that the long, true tragedy HAS ENDED—assuming that every philosophy begins as a long tragedy.

26. Every exceptional person instinctively seeks a fortress and a private refuge, somewhere FREE from the crowd, the many, the majority, where, as their exception, he can forget the people who constitute “the rule.” There is only one exception to this: a still stronger instinct may drive him straight towards such people, as a seeker of understanding in the great and exceptional sense. Anyone whose dealings with others do not sometimes turn him every green and grey shade of distress—through disgust, surfeit, sympathy, gloom, and loneliness—is certainly not a person of elevated taste. But suppose he refuses to shoulder this burden and disgust voluntarily, keeps avoiding it, and remains quietly and proudly concealed in his fortress, as I have said: then one thing is certain. He was neither made nor destined for knowledge. Had he been, he would eventually have had to tell himself, “To the devil with my good taste! ‘The rule’ is more interesting than the exception—than me, the exception!” Then he would go DOWN, and above all he would go “inside.” A prolonged, serious study of the AVERAGE human being—and therefore much disguise, self-overcoming, intimacy, and bad company (all company is bad except that of one's equals)—is a necessary part of every philosopher's life story, perhaps its most disagreeable, hateful, and disappointing part. If he is lucky, however, as a favourite child of knowledge should be, he will find suitable helpers to shorten and lighten the work. I mean the so-called cynics: people who simply acknowledge in themselves the animal, the ordinary, and “the rule,” yet possess enough spirit and sensitivity to speak about themselves and their kind BEFORE WITNESSES. Sometimes they even wallow in books as though on their own dungheap. Cynicism is the only way low souls approach what we call honesty. The higher person must listen to every coarse or subtle form of it, and count himself fortunate when the clown shamelessly exposes himself before him, or the scientific satyr speaks without restraint. Sometimes fascination mingles with the disgust: by a freak of nature, genius may be tied to just such an indiscreet billy-goat and ape. Consider the Abbe Galiani, the deepest, sharpest, and perhaps filthiest man of his century—far deeper than Voltaire, and consequently far less talkative. More often, as already suggested, a scientific head sits on an ape's body, a fine and exceptional intelligence inhabits a base soul. This is by no means rare, particularly among doctors and moral physiologists. Whenever someone speaks without bitterness, indeed quite innocently, of a human being as a belly with two needs and a head with one; whenever someone sees, seeks, and WANTS to see only hunger, sexual instinct, and vanity as the real and sole motives of human action—in short, whenever someone speaks “badly,” though not even “ill,” of humanity—the lover of knowledge should listen closely and attentively. In general, he should keep an open ear wherever people speak without indignation. The indignant person, forever biting and tearing at himself—or at the world, God, or society instead—may stand morally higher than the laughing, complacent satyr; in every other respect he is the more ordinary, less interesting, and less instructive case. And no one LIES like an indignant person.

27. Being understood is difficult, especially when one thinks and lives gangasrotogati [Footnote: Like the river Ganges: presto.] among people who think and live quite differently: kurmagati [Footnote: Like the tortoise: lento.], or at best “froglike,” mandeikagati [Footnote: Like the frog: staccato.] (I myself do everything possible to be “difficult to understand”!). We should be sincerely grateful for any goodwill shown in making interpretation a little more subtle. As for our “good friends,” though, who are always too easygoing and believe friendship entitles them to an easy time, it is wise from the start to give them a playground in which misunderstanding can romp about. That way we can still laugh. Or we can get rid of these good friends altogether—and laugh then too!

28. The hardest thing to carry from one language into another is a style's TEMPO. Its basis lies in the character of a race—or, in more physiological terms, in the average TEMPO at which that race assimilates its food. Some well-intentioned translations involuntarily vulgarise the original, almost falsify it, simply because they cannot reproduce its lively, cheerful TEMPO, which leaps over and clears away every danger in wording and expression. A German is almost incapable of PRESTO in his own language, and therefore, as one may reasonably infer, of many of the most delightful and audacious NUANCES of free, free-spirited thinking. Just as the buffoon and the satyr are foreign to his body and conscience, so Aristophanes and Petronius cannot be translated for him. Germans have cultivated an abundant variety of everything ponderous, sticky, and pompously awkward, every tedious and long-winded style. Forgive the observation that even Goethe's prose, blending stiffness with elegance, is no exception: it mirrors the “good old days” to which it belongs and expresses German taste when a “German taste” still existed—a rococo taste in moribus et artibus. Lessing is an exception, thanks to his actor's nature, which understood much and knew its way around many things. He had not translated Bayle for nothing; he gladly sheltered in the shade of Diderot and Voltaire, and more gladly still among the Roman comic playwrights. Lessing also loved freedom of spirit in TEMPO, and escape from Germany. Yet how could German, even Lessing's prose, imitate Machiavelli's TEMPO? In his “Principe,” Machiavelli lets us breathe Florence's fine, dry air, and cannot help treating the gravest matters in a boisterous allegrissimo—perhaps with a malicious artist's appreciation of the contrast he dares create: long, heavy, difficult, dangerous thoughts, delivered at a gallop, in the finest and most mischievous good humour. And who, finally, would risk translating Petronius into German? More than any great musician so far, he mastered PRESTO in invention, ideas, and language. What do the swamps of the sick, evil world—or of the “ancient world”—ultimately matter, if like him one has the feet, the rush, the breath, the liberating scorn of a wind that makes everything healthy by setting everything RUNNING! As for Aristophanes—that transfiguring, completing genius, for whose sake one FORGIVES the whole of Hellenism its existence, once one understands in full depth EVERYTHING there that needs forgiveness and transfiguration—nothing has made me ponder PLATO'S secrecy and sphinx-like character more than one fortunately preserved petit fait. Beneath the pillow of his deathbed they found no “Bible,” nothing Egyptian, Pythagorean, or Platonic, but a book by Aristophanes. How could even Plato have borne life—the Greek life he rejected—without an Aristophanes!

29. Independence is a matter for very few people; it is the privilege of the strong. Whoever attempts it, even with every right to do so but without being COMPELLED, shows himself probably not only strong but daring beyond measure. He steps into a labyrinth and multiplies a thousandfold the dangers already inherent in life. Not the least of these is that no one can see where or how he loses his way, becomes isolated, and is torn to pieces by some minotaur of conscience. If such a person comes to grief, it lies so far beyond other people's understanding that they neither feel it nor share his suffering. And he can never return! He cannot even return to the sympathy of his fellow human beings!

30. Our deepest insights must—and ought to—look like foolishness, and sometimes like crimes, when they reach, without permission, the ears of people neither fitted nor destined for them. Philosophers once distinguished the exoteric from the esoteric: among Indians as among Greeks, Persians, and Mussulmans—in short, wherever people believed in ranks and gradations, NOT in equality or equal rights. The chief difference is not simply that the exoteric stand outside and look, assess, measure, and judge from outside instead of within. More fundamentally, they look upwards from below, while the esoteric look DOWNWARDS FROM ABOVE. The soul can reach heights from which even tragedy no longer has a tragic effect. If all the world's suffering were brought together, who would dare decide that looking at it would NECESSARILY tempt and compel us to pity, thereby doubling that suffering?... What feeds or refreshes a higher kind of person must be almost poisonous to an entirely different, lower kind. An ordinary person's virtues might amount to vice and weakness in a philosopher. A highly developed person might conceivably degenerate and collapse, acquiring through that very decline qualities for which the lower world into which he had fallen would honour him as a saint. Some books have opposite effects on the soul and its health, depending on whether a lower soul and weaker vitality use them, or a higher, stronger one. For the former they are dangerous, disturbing, destabilising books; for the latter, heralds calling the bravest to THEIR particular courage. Books for everyone are invariably foul-smelling: the scent of petty people clings to them. Wherever the populace eat and drink, and even wherever they worship, there is usually a stink. Anyone wishing to breathe PURE air should stay out of churches.

31. In youth we still worship and despise without the art of NUANCE, life's finest acquisition. We rightly pay a heavy penalty for having attacked people and things with Yes and No. Everything is arranged so that the worst taste of all, THE TASTE FOR THE UNCONDITIONAL, is cruelly mocked and mistreated until we learn to put a little art into our feelings, and prefer, like genuine artists of living, to test ourselves against the artificial. Youth's angry, reverent spirit seems unable to rest until it has suitably falsified people and things in order to discharge its passion upon them. Youth itself is something falsifying and deceptive. Later, the young soul, tortured by repeated disillusionment, finally turns its suspicions on itself—still passionate and savage even in suspicion and remorse. How it berates itself, how impatiently it tears at itself, how it takes revenge for its long self-blinding, as though that blindness had been chosen! In this transition we punish ourselves by distrusting our feelings, torment our enthusiasm with doubt, and find danger even in a good conscience, as though it concealed a finer honesty from itself and expressed that honesty's weariness. Above all, we take a principled stand AGAINST “youth.”—Ten years later, we understand that all this was still—youth!

32. During the longest stretch of human history, what we call prehistory, people inferred an action's worth or worthlessness from its CONSEQUENCES. They considered neither the action itself nor its origin. Rather, much as in China today, where a child's distinction or disgrace reflects upon the parents, success or failure cast its judgment backwards and made people think well or badly of the deed. Let us call this humanity's PRE-MORAL period: the command “Know thyself!” was still unknown.—Over the last ten thousand years, however, people in certain large regions of the earth have gradually learned to judge an action's value by its origin rather than its consequences. Taken as a whole, this was a great achievement, a significant refinement of vision and standards, the unconscious result of aristocratic values gaining supremacy and of belief in “origin.” It marks the period we may call MORAL in the narrower sense: the first attempt at self-knowledge begins here. The origin instead of the consequences—what a reversal of perspective! And certainly a reversal won only through prolonged struggle and hesitation! Yet precisely this change brought a sinister new superstition to power, a peculiar narrowing of interpretation: an action's origin was understood in the most definite way possible, as its origin in an INTENTION. People agreed that the deed's value resided in the intention's value. Intention as an action's sole origin and entire prehistory: this prejudice has governed moral praise and blame, judgment and even philosophy, almost down to our own day.—But might a fresh self-awareness and sharpness of perception now require us once more to resolve upon a reversal, a fundamental shift in values? Might we stand at the threshold of a period that would initially have to be described negatively as ULTRA-MORAL? At least among us immoralists, the suspicion is growing that an action's decisive value lies precisely in what is NOT INTENTIONAL; that everything intentional in it, everything visible, perceptible, or “sensed,” belongs to its surface, its skin—which, like any skin, reveals something but CONCEALS much more. We believe, in brief, that intention is merely a sign or symptom requiring interpretation, and moreover a sign admitting so many interpretations that it means almost nothing by itself. Morality as understood until now, morality of intention, has been a prejudice—perhaps something premature or preliminary, probably on the same level as astrology and alchemy, but in any event something to overcome. The overcoming of morality, in a certain sense even morality's overcoming of itself: let that name the long-secret work reserved for today's most refined, most honest, and also most wicked consciences, the living touchstones of the soul.

33. There is no avoiding it: feelings of surrender, sacrifice for one's neighbour, and the whole morality of self-renunciation must be ruthlessly questioned and put on trial. So must the aesthetics of “disinterested contemplation,” through which today's emasculation of art seeks, with considerable cunning, to give itself a good conscience. The feelings “for others” and “NOT for myself” contain far too much enchantment and sweetness for us not to be doubly suspicious, and immediately ask, “Might these be—DECEPTIONS?” Their giving PLEASURE—to the person who feels them, the person who benefits, and the mere onlooker—is no argument in their FAVOUR. It is precisely a reason for caution. Then let us be cautious!

34. Whatever philosophical position we adopt today, the most certain thing we can see from any of them is the ERRONEOUSNESS of the world we believe we inhabit. Evidence piles upon evidence, tempting us to suspect some deceptive principle in the “nature of things.” But whoever blames thinking itself, and therefore “the spirit,” for the world's falsity—an honourable escape route used by every conscious or unconscious advocatus dei—whoever regards this world, including space, time, form, and motion, as falsely DEDUCED, would eventually have ample reason to distrust all thinking as well. Has it not played the shabbiest tricks on us until now? What guarantee could it offer that it will stop doing what it has always done? Seriously, there is something moving and worthy of respect in thinkers' innocence: even today it lets them approach consciousness and ask for HONEST answers. Is it “real,” for instance? Why does it keep the external world so firmly at a distance? And other questions of the same sort. Belief in “immediate certainties” is a MORAL NAIVETE that does credit to us philosophers—but we must now stop being “MERELY moral” people! Outside morality, such belief is foolishness that does us little credit! In respectable middle-class life, constant suspicion counts as evidence of a “bad character,” and therefore as an imprudence. But here, beyond that world and its Yeses and Nos, what prevents us from being imprudent and declaring that the philosopher, the creature most persistently fooled on earth, has finally earned a RIGHT to “bad character”? He is now OBLIGED to distrust, to peer out with the most malicious sideways glance from every abyss of suspicion.—Forgive the joke in this gloomy grimace and way of putting things. I myself learned long ago to think and judge differently about deceiving and being deceived, and I keep at least a couple of nudges in the ribs ready for the blind fury with which philosophers resist deception. Why NOT be deceived? That truth is worth more than appearance is merely a moral prejudice; indeed, it is the world's least substantiated assumption. We must concede this much: life could never have existed without perspectival judgments and appearances. If, with the virtuous enthusiasm and stupidity of many philosophers, we wished to abolish the “apparent world” entirely—well, suppose YOU could manage it—none of your “truth” would remain either! What, in fact, compels us to assume an essential opposition between “true” and “false”? Why not degrees of appearance, lighter and darker shades and tones, different valeurs, as painters say? Why could the world THAT CONCERNS US not be a fiction? If someone objected, “But a fiction needs an author,” could we not bluntly reply: WHY? Could this “needs” not also belong to the fiction? May we not at last treat the subject with a little irony, just as we do the predicate and object? Could the philosopher not rise above faith in grammar? All respect to governesses, but is it not time for philosophy to give up a governess's faith?

35. O Voltaire! O humanity! O idiocy! “Truth,” and the SEARCH for truth, are delicate matters. If someone approaches them too humanely—“il ne cherche le vrai que pour faire le bien”—I wager that he will discover nothing!

36. Suppose the only reality “given” to us is our world of desires and passions, and we cannot descend or ascend to any other “reality” than that of our drives—for thinking is merely a relationship among these drives. May we not then try asking whether this “given” reality is ENOUGH to understand even the so-called mechanical or “material” world by analogy with ourselves? I do not mean understanding it as an illusion, an “appearance,” a “representation” in Berkeley's or Schopenhauer's sense. I mean granting it the same degree of reality as our emotions: a more primitive form of the emotional world, in which everything remains locked together in a mighty unity that later branches out and develops in organic processes—and naturally also becomes more refined and weaker. Could it be a kind of instinctive life in which all organic functions, including self-regulation, assimilation, nutrition, secretion, and metabolism, remain synthetically united—a PRIMARY FORM of life? Ultimately, this experiment is not merely permissible: the conscience of LOGICAL METHOD commands it. We must not assume several kinds of causality until we have pushed the attempt to manage with one kind as far as possible—to absurdity, if I may put it that way. This is a morality of method that we may no longer reject; it follows “from its definition,” as mathematicians say. The final question is whether we really recognise the will as ACTING, whether we believe in the will's causality. If we do—and at bottom our belief IN THIS is simply our belief in causality itself—we MUST try the hypothesis that the will's causality is the only causality. “Will,” naturally, can act only upon “will,” not upon “matter”—not upon “nerves,” for example. In short, we must venture the hypothesis that wherever we recognise “effects,” will is acting upon will, and that all mechanical action, insofar as a force is active in it, is precisely the force of will, the effect of will. Suppose, finally, we succeeded in explaining our entire instinctive life as the development and branching of one fundamental form of will—the Will to Power, as my thesis names it. Suppose all organic functions could be traced back to this Will to Power, and the problem of reproduction and nutrition—they are one problem—could also be solved through it. We would then have earned the right to define ALL effective force unequivocally as WILL TO POWER. Seen from within, defined and described according to its “intelligible character,” the world would simply be “Will to Power,” and nothing else.

37. “What? In ordinary language, doesn't that mean God has been disproved, but the devil has not?”—Quite the contrary! Quite the contrary, my friends! And who the devil forces you to use ordinary language anyway!

38. Consider what eventually happened, amid all modern enlightenment, to the French Revolution. Seen close up, it was a dreadful farce, quite unnecessary; yet Europe's noble and visionary spectators, looking from a distance, read their own indignation and enthusiasm into it so passionately and for so long that THE TEXT DISAPPEARED BENEATH THE INTERPRETATION. In just this way, a noble posterity might once again misunderstand the whole past, perhaps making ITS appearance bearable only through that misunderstanding.—Or rather, has this not happened already? Were we ourselves not that “noble posterity”? And insofar as we now understand this, has it not thereby already become the past?

39. Hardly anyone readily accepts a teaching as true merely because it makes people happy or virtuous—except perhaps those amiable “Idealists” who enthuse over the good, the true, and the beautiful, letting every colourful, coarse, good-natured wish swim indiscriminately in their pond. Happiness and virtue prove nothing. Yet even thoughtful people readily forget that making people unhappy or bad is equally little a refutation. Something might be TRUE and nevertheless supremely harmful and dangerous. Existence might even be fundamentally constituted so that complete knowledge of it would destroy us. A mind's strength could then be measured by how much “truth” it could bear—or, more plainly, by how much it NEEDED truth diluted, veiled, sweetened, muted, and falsified. Undoubtedly, however, wicked and unfortunate people occupy a better position for discovering certain PARTS of truth, with greater prospects of success; let us say nothing of the wicked who are happy, a species moralists pass over in silence. Perhaps harshness and cunning favour the development of strong, independent spirits and philosophers more than the gentle, refined, accommodating kindness and easygoing habits rightly valued in a learned person. All this presupposes, of course, that “philosopher” does not mean only someone who writes books, or even puts HIS philosophy into books! Stendhal supplies one final feature for this portrait of the free-spirited philosopher. For the sake of German taste I will underline it, precisely because it OPPOSES German taste. “Pour etre bon philosophe,” says this last great psychologist, “il faut etre sec, clair, sans illusion. Un banquier, qui a fait fortune, a une partie du caractere requis pour faire des decouvertes en philosophie, c'est-a-dire pour voir clair dans ce qui est.”

40. Everything deep loves a mask; the deepest things dislike even images and likenesses. Might the OPPOSITE alone be the proper disguise in which a God's shame can walk abroad? A question worth asking! It would be odd if no mystic had already ventured something similar. Some events are so delicate that it is wise to cover them in coarseness and make them unrecognisable. After certain acts of love and extravagant generosity, nothing could be wiser than taking a stick and thoroughly beating the witness: that clouds his memory. Many people can cloud and maltreat their own memory, at least to take revenge upon this sole keeper of their secret. Shame is inventive. What we feel most ashamed of is not necessarily what is worst. Masks hide more than deceit; cunning contains so much goodness. I can imagine a man concealing something precious and fragile who rolls awkwardly through life, round as an old green wine-cask bound with heavy hoops: the delicacy of his shame requires it. Someone whose shame has depths encounters his destiny and makes his delicate decisions on paths almost no one reaches, paths whose very existence may be unknown to his closest friends. His mortal danger remains invisible to them, and so does the safety he regains. Such a hidden nature instinctively uses speech to remain silent and concealed, endlessly inventing ways to avoid communicating. He WANTS and insists that a mask of himself should take his place in his friends' hearts and minds. Even if he does not want this, one day his eyes will open to the fact that a mask is there nonetheless—and that this is as it should be. Every deep spirit needs a mask. More than that: a mask continually grows around every deep spirit because every word, every step, every sign of life is constantly misinterpreted—that is, interpreted SUPERFICIALLY.

41. We must put ourselves through our own tests of whether we are destined for independence and command, and do so at the right moment. We must not evade these tests, though they may be the most dangerous game we can play, and though ultimately we conduct them before ourselves alone, with no other judge. Do not cling to a person, however dearly loved: every person is both a prison and a hiding-place. Do not cling to a fatherland, however suffering and needy: it is even easier to detach one's heart from a victorious homeland. Do not cling to pity, even pity for higher people whose peculiar torment and helplessness chance has allowed us to glimpse. Do not cling to a science, however precious the discoveries with which it tempts us, apparently reserved for us alone. Do not cling to our own liberation, the bird's intoxicating distance and remoteness, flying ever higher to see ever more beneath it—the flier's danger. Do not cling to our own virtues, or let our whole self fall victim to one of our special gifts: our “hospitality,” for instance, the greatest danger for richly endowed and highly developed souls, who spend themselves lavishly, almost carelessly, and push generosity until the virtue becomes a vice. We must know how TO PRESERVE OURSELVES: the best test of independence.

42. A new kind of philosopher is emerging. I venture to baptise them with a name that carries some danger. As far as I understand them, and as far as they permit understanding—for by nature they WANT to remain something of a riddle—these future philosophers might rightly, perhaps also wrongly, ask to be called “tempters.” After all, the name itself is only an attempt—or, if you prefer, a temptation.

43. Will these coming philosophers be new friends of “truth”? Very probably: all philosophers until now have loved their truths. But they certainly will not be dogmatists. Their pride and taste alike must rebel against the idea that their truth should remain a truth for everyone—the secret wish and ultimate goal of every dogmatic undertaking until now. Perhaps a future philosopher will say, “My judgment is MY judgment: someone else has no ready claim to it.” We must abandon the bad taste of wanting agreement with a great many people. “Good” stops being good when our neighbour puts it in his mouth. And how could there be a “common good”! The phrase contradicts itself: whatever can be common is always worth little. In the end, things must remain as they are and always have been: greatness for the great, abysses for the deep, delicacies and shudders for the refined; in brief, everything rare for the rare.

44.
