After all this, must I explicitly say that these future philosophers will be free, VERY free spirits—and just as certainly not merely free spirits, but something more, higher, greater, and fundamentally different, something unwilling to be misunderstood or mistaken for something else? Yet in saying this I feel almost as OBLIGED to them as to ourselves—we free spirits, their heralds and forerunners—to clear away an old, foolish prejudice and misunderstanding that has clouded the idea of a “free spirit” for far too long. In every European country, and in America too, a narrow, prejudiced, fettered class of minds now misuses this name. They want almost the opposite of what our instincts and intentions urge—not to mention that, to the NEW philosophers now emerging, they must be still more like closed windows and barred doors. Briefly, and regrettably, these misnamed “free spirits” are LEVELLERS: fluent-tongued and busy-penned slaves of democratic taste and its “modern ideas.” All are men without solitude, without any solitude of their own; blunt, honest fellows whose courage and decent behaviour should not be denied. But they are not free. They are laughably superficial, especially in their instinctive preference for blaming almost ALL human misery and failure on the old forms of society—a notion that happily turns the truth completely upside down! What they strive for with all their strength is the herd's universal happiness on a green meadow, together with security, safety, comfort, and relief from life's burdens for everyone. Their two most frequently chanted songs and doctrines are “Equality of Rights” and “Sympathy with All Sufferers”; suffering itself, they believe, must be ABOLISHED. We who stand opposed, however, have opened our eyes and consciences to the question of how and where the plant “man” has grown most vigorously. We believe it has always been under contrary conditions: his situation had to become enormously more dangerous; under prolonged oppression and constraint, his inventiveness and powers of disguise—his “spirit”—had to become subtle and daring; his Will to Life had to rise into an unconditional Will to Power. We believe that harshness, violence, slavery, danger in the street and in the heart, secrecy, stoicism, the tempter's art, and every kind of devilry—that everything wicked, terrible, tyrannical, predatory, and serpentine in humanity—serves the elevation of the human species as much as its opposite. We have not said enough even in saying THIS MUCH. At any rate, in both our words and our silence we stand at the OTHER extreme from all modern ideology and the herd's ideals—perhaps at their antipodes? Is it surprising that we “free spirits” are not the most communicative spirits? That we refuse to reveal in every respect WHAT a spirit can free itself from, and WHERE it may then be driven? As for the meaning of that dangerous formula “Beyond Good and Evil,” by which we at least avoid being confused with others, we ARE different from “libres-penseurs,” “liben pensatori,” “free-thinkers,” and whatever else these honest champions of “modern ideas” choose to call themselves. We have made homes, or at least stayed as guests, in many realms of the spirit. Again and again we have escaped the gloomy, comfortable corners where preferences and prejudices, youth, ancestry, chance encounters with people and books, or even weariness from travelling seemed to imprison us. We are full of malice towards dependency's temptations concealed in honours, money, positions, or heightened sensual pleasure; grateful even for hardship and the changes brought by illness, since they continually release us from some rule and its “prejudice”; grateful to the God, devil, sheep, and worm within us; curious to a fault, investigators to the point of cruelty, with fingers unafraid of the intangible and teeth and stomachs equal to the most indigestible. We are ready for any task requiring shrewdness and sharp senses, ready for every adventure through an excess of “free will,” with souls in front and behind whose final intentions are hard to penetrate, with foregrounds and backgrounds no foot can explore to the end; hidden beneath cloaks of light; takers of possession, although we look like heirs and spendthrifts; arrangers and collectors from dawn to night; misers guarding our wealth and our crammed drawers; economical in learning and forgetting; inventive in schemes; sometimes proud of tables of categories, sometimes pedants, sometimes nocturnal workers even in broad daylight, yes, even scarecrows when necessary. And that is necessary today, because we are the born, sworn, jealous friends of SOLITUDE, of our own deepest midnight and midday solitude—this is the kind of people we free spirits are! And perhaps you coming ones resemble us a little? You NEW philosophers?

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The Religious Mood
paragraphs: 45. The human soul and its boundaries; the full range of inner experience attained so far, its heights, depths, and distances; the soul's entire history UP TO THIS MOMENT, and its possibilities still unexhausted: this is the destined hunting ground of the born psychologist who loves a “big hunt.” Yet how often he must tell himself in despair, “One person! Alas, only one person! And this immense forest, this virgin forest!” He longs for several hundred hunting assistants and finely trained hounds to send into the history of the human soul and drive HIS game towards him. In vain. Again and again he discovers, bitterly and profoundly, how hard it is to find helpers and dogs for precisely the things that awaken his curiosity. The trouble with sending scholars into new and dangerous hunting grounds, where courage, shrewdness, and subtlety of every kind are needed, is that they become useless just when the “BIG hunt” and the great danger begin. That is exactly when their sharp eyes and noses fail. To guess and establish, for example, the history that the problem of KNOWLEDGE AND CONSCIENCE has had within the souls of homines religiosi, one might oneself need an experience as deep, wounded, and vast as Pascal's intellectual conscience. Beyond that, one would still need a broad heaven of clear, malicious spirituality, capable of looking down on this mass of dangerous, painful experiences, ordering it and giving it effective formulation.—But who could perform this service for me! And who could spare the time to wait for such servants! They plainly appear too rarely; their appearance is always so improbable! In the end, to know anything, one must do everything ONESELF—which means having MUCH to do! But curiosity like mine is, once and for all, the most pleasant of vices—forgive me! I meant to say that love of truth has its reward in heaven, and already here on earth.

46. Early Christianity wanted, and often achieved, a particular kind of faith amid a sceptical world of southern free spirits, a world with centuries of conflict between philosophical schools both behind it and within it, and additionally schooled in tolerance by the Imperium Romanum. That faith is NOT the sincere, austere faith of a slave through which a Luther, a Cromwell, or another northern barbarian of the spirit perhaps clung to his God and Christianity. It is far closer to Pascal's faith, terrifyingly like reason's prolonged suicide—a tough, long-lived, wormlike reason that cannot be killed outright with one stroke. Christian faith is, from its beginning, sacrifice: the sacrifice of all freedom, pride, and spiritual confidence; simultaneously submission, self-mockery, and self-mutilation. Cruelty and religious Phoenicianism inhabit this faith, suited to a delicate, many-sided, exceptionally exacting conscience. It presupposes that subjecting the spirit causes indescribable PAIN, that the spirit's whole past and all its habits resist the absurdissimum in which “faith” presents itself. Modern people, numb to all Christian terminology, no longer grasp the terrifying extremity that ancient taste heard in the paradox “God on the Cross.” Never before, anywhere, had there been so audacious a reversal, anything at once so dreadful, so questioning, and so questionable. The formula promised a transvaluation of every ancient value. It was the East, the PROFOUND East: the Oriental slave taking revenge upon Rome, upon its noble, lighthearted tolerance and its Roman “Catholicism” of unbelief. What always enraged slaves against their masters and stirred them to rebellion was not faith but freedom from faith, that half-Stoic, smiling indifference to faith's solemn seriousness. “Enlightenment” provokes revolt. The slave wants the unconditional and understands only tyranny, even in morality; he loves as he hates, without NUANCE, to the depths, to the point of pain and sickness. His many HIDDEN sufferings make him rebel against the noble taste that seems to DENY suffering. Scepticism about suffering—at bottom simply an attitude of aristocratic morality—was also no small cause of the last great slave uprising, which began with the French Revolution.

47. Wherever religious neurosis has appeared on earth, it has been linked with three dangerous rules of living: solitude, fasting, and sexual abstinence. Yet we cannot confidently decide which is cause and which effect, or WHETHER any causal relationship exists at all. That last doubt is justified by a recurring symptom among both savage and civilised peoples: sudden, excessive sensuality, which just as suddenly turns into fits of repentance, renunciation of the world, and renunciation of the will. Could both symptoms be forms of disguised epilepsy? Yet nowhere is it MORE necessary to set explanations aside. No other type has gathered so much nonsense and superstition around it; none has so fascinated people, philosophers included. Perhaps we should become a little indifferent here, learn caution, or better still look AWAY and GO AWAY. Nevertheless, behind the most recent philosophy, Schopenhauer's, we find this dreadful question mark of religious crisis and awakening, almost as the problem itself. How is the denial of the will POSSIBLE? How is the saint possible? That seems to be the question with which Schopenhauer began and became a philosopher. It was therefore a genuinely Schopenhauerian consequence that his most convinced follower—perhaps his last, in Germany at least—Richard Wagner, ended his own life's work at precisely this point. He finally brought this terrible, eternal type to the stage as Kundry, type vecu, showing it as it loved and lived. This happened just when alienists in almost every European country could study the type at close range, as religious neurosis—or, as I call it, “the religious mood”—made its latest epidemic appearance in the “Salvation Army.” But what has so intensely interested every kind of person in every age, philosophers included, in the whole phenomenon of the saint? Undoubtedly its apparently miraculous character: the immediate SUCCESSION OF OPPOSITES, of states of soul thought to be morally contrary. People considered it self-evident that a “bad man” had suddenly become a “saint,” a good man. Psychology as it then existed foundered here. Might the principal reason be that psychology had submitted to morality, BELIEVED in opposing moral values, and seen, read, and INTERPRETED those oppositions into the text and the facts? What? The “miracle” merely a mistaken interpretation? A failure of philology?

48. The Latin peoples seem far more deeply bound to their Catholicism than we Northerners are to Christianity in general. Consequently, unbelief means something entirely different in Catholic countries than among Protestants: there it is a kind of rebellion against the spirit of the race; with us it is more a return to that spirit—or lack of spirit. We Northerners unquestionably descend from barbarous races, even in our religious gifts: our gifts here are POOR. The Celts may be excepted; they have also provided the North's most fertile ground for Christian infection. In France the Christian ideal flowered as fully as the pale northern sun permitted. How oddly devout, to our taste, even the later French sceptics remain whenever Celtic blood runs through them! How Catholic, how un-German, Auguste Comte's Sociology appears to us, with the Roman logic of its instincts! How Jesuitical that amiable, clever guide to Port Royal, Sainte-Beuve, remains despite all his hostility to the Jesuits! And Ernest Renan too: how inaccessible his language seems to us Northerners, when the slightest religious shiver immediately unsettles his refined, voluptuous soul, reclining so comfortably! Let us repeat these beautiful sentences of his—and what malice and pride they at once call forth in reply from our probably less beautiful but harder, more German souls!—“DISONS DONC HARDIMENT QUE LA RELIGION EST UN PRODUIT DE L'HOMME NORMAL, QUE L'HOMME EST LE PLUS DANS LE VRAI QUANT IL EST LE PLUS RELIGIEUX ET LE PLUS ASSURE D'UNE DESTINEE INFINIE.... C'EST QUAND IL EST BON QU'IL VEUT QUE LA VIRTU CORRESPONDE A UN ORDER ETERNAL, C'EST QUAND IL CONTEMPLE LES CHOSES D'UNE MANIERE DESINTERESSEE QU'IL TROUVE LA MORT REVOLTANTE ET ABSURDE. COMMENT NE PAS SUPPOSER QUE C'EST DANS CES MOMENTS-LA, QUE L'HOMME VOIT LE MIEUX?”... To my ears and habits of thought these sentences lie so completely at the ANTIPODES that, on first encountering them, I angrily wrote in the margin, “LA NIAISERIE RELIGIEUSE PAR EXCELLENCE!” Later, in a further fit of anger, I even grew fond of them, these sentences that turn truth entirely upside down! How pleasant, how distinctive, to have antipodes of one's own!

49. The astonishing feature of ancient Greek religious life is its unstoppable outpouring of GRATITUDE. It takes a very superior kind of human being to adopt SUCH an attitude towards nature and life. Later, when the populace gained control in Greece, FEAR spread through religion as well; Christianity was getting ready to emerge.

50. Passion for God comes in boorish, honest-hearted, importunate forms, like Luther's: all Protestantism lacks the southern DELICATEZZA. It can take the form of an Oriental exaltation of spirit, resembling a slave favoured or promoted beyond his deserts. St. Augustine, for instance, offensively lacks any nobility of bearing or desire. It can contain a feminine tenderness and sensuality, modestly and unconsciously yearning for a UNIO MYSTICA ET PHYSICA, as with Madame de Guyon. Curiously often it disguises the puberty of a girl or boy; here and there it is even an old maid's hysteria, or her final ambition. In such cases the Church has frequently made the woman a saint.

51. The most powerful people have always bowed reverently before the saint, that enigma of self-mastery and utterly voluntary deprivation. Why did they bow? Behind his frail, miserable, questionable appearance they sensed a superior force seeking to test itself through such subjection. In his strength of will they recognised and knew how to honour their own strength and love of power. Honouring the saint, they honoured something in themselves. His presence also awakened a suspicion: surely such immense self-denial and opposition to nature cannot have been desired for nothing, they asked themselves. Perhaps there is a reason, some tremendous danger about which the ascetic hopes to learn more from his secret visitors and companions in conversation? In short, the world's mighty learned a new fear before him. They sensed a new power, a strange enemy still unconquered. It was the “Will to Power” that made them stop before the saint. They had to question him.

52. The Jewish “Old Testament,” the book of divine justice, contains people, events, and sayings on a scale so immense that neither Greek nor Indian literature can rival it. We stand in fear and reverence before those gigantic remains of what humanity once was, and think sadly of old Asia and its little projecting peninsula, Europe, so determined to parade before Asia as “The Progress of Mankind.” Of course, someone who is merely a delicate, tame domestic animal and knows only domestic-animal needs—like our cultivated people today, including the Christians of “cultivated” Christianity—need feel neither amazement nor sadness among these ruins. Taste for the Old Testament is a touchstone of “great” and “small.” Perhaps such a person will find the New Testament, the book of grace, more appealing to his heart: it carries much of the scent of the genuine, tender, foolish prayer-mumbler and petty soul. Binding this New Testament, a ROCOCO of taste in every respect, together with the Old Testament as the “Bible,” as “The Book in Itself,” may be literary Europe's greatest act of audacity and greatest “sin against the Spirit.”

53. Why atheism today? God's “father” has been thoroughly refuted, as have his “judge” and “rewarder.” So has his “free will”: he does not hear, and even if he did, he would not know how to help. Worst of all, he seems unable to make himself clearly understood. Is he unsure of himself? From questions asked and conversations overheard, this is what I have gathered about the decline of European theism. To me, the religious instinct seems to be growing vigorously, while profoundly distrusting and rejecting the satisfaction theism offers it.

54. What is modern philosophy chiefly doing? Since Descartes—more in defiance of him, indeed, than by following his method—philosophers have made an ATTENTAT, an assault, on the old conception of the soul, disguised as a critique of subject and predicate. In other words, they have attacked Christian teaching's fundamental assumption. As a sceptical theory of knowledge, modern philosophy is secretly or openly ANTI-CHRISTIAN, though, for sharper ears, by no means anti-religious. People once believed in “the soul” just as they believed in grammar and the grammatical subject. “I,” they said, is the condition; “think” is the predicate and depends upon it. Thinking is an activity, so one MUST posit a subject as its cause. Then, with extraordinary persistence and subtlety, they tried to escape this net by asking whether the reverse might be true: “think” the condition, “I” the dependent result; “I” therefore merely a synthesis MADE by thinking itself. KANT really wanted to show that beginning with the subject could prove neither the subject nor the object. Perhaps he was not always a stranger to the possibility that the subject, and hence “the soul,” has only an APPARENT EXISTENCE—that thought which once exercised immense power on earth as Vedanta philosophy.

55. Religious cruelty has a great ladder with many rungs, but three matter most. Once, people sacrificed human beings to their God, perhaps the very people they loved best. Here belong the sacrifices of firstborn children in all primitive religions, and the sacrifice of Emperor Tiberius in the Mithra-Grotto on Capri, that most terrible of Roman anachronisms. Later, during humanity's moral epoch, people offered their strongest instincts, their “nature,” to their God. THIS festive joy shines in the cruel eyes of ascetics and “anti-natural” fanatics. Finally, what was left to sacrifice? Must they not ultimately surrender everything comforting, sacred, healing—all hope, all faith in hidden harmonies, in future happiness and justice? Must they not sacrifice God himself and, in cruelty towards themselves, worship stone, stupidity, gravity, fate, nothingness? Sacrificing God to nothingness: this paradoxical mystery of ultimate cruelty has been reserved for the generation now emerging. We all already know something of it.

56. Whoever, like me, has been driven by some mysterious desire to pursue pessimism to its foundations and release it from the half-Christian, half-German narrowness and stupidity in which it finally appeared in this century—as Schopenhauer's philosophy; whoever has looked with an Asiatic and more-than-Asiatic eye inside and through the most world-denying of all possible ways of thinking, beyond good and evil, no longer, like Buddha and Schopenhauer, ruled and deceived by morality—may precisely through this have opened his eyes, quite unintentionally, to the opposite ideal. It is the ideal of the most exuberant, lively, world-affirming person, who has not merely learned to compromise with and accommodate what was and is, but wants it back AS IT WAS AND IS, throughout eternity. Insatiably he calls da capo, not just to himself but to the entire piece and performance; and not just to the performance but to whoever needs it and makes it necessary, because he continually needs himself anew and makes himself necessary.—What? Would this not be—circulus vitiosus deus?

57. As our intellectual sight and insight grow stronger, the distances and the space around us expand: our world deepens, and new stars, new riddles, and new conceptions keep appearing. Perhaps everything upon which the mind's eye has exercised its sharpness and depth was merely an opportunity for exercise, a sort of game, something for children and childish minds. Perhaps the gravest concepts, those responsible for the most conflict and suffering—“God” and “sin”—will one day matter to us no more than a child's toy or pain matters to an old man. And perhaps that “old man” will then need another toy and another pain—still childish enough, an eternal child!

58. Has anyone noticed how much outward idleness, or half-idleness, a truly religious life requires? It needs it both for its favourite microscopic work of self-examination and for the gentle stillness called “prayer,” that perpetual readiness for the “coming of God.” I mean idleness with a good conscience, ancient idleness inherited in the blood, not entirely unfamiliar with the aristocratic feeling that work is DISHONOURING, that it makes body and soul common. Has anyone noticed, then, that modern industriousness—noisy, all-consuming, conceited, foolishly proud—trains and prepares people for “unbelief” more than anything else? Among Germans now living apart from religion, for instance, I find “free-thinkers” of many kinds and origins, but above all a majority whose religious instincts have been dissolved by generations of hard work. They no longer know what religions are for and register their existence with a dull astonishment. These good people feel completely occupied already, whether by business or pleasure—not to mention the “Fatherland,” newspapers, and “family duties.” Apparently they have no time left for religion. Above all, they cannot tell whether it is some new business or some new pleasure; surely, they tell themselves, people cannot go to church simply to put themselves in a bad mood. They have no hostility towards religious customs. If circumstances—state affairs, perhaps—require their participation, they comply as they comply with so much else: patiently, seriously, without pretension, and without much curiosity or unease. They live too far outside it all to feel any need to be FOR or AGAINST. Today's indifferent include most middle-class German Protestants, especially in the great, industrious centres of trade and commerce; most hardworking scholars; and the entire university workforce, except the theologians, whose presence and very possibility keep offering psychologists ever subtler puzzles. Devout people, or merely regular churchgoers, seldom realise HOW MUCH goodwill—one might say deliberate will—is now needed for a German scholar to take religion seriously as a problem. His entire profession, and, as I said, the workmanlike diligence his modern conscience demands, incline him towards a lofty, almost charitable unconcern about religion. Sometimes this carries a slight contempt for the spiritual “uncleanliness” he assumes in anyone who still professes loyalty to the Church. Only history, NOT his own experience, allows the scholar to attain a respectful seriousness and a certain timid deference towards religions. Even if his feelings develop into gratitude, he has personally moved no closer to what still exists as Church or piety; perhaps he has moved farther away. Born and raised amid practical indifference to religious questions, he usually refines that indifference into a cautious fastidiousness that avoids religious people and things. The very depth of his tolerance and humanity may lead him to avoid the delicate trouble that tolerance itself entails.—Every age has its own divine form of naivete, whose discovery other ages may envy. How much naivete—adorable, childlike, endlessly foolish naivete—lies in the scholar's belief in his own superiority, in the good conscience of his tolerance, in the innocent certainty with which his instinct treats the religious person as a lower, less valuable type beyond which, ahead of which, ABOVE which he himself has developed: this arrogant little dwarf and herd-man, this industriously alert drudge, working with head and hands upon “ideas,” upon “modern ideas”!

59. Anyone who has looked deeply into the world has surely sensed the wisdom in human superficiality. The instinct of self-preservation teaches us to be flighty, lighthearted, and false. Among philosophers and artists alike we sometimes encounter a passionate, excessive worship of “pure forms.” Whoever NEEDS the cult of surfaces so badly has surely, at some point, made an unfortunate dive BENEATH them. Perhaps even these burned children have their order of rank: born artists who can enjoy life only by trying to FALSIFY its image, as though taking a wearisome revenge on it. We might judge how deeply life has disgusted them by how far they want its image falsified, softened, lifted beyond this world, and deified. The homines religiosi might count as artists of the HIGHEST rank. It is the deep, suspicious fear of incurable pessimism that makes whole centuries sink their teeth into a religious interpretation of existence: fear born of an instinct sensing that truth might be reached TOO soon, before humanity has grown strong enough, hard enough, artistic enough.... Seen this way, piety, “Life in God,” would be FEAR of truth's most elaborate and ultimate product: the artist's worship and intoxication before the most consistent of all falsifications, the will to turn truth upside down, to have untruth at any price. Perhaps piety has so far been the most effective way to beautify human beings. Through it they can become so artful, superficial, shimmering, and good that the sight of them no longer offends.

60. Loving humanity FOR GOD'S SAKE has so far been the noblest and most far-reaching feeling humanity has attained. Love of humanity without some redeeming purpose behind it is merely one MORE stupidity and piece of brutishness. The inclination to love must first receive its proportion, delicacy, grain of salt, and sprinkling of ambergris from a higher inclination. Whoever first perceived and “experienced” this, however his tongue stumbled in trying to express so delicate a matter, deserves for ever to be held sacred and honoured: he has flown higher than anyone yet, and gone astray in the most beautiful fashion!

61. The philosopher as WE free spirits understand him—the person with the greatest responsibility, whose conscience embraces humanity's overall development—will use religion in his work of discipline and education, just as he uses the political and economic circumstances of his time. Religion can select and discipline, destroy as well as create and shape, in many different ways, depending on the people brought under its spell and protection. For strong, independent people, destined and trained to command, embodying a ruling race's judgment and skill, religion offers another means of overcoming resistance to authority. It binds rulers and subjects together, betraying and delivering the subjects' consciences, their innermost hearts that would gladly escape obedience, into the rulers' hands. And exceptional people of noble origin may, through superior spirituality, prefer a more secluded and contemplative life, keeping only the finer forms of government for themselves—over selected disciples or members of an order. Religion can then give them peace from the noise and trouble of administering COARSER affairs, and protect them from the UNAVOIDABLE filth of political agitation. The Brahmins understood this. Religious organisation secured their power to appoint kings for the people, while their own feelings kept them aloof, conscious of a higher, more-than-royal mission. At the same time, religion encourages some subjects and gives them the opportunity to prepare for future command: the slowly rising ranks and classes whose favourable marriage customs strengthen the will and the pleasure of self-control. Religion provides them with incentives and temptations enough to seek higher intellectual life and experience sovereign self-mastery, silence, and solitude. Asceticism and Puritanism are almost indispensable ways of educating and ennobling a race that wants to overcome its inherited low condition and work towards future supremacy. Finally, for ordinary people, the majority, who exist to serve and be generally useful, and are entitled to exist only to that extent, religion gives priceless satisfaction with their station and circumstances, peace of heart, a nobler sense of obedience, more social happiness and fellow-feeling. It adds something transfiguring and beautifying, something justifying all the ordinariness, meanness, and half-animal poverty of their souls. Religion and the religious meaning of life cast sunshine over these perpetually burdened people, making even their own appearance bearable to them. It acts upon them much as Epicurean philosophy usually acts on sufferers of a higher kind: refreshing and refining them, almost TURNING suffering TO ADVANTAGE, finally even sanctifying and vindicating it. Perhaps Christianity and Buddhism offer nothing more admirable than this art: teaching even the lowest to raise themselves through piety into an apparently higher order, and so remain satisfied with the actual world in which living is difficult enough for them—precisely that difficulty being necessary.

62. To be sure, we must also enter the negative side of religion's account and expose its hidden dangers. The price is always excessive and terrible when religions cease to serve as instruments of education and discipline in the philosopher's hands and instead rule on their own authority and SUPREMELY, wishing to be the final end rather than one means among others. Among human beings, as among every other animal, defective, diseased, degenerating, weak, and inevitably suffering individuals exist in excess. Successful cases are always exceptional among humans too—and, since the human being is THE ANIMAL NOT YET PROPERLY ADAPTED TO HIS ENVIRONMENT, rare exceptions. Worse still: the higher the type a person represents, the less likely he is to SUCCEED. Chance, the law of irrationality governing humanity as a whole, shows itself most terribly in the destruction of higher people, whose conditions of life are delicate, varied, and hard to establish. How, then, do the two great religions just mentioned respond to this SURPLUS of life's failures? They try to preserve and keep alive whatever can be preserved. As religions FOR SUFFERERS, they take their side on principle, always favouring those who experience life as a disease, and wishing to dismiss every other experience as false and impossible. We may esteem this compassionate, protective care very highly, especially because, among others, it has also benefited—and still benefits—the highest and usually most suffering human type. Nevertheless, the religions that have ruled SUPREMELY until now are, on a general assessment, among the chief reasons the type “man” has remained low: they have preserved too much THAT SHOULD HAVE PERISHED. We owe them gratitude for invaluable services. Who could be so rich in gratitude that he would not feel poor before all Christianity's “spiritual men” have done for Europe! Yet after comforting sufferers, heartening the oppressed and despairing, giving the helpless a staff and support, and drawing the broken-hearted and distracted out of society into convents and spiritual penitentiaries, what else did they need to do? To preserve all the sick and suffering systematically in this way and with a good conscience meant, in plain truth, working for the DETERIORATION OF THE EUROPEAN RACE. They had to REVERSE every valuation—that is what they had to do! They had to break the strong, spoil great hopes, cast suspicion upon delight in beauty, and turn everything independent, manly, conquering, and commanding—all instincts natural to the highest and most successful human type—into uncertainty, troubled conscience, and self-destruction. In short, they had to transform every love of earthly life and earthly mastery into hatred of the earth and its concerns. THAT was the task the Church imposed upon itself, and had to impose, until in its scale of values “unworldliness,” “unsensuousness,” and “higher man” merged into one feeling. If we could watch European Christianity's strangely painful comedy, equally coarse and refined, with an Epicurean god's mocking, impartial eye, I imagine we would never stop wondering and laughing. Does it not seem that one will has governed Europe for eighteen centuries in order to turn humanity into a SUBLIME ABORTION? But someone with opposite demands, no longer Epicurean, approaching this almost voluntary degeneration and stunting exemplified by the European Christian—Pascal, for instance—with a divine hammer in his hand: would he not cry out in rage, pity, and horror, “Oh, you bunglers, presumptuous, pitiable bunglers, what have you done! Was this work meant for your hands? How you have hacked and spoiled my finest stone! What have you dared to do!” I would say that Christianity has been the most momentous presumption so far. People neither great nor hard enough to be entitled to shape MAN as artists; people insufficiently strong and farsighted to ALLOW, with sublime self-restraint, the obvious law of failures and perishings by the thousand to prevail; people not noble enough to perceive the fundamentally different ranks and distances of rank separating one human being from another: SUCH people, with their “equality before God,” have governed Europe's fate until finally they produced a stunted, almost ridiculous species—a herd animal, obliging, sickly, mediocre: the European of today.

paragraphs: 63. A teacher through and through takes things seriously—even himself—only insofar as they concern his pupils.
64. “Knowledge for its own sake”: morality's final trap. Through it we become thoroughly caught in morality's web all over again.
65. Knowledge would have little allure if reaching it did not require us to overcome so much shame. 65A. We treat our God most dishonourably: we do not ALLOW him to sin.
66. Someone's readiness to be humiliated, robbed, deceived, and exploited may express the shy reserve of a God living among human beings.
67. Loving just one person is barbarous, since it comes at everyone else's expense. The same goes for love of God!
68. “I did it,” my memory tells me. “I cannot have done it,” my pride insists, refusing to yield. At last—memory gives way.
69. Anyone who has missed the hand that kills through kindness has looked at life without paying attention.
70. A person with a character also has a characteristic experience, one that returns again and again.
71. THE SAGE AS ASTRONOMER.—As long as the stars feel like something “above you,” you still lack the discerning person's eye.
72. Great people are made by the endurance of great feelings, rather than by their intensity.
73. Whoever reaches his ideal has, by that very act, gone beyond it. 73A. Many a peacock conceals his tail from everyone—and calls that his pride.
74. Genius makes a person intolerable unless at least two other qualities accompany it: gratitude and purity.
75. The kind and degree of a person's sensuality reach even into the highest regions of his spirit.
76. In times of peace, the combative person turns his attacks upon himself.
77. We use principles to rule, justify, honour, reproach, or hide our habits. Two people holding identical principles probably pursue fundamentally different purposes through them.
78. Even someone who despises himself still values himself in the role of despiser.
79. A soul that knows it is loved but feels no love in return reveals what has settled at its bottom: the dregs rise.

80. Once something has been explained, it stops troubling us. What did the God intend by advising, “Know thyself!” Perhaps, “Stop troubling yourself about yourself! Become objective!”—And Socrates? And the “scientific man”?
81. Dying of thirst at sea is dreadful. Must you add so much salt to your truth that it can no longer quench anyone's thirst?
82. “Sympathy for everyone” would mean cruelty and tyranny towards YOU, my dear neighbour.
83. INSTINCT.—When the house burns, we forget even our dinner. Yes—but afterwards we retrieve it from the ashes.
84. A woman learns to hate as she forgets how to charm.
85. Men and women share the same emotions, but at different TEMPOS. That is why they never stop misunderstanding one another.
86. Behind all their personal vanity, women still retain an impersonal contempt of their own—for “woman.”

87. FETTERED HEART, FREE SPIRIT.—Keep your heart firmly chained and imprisoned, and you can give your spirit many freedoms: I have said this before. But people do not believe me unless they already know it themselves.
88. When exceptionally clever people grow embarrassed, we begin to suspect them.
89. Terrible experiences make us wonder whether the person undergoing them is not something terrible too.
90. Heavy, melancholy people become lighter and briefly rise to their own surface through precisely what weighs others down: hatred and love.
91. He is so cold, so icy, that touching him burns your finger! Every hand that grasps him recoils! Precisely for that reason, many people suppose he is red-hot.
92. Who has not, at some point or other, sacrificed himself to preserve his good reputation?
93. Friendliness contains no hatred of humanity; for that very reason, it contains far too much contempt for humanity.
94. Human maturity means recovering the seriousness we once brought to our games as children.
95. Shame at one's immorality is a rung on a ladder that ends in shame at one's morality too.
96. We should take leave of life as Ulysses took leave of Nausicaa: blessing it, rather than being in love with it.
97. What, a great man? All I ever see is someone acting out his own ideal.
98. A trained conscience gives you kisses even as it bites you.
99. THE DISAPPOINTED ONE SPEAKS.—“I was listening for an echo; all that reached me was praise.”
100. We all pretend to ourselves that we are less complicated than we really are; this gives us relief from our fellows.
101. A discerning person today might easily see himself as God transformed into an animal.
102. Learning that his love is returned ought really to disillusion the lover about his beloved. “What! She is humble enough to love even you? Or foolish enough? Or—or—”
103. THE DANGER IN HAPPINESS.—“Everything now works out for the best for me; I love every fate now. Who would like to become my fate?”
104. Today's Christians refrain from burning us because their love is powerless, not because they love humanity.

105. The pia fraus offends the taste—the “piety”—of the free spirit, the “pious man of knowledge,” even more than the impia fraus. Hence the type's profound lack of judgment compared with the Church: this is ITS lack of freedom.
106. Through music, even the passions themselves find pleasure in their own existence.
107. Strong character shows itself in closing one's ears, once a decision is made, even to the finest objections. Thus it sometimes wills stupidity.
108. Phenomena themselves are never moral; what is moral is only our interpretation of them.
109. Often the criminal is not worthy of his own deed: he belittles it and speaks badly of it.
110. A criminal's defenders are seldom artists enough to make the deed's beautiful horror tell in favour of the person who committed it.
111. Vanity is hardest to hurt precisely at the moment when our pride has been injured.
112. Someone who feels destined to contemplate rather than believe finds every believer too loud and intrusive, and keeps them at a distance.
113. “Do you want to win his favourable opinion? Then show embarrassment in his presence.”
114. Women's enormous expectations of sexual love, and their coyness about those expectations, distort all their perspectives from the very beginning.
115. When neither love nor hatred is at stake, a woman's performance in the game is mediocre.
116. Our life's great turning points come when we dare to rename our bad qualities as what is best in us.
117. The wish to conquer an emotion is, ultimately, simply the wish of another emotion, or of several others.
118. Admiration has its innocence: it belongs to someone who has never yet considered that he too might one day be admired.
119. We can loathe dirt so intensely that we cannot bring ourselves to wash—to “justify”—ourselves.
120. Sensuality often drives love to grow too quickly, leaving its roots weak and easily pulled out.
121. How curious that God chose to learn Greek when he wanted to become an author—and did not learn it any better.
122. Pleasure in being praised often expresses nothing but the heart's courtesy, the very opposite of the spirit's vanity.
123. Even concubinage has suffered corruption—at the hands of marriage.
124. Someone who rejoices at the stake has not defeated pain. He triumphs because the pain he expected is absent. Here is a parable.
125. Whenever we must revise our opinion of someone, we make him pay dearly for the inconvenience he has caused us.
126. A nation is nature's roundabout route to producing six or seven great men. Yes—and then to getting around those men.
127. Every true woman sees science as an enemy of modesty. It feels as though someone wanted to use it to peek beneath her skin—or, worse still! beneath her clothes and finery.
128. The more abstract the truth you aim to teach, the more you must draw the senses towards it.
129. The devil has the widest perspectives on God, which is why he keeps so far away from him. The devil, in fact, as knowledge's oldest friend.
130. What someone IS starts to show when his talent fades, when he stops displaying what he CAN do. Talent is also an ornament, and ornaments also conceal.

131. The sexes misunderstand one another because each really honours and loves only itself—or, more pleasantly put, its own ideal. Thus men want women to be peaceful. Yet a woman is ESSENTIALLY unpeaceful, like a cat, however successfully she may have adopted a peaceful appearance.
132. It is for our virtues that we receive the finest punishments.
133. Whoever cannot discover the path to HIS ideal lives more frivolously and shamelessly than someone who has no ideal at all.
134. Everything trustworthy, every good conscience, every proof of truth originates in the senses.
135. Pharisaism is not what happens when a good man deteriorates; a substantial measure of it is an essential condition of goodness.
136. One person wants an accoucheur, a midwife for his thoughts; another wants someone he can help. That is how good conversation begins.
137. With scholars and artists, we easily make opposite mistakes. An outstanding scholar quite often proves a mediocre human being, while even a mediocre artist often proves a very remarkable one.
138. Awake, we do just what we do in dreams: invent and imagine the person we are dealing with—and immediately forget that we have done so.
139. In matters of revenge and love, woman is more barbarous than man.
140. ADVICE IN A RIDDLE.—“If the bond must not break, first bite it—make it secure!”
141. The belly explains why a human being cannot so easily mistake himself for a God.
142. The most chaste remark I have ever heard: “Dans le veritable amour c'est l'ame qui enveloppe le corps.”
143. Vanity wants our easiest accomplishments to be taken for what costs us the greatest effort. A contribution to the origins of many moral systems.

144. A woman's scholarly interests generally suggest something amiss in her sexual nature. Barrenness itself encourages a certain masculine taste; man, indeed, if I may say so, is “the barren animal.”
145. Comparing the sexes in general, we might say that woman's genius for adornment depends upon her instinct for the SECONDARY role.
146. Whoever battles monsters must take care not to become a monster in the process. And when you look into an abyss for a long time, the abyss looks back into you.
147. From old Florentine tales—and, indeed, from life: Buona femmina e mala femmina vuol bastone.—Sacchetti, Nov. 86.
148. To charm a neighbour into forming a favourable opinion, then believe that opinion unreservedly oneself: who performs this conjuring trick better than women?
149. What an age calls evil is generally an ill-timed echo of something once called good: an old ideal returning through atavism.
150. Around a hero, everything turns into tragedy; around a demigod, into a satyr play; around God, into—what? Perhaps a “world”?
151. Having a talent is insufficient: one must also obtain your permission to have it. Isn't that so, my friends?
152. “Paradise is always where the tree of knowledge stands”: that is what both the oldest and the newest serpents tell us.
153. Whatever we do from love always happens beyond the bounds of good and evil.
154. Objection, evasion, cheerful suspicion, and a taste for irony show health; everything absolute belongs in the realm of pathology.
155. Our feeling for tragedy rises and falls along with our sensuousness.
156. Madness is rare in an individual, but among groups, parties, nations, and historical ages it is the norm.
157. The thought of suicide offers great comfort: it helps us make it through many a miserable night.
158. Our conscience, no less than our reason, bows before our strongest drive, the tyrant within us.
159. We MUST repay kindness and injury—but why necessarily to the same person who treated us well or badly?
160. Once we have shared what we know, we no longer love that knowledge quite enough.
161. Poets treat their own experiences without shame: they turn them to account.
162. “Our fellow human being is not our neighbour, but our neighbour's neighbour”: every nation thinks this way.
163. Love reveals a lover's noble, hidden qualities, his rare and exceptional traits. It can therefore mislead us about what his character is ordinarily like.
164. Jesus told his Jews: “The law was meant for servants. Love God as I do, as his Son! What business do we Sons of God have with morals!”
165. BEFORE EVERY PARTY.—Every shepherd needs a bell-wether; otherwise he must occasionally play the wether himself.
166. We can lie with our mouths, certainly, but the expression accompanying the lie still speaks the truth.
167. For vigorous people, intimacy carries shame—and is something to treasure.
168. Christianity made Eros drink poison. He did not die, admittedly, but he declined into Vice.
169. Talking endlessly about oneself can be another way of keeping oneself hidden.
170. Praise intrudes upon us more than blame does.
171. Pity strikes a person of knowledge as almost ridiculous, like gentle hands laid upon a Cyclops.
172. Sometimes we embrace a particular person out of love for humanity, since we cannot embrace everyone. But we must never admit this to the person concerned.
173. We do not hate someone while we consider him beneath us, only when we see an equal or superior.
174. You Utilitarians also love the UTILE only as a VEHICLE for your inclinations; you too really find the rattling of its wheels unbearable!
175. What we ultimately love is our desire, rather than its object.
176. Other people's vanity offends our taste only when it conflicts with our own vanity.
177. Perhaps no one has ever been truthful enough about what “truthfulness” actually means.
178. People refuse to believe in clever men's follies: what a denial of human rights!
179. Our deeds' consequences seize us by the forelock, utterly unconcerned that we have “reformed” in the meantime.
180. There is a way of lying innocently that shows genuine faith in one's cause.
181. To offer blessings while being cursed is something inhuman.
182. Familiarity from our superiors leaves us bitter, because we are forbidden to respond in kind.
183. “What troubles me is not your having deceived me, but my inability to believe you any longer.”
184. Some kindness has an arrogance that makes it look like wickedness.
185. “I dislike him.”—Why?—“Because I cannot match him.”—Has anyone ever given that answer?

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — The Natural History of Morals
paragraphs: 186. Europe's moral feeling today may be as subtle, late-developed, varied, sensitive, and refined as its corresponding “Science of Morals” is new, preliminary, awkward, and clumsy. An interesting contrast, sometimes embodied quite visibly in a moralist himself. Indeed, “Science of Morals” is a far too presumptuous name for what it denotes, and offends GOOD taste, which always anticipates more modest expressions. We should honestly acknowledge WHAT will still be needed here for a long time, WHAT alone is appropriate now: collecting material, surveying and classifying the immense field of delicate feelings and distinctions of value that live, grow, reproduce, and die. Perhaps we might also try to describe the recurring, commoner forms of these living crystallisations, in preparation for a THEORY OF TYPES of morality. Until now, people have certainly not been so modest. Whenever philosophers addressed morality as a science, they demanded something much grander, more pretentious, more ceremonious of themselves, with pedantic, ridiculous solemnity. They wanted to GIVE MORALITY A FOUNDATION—and every philosopher has believed he provided one, while treating morality itself as something “given.” How remote from their clumsy pride was the apparently insignificant problem, abandoned to dust and decay, of describing the forms of morality: a task for which the finest hands and senses would scarcely be fine enough! Moral philosophers knew the moral facts only imperfectly, through an arbitrary digest or accidental selection—perhaps the morality of their own surroundings, position, church, Zeitgeist, climate, or region. Precisely because they knew so little about peoples, eras, and earlier ages, and had little desire to learn, they never even glimpsed the real problems of morality, which emerge only by comparing MANY moralities. Strange as it sounds, every “Science of Morals” so far has OMITTED the problem of morality itself. No one suspected that anything was problematic here! Properly examined, what philosophers called “giving morality a foundation” was merely a learned form of good FAITH in the prevailing morality, a fresh way of EXPRESSING it. It was therefore just another fact within a particular morality, and, in its deepest motive, a denial that questioning that morality was PERMISSIBLE—certainly the opposite of testing, analysing, doubting, and dissecting that faith. Listen to the almost admirable innocence with which Schopenhauer describes his task, and judge how scientific a “Science” can be when its latest master still speaks like children and old wives. “The principle,” he says on page 136 of the Grundprobleme der Ethik, [Footnote: Pages 54-55 of Schopenhauer's Basis of Morality, translated by Arthur B. Bullock, M.A. (1903).] “the axiom on whose meaning all moralists PRACTICALLY agree: neminem laede, immo omnes quantum potes juva—is REALLY the proposition all moral teachers seek to establish, ... the REAL foundation of ethics, sought for centuries like the philosopher's stone.” Establishing that proposition may indeed be difficult; Schopenhauer's own failure is well known. Anyone who has fully grasped its absurd falsity and sentimentality in a world whose essence is Will to Power may recall that this pessimist ACTUALLY played the flute... every day after dinner, as his biography relates. An incidental question: a pessimist who rejects God and the world but STOPS SHORT at morality, assents to it, and plays the flute to laede-neminem morals—what? Is that really a pessimist?

187. Quite apart from the worth of claims such as “there is a categorical imperative within us,” we can always ask what such a claim reveals about its author. Some moral systems aim to justify their author before others; some soothe him and leave him pleased with himself. Through others he seeks to crucify and humble himself, to take revenge, to hide, or to glorify himself and gain superiority and distinction. One morality helps its author forget; another makes him, or something about him, forgotten. Many moralists want power and creative freedom over humanity. Others—perhaps Kant above all—use morality to tell us, “What deserves respect in me is that I know how to obey—and things SHALL be no different for you!” In short, moral systems are merely a SIGN-LANGUAGE OF THE EMOTIONS.

188. Set against laisser-aller, every morality is a kind of tyranny over “nature” and over “reason.” But this is no objection unless we again use some morality to decree that every tyranny and irrationality is forbidden. What is essential and priceless in any morality is its prolonged constraint. To understand Stoicism, Port Royal, or Puritanism, recall the discipline through which every language gained strength and freedom: metrical constraint, the tyranny of rhyme and rhythm. What pains the poets and orators of every nation have taken! This includes some present-day prose writers, whose ears harbour an unyielding conscientiousness. “For the sake of nonsense,” say utilitarian bunglers, imagining this makes them wise; “in submission to arbitrary laws,” say anarchists, imagining this makes them “free,” even free-spirited. Yet the remarkable fact remains: everything that exists or has existed in the way of freedom, elegance, daring, dance, and masterly assurance—in thought itself, government, speech and persuasion, art as much as conduct—developed only under the tyranny of such arbitrary laws. Seriously, it is quite possible that THIS is “nature” and “natural,” rather than laisser-aller! Every artist knows how far his “most natural” state is from letting himself go: in moments of “inspiration,” freely arranging, placing, disposing, and constructing, he obeys a thousand laws with strictness and delicacy. Their very rigidity and precision defeat any attempt to formulate them in concepts; beside them even the firmest concept seems fluid, multiple, and ambiguous. The essential thing “in heaven and on earth,” apparently—to repeat it—is prolonged OBEDIENCE in one direction. In the long run this produces, and always has produced, something that makes life worth living: virtue, art, music, dance, reason, spirituality—something transfiguring, refined, foolish, or divine. The spirit's long servitude; the suspicious restrictions on communicating thoughts; the discipline thinkers imposed on themselves to follow a church's or court's rules, or Aristotelian premises; the persistent spiritual determination to read every event through a Christian scheme and rediscover and justify the Christian God in everything: all this violence, arbitrariness, harshness, terror, and irrationality trained the European spirit into its strength, relentless curiosity, and subtle agility. Admittedly, much irreplaceable strength and spirit had to be crushed, stifled, and ruined along the way. Here, as everywhere, “nature” shows herself in all her extravagant, INDIFFERENT magnificence, shocking yet noble. For centuries Europeans thought only to prove something—whereas now we distrust any thinker who “wants to prove something.” The result their most rigorous thinking WAS TO reach was fixed beforehand, as perhaps in ancient Asiatic astrology, or still today in the innocent Christian-moral interpretation of immediate personal events “for God's glory” or “for the soul's good.” This tyranny, this arbitrariness, this stern and magnificent stupidity EDUCATED the spirit. Slavery, both coarse and subtle, apparently remains indispensable even to spiritual education and discipline. Every morality can be viewed this way: “nature” within it teaches hatred of laisser-aller and excessive freedom, creates the need for restricted horizons and immediate duties, teaches the NARROWING OF PERSPECTIVES. Thus, in a sense, it teaches that stupidity is a condition of life and growth. “You must obey someone, and for a long time; OTHERWISE you will come to grief and lose all respect for yourself”: this seems to me nature's moral imperative. It is certainly not “categorical,” as old Kant wanted—hence the “otherwise”—nor is it addressed to individuals (what does nature care about an individual!), but to peoples, races, ages, and ranks, and above all to the animal “man” as a whole, to HUMANITY.

189. Industrious peoples find idleness very hard to bear. ENGLISH instinct performed a masterstroke by making Sunday so sacred and gloomy that an Englishman unconsciously longs for the weekday and working day again. It is a cleverly devised, cleverly inserted FAST, of a kind often found in antiquity too, though, appropriately for southern peoples, not specifically a fast from work. Many kinds of fasting are needed. Wherever powerful influences and habits prevail, lawmakers must arrange intervening days when those drives are restrained and learn to hunger afresh. Seen from above, entire generations and eras infected by moral fanaticism resemble these inserted periods of restraint and fasting. A drive learns to humble and submit itself—and also to PURIFY and SHARPEN itself. Certain philosophical sects invite the same interpretation: the Stoa, for instance, amid Hellenic culture's atmosphere, thick and overcharged with Aphrodisiacal scents. This also suggests an explanation for a paradox: why the sexual drive was sublimated into love, amour-passion, precisely during Europe's most Christian period, and generally only under the pressure of Christian feelings.

190. Something in Plato's morality does not truly belong to Plato; it appears in his philosophy almost despite him. This is Socratism, for which he himself was too noble. “Nobody wishes to harm himself; therefore every evil deed is done unknowingly. The evil person injures himself, but would not do so if he knew that evil was evil. He is therefore evil only through error. Free him from error and you necessarily make him—good.” This reasoning smells of the POPULACE, who notice only wrongdoing's unpleasant consequences and effectively conclude, “Doing wrong is STUPID.” Without further thought they equate “good” with “useful and pleasant.” We can immediately suspect the same origin in every utilitarian system and follow the trail; we shall seldom be mistaken. Plato did everything possible to read refinement and nobility into his teacher's doctrines, and above all to read himself into them. This most daring interpreter lifted the whole Socrates out of the street like a popular tune and song, presenting him in endless, impossible variations: in all Plato's own disguises and multiplicities. Speaking playfully, and in Homeric language, what is Plato's Socrates if not—[Greek words inserted here.]

191. The old theological question of “Faith” and “Knowledge”—more plainly, instinct and reason—asks whether instinct should hold greater authority in evaluating things than rationality, which wants to assess and act on motives, on a “Why,” that is, according to purpose and usefulness. It is the same old moral problem that first appeared in Socrates and divided minds long before Christianity. Naturally following the inclination of his talent, that of an unsurpassed dialectician, Socrates initially sided with reason. Indeed, what did he do all his life but mock the awkward helplessness of noble Athenians, instinctive people like all nobles, who could never satisfactorily explain why they acted as they did? Ultimately, though silently and secretly, he laughed at himself as well. His finer conscience and self-examination revealed the same difficulty and incapacity within him. “But why,” he asked himself, “should that make us abandon the instincts! We must set them right, and reason TOO: follow the instincts, but persuade reason to support them with sound arguments.” This was the great, mysterious ironist's real FALSENESS. He trained his conscience to be satisfied with a kind of self-trickery; in fact, he recognised the irrationality within moral judgment. Plato, more innocent in these matters and lacking the plebeian's cunning, spent all his strength—the greatest any philosopher had ever expended—trying to prove to himself that reason and instinct spontaneously converge on the good, on “God.” Since Plato, theologians and philosophers have all followed that road. This means instinct—or what Christians call “Faith,” and I call “the herd”—has so far prevailed in morality. One might except Descartes, rationalism's father and therefore the Revolution's grandfather, who acknowledged only reason's authority. But reason is merely an instrument, and Descartes was superficial.

192. Anyone who has traced the history of a single science will find in its development a clue to the oldest, commonest processes of all “knowledge and cognition.” There, as here, the first things to develop are premature hypotheses, fictions, the good, foolish will to “believe,” and a lack of patience and suspicion. Our senses learn late, and never completely, to become subtle, trustworthy, cautious instruments of knowledge. In any given case, the eye finds it easier to reproduce an often-produced image than to grasp what is different and new in an impression; the latter takes more strength, more “morality.” Hearing something new is difficult and painful for the ear; unfamiliar music reaches us badly. Listening to a foreign language, we automatically try to shape its sounds into words we know better. Thus Germans turned the spoken ARCUBALISTA into ARMBRUST, cross-bow. Our senses too resist and dislike novelty. Even in the “simplest” sensations, emotions generally RULE: fear, love, hatred, and the passive feeling of laziness. A modern reader scarcely reads every word on a page, much less every syllable; instead, he picks out perhaps five of every twenty words at random and “guesses” their likely meaning. In much the same way, we do not see a tree's leaves, branches, colour, and shape fully and accurately. Imagining a rough approximation of a tree is much easier. We do the same even amid the most extraordinary experiences: we invent most of the experience, and can hardly be persuaded to contemplate an event EXCEPT as its “inventors.” All this shows that, by our fundamental nature and from the remotest times, we have been ACCUSTOMED TO LYING. Or, more politely and hypocritically—in short, more pleasantly—we are far more artistic than we realise. During a lively conversation, I often see the other person's face with astonishing clarity, shaped by the thought he expresses or that I believe his mind contains. The detail exceeds my eyesight's actual POWER, so I MUST have imagined the subtle movements of muscles and expression in the eyes. Probably he wore an entirely different expression, or none at all.

193. Quidquid luce fuit, tenebris agit—but the reverse is true as well. Experiences in dreams, if repeated often enough, eventually belong to our soul's possessions as fully as anything “actually” experienced. They make us richer or poorer, add or remove a need; ultimately, even in broad daylight and the clearest moments of waking, our dreams' character governs us to some degree. Suppose someone has often flown in dreams until, whenever he dreams, he recognises the power and art of flight as his privilege, his own enviable happiness. He believes the slightest impulse lets him describe any curve or angle; he knows a divine lightness, an “upward” without effort or constraint, a “downward” without descent or abasement—without TROUBLE! How could someone with these dream experiences and habits fail to find “happiness” differently coloured and defined even while awake! How could he fail to long DIFFERENTLY for happiness? Compared with his own “flying,” the “flight” poets describe must seem far too earthly, muscular, violent, and “troublesome.”

194. People differ not only in their lists of desirable things—in which goods they consider worth pursuing, and in the greater or lesser value and ranking they assign to generally recognised goods. They differ much more in what they count as actually HAVING and POSSESSING something desirable. With a woman, for instance, a more modest man considers control over her body and sexual pleasure sufficient proof of ownership. Another, more suspicious and ambitious in his desire to possess, sees how questionable and merely apparent such ownership is. He wants subtler tests, particularly whether she not only gives herself to him but also gives up for him what she has or would like to have. Only THEN does he consider her “possessed.” A third man's distrust and appetite for possession do not stop even there. He wonders whether, in surrendering everything, she is perhaps surrendering to a phantom of him. He first wants to be known thoroughly, indeed profoundly; to be loved at all, he dares let himself be discovered. Only when she no longer deceives herself about him, loving his devilry and hidden insatiability as much as his goodness, patience, and spirituality, does he feel she belongs entirely to him. One man wants to possess a people and finds every higher art of Cagliostro and Catalina suited to the task. Another, with a more refined appetite, tells himself, “Where we want to possess, we must not deceive.” The thought of a mask of himself ruling the people's hearts makes him impatient and angry: “Then I must MAKE myself known, and first learn to know myself!” Helpful, charitable people almost always display a clumsy cunning: they first dress up the person they will help as someone “deserving,” seeking precisely THEIR assistance, who will respond with profound gratitude, attachment, and submission. Through these fancies they take possession of the needy, just as their charity and helpfulness generally spring from the desire to own. Interfere with their benevolence, or get there first, and they become jealous. Parents involuntarily shape their children into something resembling themselves, calling it “education.” Deep down, no mother doubts that giving birth makes the child her property; no father questions his right to HIS OWN ideas and valuations. In earlier times, fathers even claimed discretion over a newborn's life or death, as among the ancient Germans. Like the father, teacher, class, priest, and prince still regard each new person as an unquestionable opportunity for fresh ownership. The consequence is...

195. The Jews—a people “born for slavery,” according to Tacitus and the entire ancient world, “the chosen people among the nations,” according to their own belief and declaration—performed the miracle of reversing valuations. Through it, earthly life acquired a new, dangerous attraction for a couple of thousand years. Their prophets merged “rich,” “godless,” “wicked,” “violent,” and “sensual” into a single meaning, and first made “world” a word of reproach. This reversal, which also made “poor” synonymous with “saint” and “friend,” contains the significance of the Jewish people. With THEM begins the SLAVE REVOLT IN MORALITY.

196. We must INFER that innumerable dark bodies exist near the sun, bodies we shall never see. Between ourselves, this is an allegory. The psychologist of morals reads the entire writing of the stars merely as a language of allegory and symbols, in which much may remain unstated.

197. Predatory animals and predatory people—Caesar Borgia, for instance—remain fundamentally misunderstood, and “nature” remains misunderstood, whenever we look for “disease” in these healthiest tropical monsters and growths, or even for an inborn “hell,” as almost every moralist has done. Do moralists not seem to hate the virgin forest and the tropics? Must they discredit “tropical man” at any price, portraying him as humanity's sickness and decline, or as his own hell and self-torment? Why? For the benefit of the “temperate zones”? Of temperate people? The “moral”? The mediocre?—A contribution to the chapter “Morality as Timidity.”

198. All moral systems addressing individuals in the name of their so-called “happiness”—what are they but advice on behaviour suited to the degree of DANGER those individuals pose to themselves? Recipes for their passions, their good and bad tendencies, insofar as these possess the Will to Power and want to rule; small and large expedients and elaborations, permeated by the stale smell of family remedies and old wives' wisdom. Their form is always grotesque and absurd because they address “everyone,” generalising where no generalisation is warranted. They all speak unconditionally and take themselves unconditionally. All need more than one grain of salt: they become tolerable, sometimes even seductive, only when heavily seasoned and beginning to smell dangerously, especially of “the other world.” Intellectually considered, this has little value and is far from “science,” much less “wisdom.” Let it be repeated three times: expediency, expediency, expediency, mixed with stupidity, stupidity, stupidity. It may be the indifference and statue-like coldness towards the emotions' heated folly that the Stoics taught and cultivated; or Spinoza's no-more-laughing and no-more-weeping, his naively recommended destruction of emotions through analysis and dissection; or reducing emotion to a harmless middle level where it can be satisfied—the Aristotelianism of morality. It may even be morality as enjoyment of emotions voluntarily diluted and spiritualised through artistic symbolism, perhaps music, or love of God and love of humanity for God's sake—for religion releases the passions again, provided that... Or finally it may be the easy, reckless surrender to emotions taught by Hafis and Goethe: boldly dropping the reins, spiritual and bodily licentia morum in the exceptional case of wise old fellows and drunkards for whom “there is no longer much danger.” This too belongs in the chapter “Morality as Timidity.”

199. Throughout human existence there have always been human herds—family associations, communities, tribes, peoples, states, churches—and always many who obey for every few who command. Since obedience has been practised and cultivated more than anything else, we may reasonably suppose that the need to obey is now generally innate: a kind of FORMAL CONSCIENCE commanding, “You shall unconditionally do something, unconditionally refrain from something”—in short, “You shall.” This need tries to satisfy itself, to fill its form with content. According to its strength, impatience, and eagerness, it seizes indiscriminately, with an omnivorous appetite, whatever assorted commanders shout into its ear: parents, teachers, laws, class prejudices, public opinion. Human development's extraordinary limitations, hesitation, slowness, frequent reversals, and detours arise because the herd instinct of obedience is transmitted most successfully, at the expense of the art of command. Imagine it growing to its utmost: eventually no commanders or independent individuals would remain, or they would suffer from a guilty conscience and first have to deceive themselves before they could command, pretending that they too were merely obeying. This is Europe's actual condition today: I call it the moral hypocrisy of the commanding class. They can protect themselves from their guilty conscience only by playing executors of older or higher commands—those of predecessors, the constitution, justice, law, or God himself—or by justifying themselves with slogans from current herd opinion, as “first servants of their people” or “instruments of public welfare.” Meanwhile, the European herd-person of today adopts the air of someone who believes that his kind is the only kind of human being whose existence ought to be permitted. He glorifies as the distinctively human virtues those qualities that make him gentle, bearable, and useful to the herd: public spirit, kindness, deference, diligence, moderation, modesty, indulgence, sympathy. Where people still think a leader and bell-wether indispensable, repeated efforts are made to replace commanders with an aggregate of clever herd-people; all representative constitutions, for example, come from this impulse. Yet the appearance of an absolute ruler is a blessing to these herd-Europeans, a release from an increasingly unbearable burden. Napoleon's impact was the last great demonstration. The history of his influence is almost the history of the higher happiness the entire century attained in its finest people and periods.

200. In an age of dissolution and intermingling races, a person may carry in his body the inheritance of many ancestries: opposing instincts and valuations—often more than merely opposing—that struggle and seldom rest. Such a person, belonging to a late culture and fractured light, will generally be weak. His deepest wish is for the war WITHIN HIM to end. Happiness appears as a soothing medicine and way of thinking, Epicurean or Christian, for instance. Above all it means rest, freedom from disturbance, fullness, final unity: the “Sabbath of Sabbaths,” in the words of the holy rhetorician St. Augustine, himself just such a person. But suppose the opposition and conflict in these natures provide an ADDITIONAL stimulus to life. Suppose, alongside their powerful, irreconcilable instincts, they have inherited and learned the mastery and subtlety needed to wage war within themselves—the capacities for self-control and self-deception. Then arise those marvellously incomprehensible, inexplicable beings, those riddles of men destined to conquer and outmanoeuvre others. The finest examples are Alcibiades and Caesar; I would add the FIRST European to my taste, the Hohenstaufen Frederick the Second, and among artists perhaps Leonardo da Vinci. They emerge in precisely the periods when the weaker type, longing for repose, comes to the foreground. The two types complement one another and spring from the same causes.

201. So long as usefulness in moral judgment means only usefulness to the herd, so long as preserving the community is the sole concern and immorality means exclusively whatever threatens its survival, there can be no “morality of loving one's neighbour.” Let us grant that consideration, sympathy, fairness, gentleness, and mutual assistance are already exercised to some small but regular extent. Let us grant, too, that even at this stage of society all the instincts later given the honourable title of “virtues” are already at work, instincts that eventually come almost to coincide with the very concept of “morality.” Even so, at that earlier time these instincts do not yet belong to the domain of moral valuation at all: they remain ULTRA-MORAL. In Rome's finest period, for instance, an act of sympathy is called neither good nor bad, neither moral nor immoral. Even praise for it may carry a resentful contempt as soon as it is compared with an action benefiting the whole, the RES PUBLICA. “Love of our neighbour” is, after all, always secondary, partly conventional and arbitrary beside our FEAR OF OUR NEIGHBOUR. Once society's fabric seems established and secure from external danger, this fear creates new perspectives in moral judgment. Powerful, dangerous instincts—enterprise, recklessness, revenge, cunning, rapacity, lust for power—previously had to be honoured for their public usefulness, under other names of course, and actively cultivated, because common danger and common enemies continually required them. Without outlets, their danger now feels doubly strong; gradually they are branded immoral and slandered. Opposite instincts and inclinations gain moral prestige, and the herd instinct draws its conclusions. How much danger an opinion, condition, emotion, disposition, or talent presents to the community or to equality now becomes the moral perspective. Once again, fear is morality's mother. When the highest, strongest instincts erupt passionately and carry a person far above the average and the herd conscience's low level, they destroy the community's confidence. Its belief in itself, its backbone, breaks; these very instincts therefore suffer the worst branding and defamation. High, independent spirituality, the will to stand alone, even compelling reason, are felt as threats. Everything raising an individual above the herd and frightening his neighbour is henceforth EVIL. Tolerance, modesty, adaptability, making oneself equal to others, MEDIOCRITY of desire—these win moral honour. Finally, under very peaceful conditions, opportunities and needs for training severity and rigour in feeling diminish. Every harshness, even in justice, begins to trouble the conscience. Lofty, stern nobility and responsibility for oneself almost offend and awaken suspicion; “the lamb,” and still more “the sheep,” commands respect. Society's history reaches a stage of diseased softness and effeminacy when society itself sincerely and seriously sides with whoever harms it, with the CRIMINAL. Punishment seems somehow unjust; certainly “punishment” and “the duty to punish” now cause pain and alarm. “Isn't making the criminal HARMLESS enough? Why punish him as well? Punishment itself is dreadful!” In these questions herd morality, the morality of fear, reaches its final conclusion. Eliminate danger altogether, the cause of fear, and this morality would disappear too: it would no longer be needed, nor WOULD IT THINK ITSELF needed! Examine the modern European conscience and from its thousand moral folds and hiding places the same command emerges, the herd's timidity speaking: “We want a day when there is NOTHING LEFT TO FEAR!” Someday—the will and the road TOWARDS that day are now called “progress” throughout Europe.

202. Let us immediately repeat what we have said a hundred times, since modern ears resist such truths—OUR truths. We know how offensive it sounds to place human beings plainly among animals, without metaphor. But it will count almost as a CRIME that we have consistently used “herd,” “herd instincts,” and similar expressions precisely of people with “modern ideas.” What use is protesting? We cannot help it: this is exactly where our new insight lies. We have discovered that Europe has reached agreement on all its principal moral judgments, and this agreement extends as well to the countries beyond Europe in which European influence prevails. Europeans evidently KNOW what Socrates thought he did not know and what the famous ancient serpent promised to teach: today they “know” good and evil. So it must sound harsh and disagreeable when we insist that what thinks it knows, glorifies itself through praise and blame, and calls itself good is the instinct of the human herd animal. That instinct increasingly advances towards dominance and supremacy over other instincts, in keeping with the growing physiological convergence and similarity of which it is a symptom. EUROPEAN MORALITY TODAY IS HERD-ANIMAL MORALITY: as we understand it, therefore, only one human morality, beside, before, and after which many others—and above all HIGHER ones—are or should be possible.
