Against this “possible” and this “should,” however, it defends itself with all its strength, stubbornly insisting, “I am morality itself; nothing else is morality!” A religion flattering and indulging the herd animal's loftiest desires has helped bring us to the point where this morality becomes increasingly visible even in political and social institutions. The DEMOCRATIC movement inherits the Christian movement. Yet its TEMPO is too slow and sleepy for the impatient, for those made sick and distraught by the herd instinct. Witness the increasingly furious howling and ever less concealed gnashing of teeth from anarchist dogs prowling Europe's cultural highways. They seem opposed to peaceful, industrious democrats and revolutionary ideologues, and still more to the clumsy would-be philosophers and dreamers of brotherhood who call themselves Socialists and want a “free society.” In fact, all share a deep, instinctive hostility to any society except the AUTONOMOUS herd, even rejecting “master” and “servant”—ni dieu ni maitre, as a socialist formula puts it. All stubbornly oppose special claims, rights, and privileges, ultimately EVERY right, since equal people no longer need “rights.” All distrust punitive justice, as though it violated the weak and wronged the NECESSARY outcomes of previous society. All equally share the religion of sympathy, compassion for everything that feels, lives, and suffers, down to animals and up to “God”: the extravagance of “sympathy for God” belongs to a democratic age. They share pity's cries and impatience, deadly hatred of suffering itself, an almost feminine inability to witness or ALLOW it; share involuntary gloom and soft-heartedness, whose spell seems to threaten Europe with a new Buddhism. All believe in MUTUAL sympathy as morality itself, humanity's summit, its ATTAINED summit, the future's only hope, the present's comfort, the great release from every obligation to the past. All believe the community is the DELIVERER: the herd, and therefore “themselves.”

203. We who believe differently, who see the democratic movement not merely as a degeneration of political organisation but as the degeneration and decline of the human type, its reduction to mediocrity and loss of worth—where can WE place our hopes? In NEW PHILOSOPHERS: nowhere else. In minds strong and original enough to begin opposing valuations, to transvalue and reverse “eternal values”; in forerunners, people of the future who will impose constraints and tie knots now that force millennia onto NEW paths. Humanity must be taught to see its future as its WILL, dependent on human willing. Vast, dangerous enterprises and collective experiments in breeding and education must be prepared, to end the terrible rule of folly and chance hitherto called “history”—the folly of the “greatest number” is only its latest form. This will someday require a new kind of philosopher and commander, before whose very conception every hidden, terrible, and benevolent being so far imagined might look pale and small. The image of such leaders hovers before OUR eyes—may I say this aloud, free spirits? The conditions for their emergence, partly to be created and partly used; the likely methods and tests by which a soul could grow so high and powerful that it felt COMPELLED to these tasks; a transvaluation of values whose new pressure and hammer would steel a conscience and turn a heart to brass, strong enough to bear such responsibility; and, conversely, the need for these leaders, the dreadful danger of their absence, failure, or degeneration: these are OUR real anxieties and dark thoughts, as you well know, free spirits! These are the heavy, distant thoughts and storms passing across OUR life's sky. Few pains compare with seeing, sensing, or experiencing an exceptional person lose his way and deteriorate. But someone with the rare eye for the general danger of “man” himself DETERIORATING, someone who recognises, as we do, the extraordinary chance that has so far played with humanity's future—a game untouched by either the hand or even a “finger of God”!—someone who senses the fate concealed beneath the foolish carelessness and blind confidence of “modern ideas,” and still more beneath the whole of Christian-European morality, suffers an anguish beyond comparison. At a glance he sees all that might still BE MADE OF HUMANITY through a favourable concentration and increase of human powers and arrangements. He knows with the full certainty of conviction how far humanity remains from exhausting its greatest possibilities, and how often the human type has faced mysterious decisions and new roads. From his most painful memories he knows even better the wretched obstacles on which the most promising, highest developments have usually shattered, collapsed, sunk, and become contemptible. Humanity's UNIVERSAL DEGENERATION to the “man of the future,” as socialist fools and shallow minds idealise him; its decline and stunting into an entirely herd-like animal, or, as they say, a person of “free society”; its brutalisation into a pygmy with equal rights and claims—all this is undeniably POSSIBLE! Anyone who has thought that possibility through to its final conclusion knows ANOTHER disgust, unknown to the rest of humanity—and perhaps a new MISSION as well!

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — We Scholars
paragraphs: 204. At the risk that moralizing will show itself here, too, as what it has always been—namely, a determined MONTRER SES PLAIES, in Balzac's phrase—I venture to protest against an unjust and harmful reversal of rank. Almost unnoticed, and apparently with a perfectly clear conscience, this reversal now threatens to establish itself in the relationship between science and philosophy. What I mean is that one must have earned, through one's own EXPERIENCE—and doesn't experience, as I understand it, always mean unhappy experience?—the right to discuss so important a question of rank. Otherwise one talks about colour like a blind man, or talks AGAINST science like women and artists (“Ah! this dreadful science!” their instinct and their shame sigh, “it always FINDS THINGS OUT!”). The scientific man's declaration of independence, his emancipation from philosophy, is one of the subtler consequences of democratic organization and disorganization. Everywhere the scholar's self-glorification and self-importance are now in full bloom, enjoying their finest spring—which is not to suggest that self-praise smells sweet in this instance. Here, too, the instinct of the populace shouts, “Freedom from all masters!” Science resisted theology, whose “hand-maid” it had been for far too long, with the happiest results. Now, in its recklessness and lack of discretion, it proposes to legislate for philosophy and become the “master” in its turn—what am I saying! to act as the PHILOSOPHER on its own authority. My memory—the memory of a scientific man, if you please!—overflows with the innocently insolent remarks about philosophy and philosophers I have heard from young naturalists and elderly doctors. I need hardly mention the most cultivated and conceited of all scholars, philologists and schoolmasters, who are both by profession. Sometimes it was the specialist, the Jack Horner in his corner, instinctively defending himself against every task and ability that brings things together. Sometimes it was the industrious worker, who had detected OTIUM and a refined taste for luxury in the philosopher's inner household, and felt hurt and diminished by them. At other times it was the utilitarian's colour-blindness: he sees in philosophy only a succession of REFUTED systems and an extravagant expense that “does nobody any good”. Sometimes what stood out was fear of concealed mysticism and of efforts to redraw the boundaries of knowledge; sometimes contempt for particular philosophers had inadvertently grown into contempt for philosophy itself. Most often, behind young scholars' proud disdain for philosophy, I found the damaging after-effect of one particular philosopher. They had generally renounced allegiance to him, but had not escaped the spell of his scornful judgments of other philosophers; the result was hostility to philosophy as a whole. (This, for example, seems to me Schopenhauer's effect on the newest Germany. His unintelligent fury against Hegel succeeded in cutting an entire recent generation of Germans off from German culture. Taken as a whole, that culture had raised the HISTORICAL SENSE and refined it into something almost prophetic; yet precisely here Schopenhauer himself was impoverished, unreceptive, and un-German to a positively ingenious degree.) Broadly speaking, perhaps the modern philosophers' own humanity, their all-too-human character—in short, their contemptible qualities—has done the deepest damage to respect for philosophy, throwing the doors open to the instinct of the populace. Just acknowledge how far our modern world has departed from the whole manner of Heraclitus, Plato, Empedocles, and all those other royal, magnificent hermits of the spirit, whatever their names. Acknowledge, too, how justly an honest man of science MAY feel himself better born and bred when he looks at the representatives of philosophy whom current fashion places as high as they actually stand low: in Germany, for instance, those two Berlin lions, the anarchist Eugen Duhring and the amalgamist Eduard von Hartmann. Above all, the spectacle of these patchwork philosophers who call themselves “realists” or “positivists” is calculated to plant a dangerous distrust in an ambitious young scholar's soul. At best these philosophers are themselves only scholars and specialists: that much is plain! They have all been defeated and BROUGHT BACK AGAIN under the rule of science. At some point they demanded more of themselves, without having a right to that “more” or to the responsibility it involves. Now, with conviction, resentment, and a desire for revenge, their words and actions express DISBELIEF in philosophy's ruling task and supremacy. After all, how could things be otherwise? Science flourishes today, its clear conscience written openly on its face. Meanwhile the condition to which the whole of modern philosophy has gradually declined, the little that remains of philosophy today, provokes distrust and displeasure, if not contempt and pity. Philosophy reduced to a “theory of knowledge”, little more in fact than a timid science of periods and a doctrine of restraint; philosophy that never gets past the threshold and sternly DENIES itself permission to enter—that is philosophy in its death throes, an ending, an agony, something to arouse pity. How could philosophy of that kind—RULE!

205. Today the philosopher faces so many dangers in his development that one might doubt whether this fruit can still ripen at all. The sciences have expanded enormously in breadth and in the height of their structure. With that expansion grows the likelihood that the philosopher will become exhausted while still a learner, or settle somewhere and “specialize”, never reaching his own height: his superspection, circumspection, and DESPECTION—the vantage from which he can look above, around, and down. Or he reaches that height too late, after the best of his maturity and strength has gone, or when he has been damaged, coarsened, and worn down, so that his view, his overall judgment of things, no longer counts for much. Perhaps it is precisely the delicacy of his intellectual conscience that makes him hesitate and linger along the way. He fears becoming a dilettante, a millepede, a milleantenna—a creature with a thousand feet and a thousand antennae. He knows only too well that a discerning man who has lost his self-respect can no longer command, no longer LEAD—unless he intends to become a grand actor, a philosophical Cagliostro and spiritual rat-catcher: in short, someone who leads people astray. In the last resort this is a question of taste, unless it has really been a question of conscience all along. To double the philosopher's difficulties once more, he also demands a verdict from himself, a Yes or No, about life and life's value rather than about science. Reluctantly he learns to believe that obtaining this verdict is his right, even his duty. He must find his way to that right and that belief through the widest range of experiences, perhaps experiences that unsettle and destroy him, often hesitating, doubting, and struck dumb. Indeed, for a long time the multitude has mistaken the philosopher either for the scientist and ideal scholar, or for the religious visionary, raised above sensuality and the world, intoxicated with God. Even now, to praise someone for living “wisely” or “as a philosopher” usually means little more than “cautiously and in seclusion”. Wisdom seems to the populace a kind of escape, a device and a skill for withdrawing successfully from a bad game. But the GENUINE philosopher—doesn't this seem true to US, my friends?—lives “unphilosophically” and “unwisely”, above all IMPRUDENTLY. He feels the obligation and the burden of a hundred trials and temptations in life; he continually stakes HIMSELF, and plays THIS bad game.

206. Beside a genius—a being who either ENGENDERS or PRODUCES, both words taken in their fullest sense—the learned man, the average scientific man, always has something of the old maid about him. Like her, he has no practical acquaintance with humanity's two principal functions. Naturally we grant respectability to both scholar and old maid, almost as compensation—in these cases we lay particular stress on respectability—and yet our obligation to make this concession carries the same touch of irritation in each case. Let us look more closely: what is the scientific man? First, an ordinary sort of person with ordinary virtues: a type who neither rules nor speaks with authority nor stands independently. He is hardworking, patiently adaptable to his place in the ranks, even-tempered and moderate in both abilities and demands. He has an instinct for people of his own kind and for what they need: for example, their patch of independence and green meadow, without which there is no rest from work; their claim to honour and consideration, which above all requires being recognized and recognizable; the sunshine of a good reputation; and the constant confirmation of their value and usefulness. Such confirmation must repeatedly overcome the inner DISTRUST rooted in the hearts of all dependent people and herd animals. As one would expect, the learned man also has ailments and faults of an ignoble sort. Petty envy fills him, and he has a lynx's eye for weaknesses in people whose heights he cannot reach. He is trusting, but only like someone who lets himself go without ever beginning to FLOW. Precisely before a man who is a mighty current, he grows colder and more guarded; his eye becomes a still, unresponsive lake, no longer stirred by enthusiasm or fellow-feeling. The worst and most dangerous thing a scholar can do springs from his type's instinct for mediocrity, from the Jesuitism of mediocrity. This instinctively works to destroy exceptional people and tries to break—or, better still, slacken—every drawn bow. Slacken it, of course, with consideration, and naturally with a gentle hand: to RELAX it through trusting sympathy is the true art of Jesuitism, which has always known how to present itself as the religion of sympathy.

207. However gratefully we welcome the OBJECTIVE spirit—and who hasn't grown sick to death of subjectivity and its damned IPSISIMOSITY!—we must eventually learn to be cautious even about our gratitude. We must put an end to the extravagant celebration of the spirit's loss of self and personality, as though this were an end in itself, salvation and transfiguration. Such celebrations are especially customary among pessimists, who in their turn have good reasons for heaping the highest honours on “disinterested knowledge”. The objective man no longer curses and complains like the pessimist. He is the IDEAL scholar, in whom the scientific instinct at last flowers fully after a thousand total or partial failures. Certainly he is among the most precious instruments in existence, but he belongs in the hands of someone more powerful. He is only an instrument, we might say, a MIRROR—not a “purpose in himself”. In truth the objective man is a mirror trained to bow down before everything that wants to be known. His only desires are those involved in knowing or “reflecting”. He waits for something to arrive, then sensitively opens himself to it, so that even the lightest footsteps and the gliding passage of spiritual beings leave their trace on his surface and film. Whatever “personality” he still has seems accidental to him, arbitrary, or more often a disturbance: so thoroughly has he learned to regard himself as a channel and reflection for external forms and events. Remembering “himself” costs him an effort, and he often gets it wrong. He readily confuses himself with other people and misunderstands his own needs; in this one matter he is insensitive and careless. Perhaps he worries about his health, or about the pettiness and narrow atmosphere of his wife and friend, or about lacking companions and society. He actually sets out to think about his suffering, but in vain! Already his thoughts wander towards the MORE GENERAL case, and tomorrow he will know no better than yesterday how to help himself. He no longer takes himself seriously or gives himself time. He is serene, NOT because he has no troubles, but because he cannot grasp and attend to HIS troubles. His habitual readiness to accommodate every object and experience, the radiant, impartial hospitality with which he welcomes everything coming his way, his thoughtless good nature and dangerous indifference between Yes and No: alas! there are plenty of occasions when he must pay for these virtues! As a human being in general, he becomes all too easily the CAPUT MORTUUM of such virtues. Ask him for love or hatred—love and hatred as God, woman, and animal understand them—and he will do and supply what he can. But don't be surprised if it amounts to little, if precisely here he proves false, fragile, dubious, and diminished. His love is forced; his hatred is manufactured, a kind of UN TOUR DE FORCE, a little display and exaggeration. He is genuine only insofar as he can be objective; only in his serene completeness does he remain “nature” and “natural”. His soul, forever reflecting and polishing itself, no longer knows how to affirm or deny. He issues no commands and destroys nothing. “JE NE MEPRISE PRESQUE RIEN”, he says with Leibniz: let us neither overlook nor underestimate that PRESQUE! Nor is he an exemplary man. He leads no one and follows no one; generally he stands too far away to have any reason to take the side of good or evil. If he has so long been confused with the PHILOSOPHER, with the Caesarian educator and dictator of civilization, he has received far too much honour. What matters more in him has been missed: he is an instrument, something like a slave, certainly the most exalted kind of slave, but nothing in himself—PRESQUE RIEN! The objective man is an instrument, an expensive measuring and reflecting apparatus, easily damaged and tarnished, to be cared for and respected. But he is no goal, no movement outward or upward, no completing human being in whom the REST of existence finds its justification, no ending—and still less a beginning, a begetting or first cause. He is nothing tough, powerful, centred in himself, and eager to rule. He is more like a soft, swollen, delicate, movable potter's form, waiting for some content and framework to which it can “shape” itself: usually a man without framework or content, a “selfless” man. Consequently he is also no use to women, IN PARENTHESI.

208. When a philosopher today announces that he is no skeptic—I hope the preceding description of the objective spirit has made that clear?—everyone listens impatiently. This admission makes people somewhat afraid of him; they would like to ask so very many questions... Indeed, timid listeners, who are so numerous now, henceforth call him dangerous. His rejection of skepticism seems to let them hear a distant, threatening noise, as though somebody somewhere were testing a new explosive, a dynamite of the spirit, perhaps a newly discovered Russian NIHILINE, a pessimism BONAE VOLUNTATIS. Such pessimism does not merely deny and intend denial, but—terrible thought!—PUTS denial INTO PRACTICE. Against this kind of “good-will”, a will to the actual, effective negation of life, everyone nowadays acknowledges that no sleeping draught or sedative works better than skepticism: the gentle, agreeable, soothing poppy of skepticism. Today's doctors even prescribe Hamlet as an antidote to the “spirit” and its underground rumblings. “Aren't our ears already full of evil noises?” the skeptics ask, loving their peace and acting almost as a sort of security police. “This underground No is dreadful! Quiet, you pessimistic moles!” The skeptic really is a delicate creature, frightened far too easily. His conscience has been trained to jump at every No, and even at a sharp, decisive Yes, as though something had bitten him. Yes! and No!—both seem to him contrary to morality. Instead he likes to celebrate his virtue through a noble detachment, perhaps saying with Montaigne, “What do I know?” Or with Socrates, “I know that I know nothing.” Or, “Here I don't trust myself; no door stands open for me.” Or, “Even if the door were open, why should I go straight in?” Or, “What good are hasty hypotheses? Perhaps making no hypotheses at all would show perfectly good taste. Must you immediately straighten everything crooked, plug every hole with some sort of oakum? Isn't there time enough for that? Doesn't time itself have leisure? Oh, you demons, can't you WAIT at all? Uncertainty has its charms too; the Sphinx is also a Circe, and Circe was also a philosopher.”—That is how a skeptic consoles himself, and he does indeed need consolation. For skepticism is the most spiritual expression of a particular, many-sided physiological constitution, usually called nervous weakness and sickliness. It develops whenever races or classes long kept apart suddenly and decisively mix. The new generation has inherited, as it were in its blood, different standards and valuations; everything in it is unrest, disorder, doubt, and tentative experiment. Its best powers check one another, its very virtues prevent one another from growing strong. Body and soul lack balance, ballast, and upright stability. But what is most diseased and degenerate in these mixed beings is the WILL. They no longer know independent decision or the brave pleasure of willing; even in their dreams they doubt “freedom of the will”. Present-day Europe is the scene of a senseless, hurried attempt to mix classes radically, and CONSEQUENTLY races as well. It is therefore skeptical from its highest levels to its lowest. Sometimes its skepticism is restless, hopping impatiently and recklessly from branch to branch; sometimes it looks gloomy, like a cloud loaded with question marks—and often it is sick to death in its will! Paralysis of the will: where today do we fail to find this cripple sitting! And how dressed up it often is, how seductively decorated! The finest festive clothes and disguises are available for this disease. For instance, most of what now appears in the display windows as “objectiveness”, “the scientific spirit”, “L'ART POUR L'ART”, and “pure voluntary knowledge” is merely skepticism and paralysis of will in costume. I am prepared to stand behind this diagnosis of Europe's illness. The disease of the will is unevenly spread across Europe. It is worst and most varied where civilization has ruled longest; it diminishes wherever “the barbarian” still—or once again—asserts his claims beneath the loose garments of Western culture. Thus, as one can readily establish and understand, the will is weakest in today's France. France has always possessed a masterly gift for turning even the ominous crises of its spirit into something charming and seductive. Now it emphatically demonstrates its intellectual ascendancy over Europe by serving as the school and exhibition of all skepticism's charms. The capacity to will, and to hold to a decision, is already somewhat stronger in Germany; within Germany it is stronger in the North than in the centre. It is considerably stronger in England, Spain, and Corsica, associated with a sluggish temperament in the first and with hard heads in the latter two. I leave aside Italy, still too young to know what it wants, which must first show whether it can exercise a will at all. But the strongest and most astonishing instance is the immense middle empire where Europe seems to flow back into Asia: Russia. There the strength to will has long been stored and accumulated; there the will, uncertain whether to affirm or deny, waits menacingly for its discharge, to borrow our physicists' favourite expression. Perhaps freeing Europe from its greatest danger would require more than wars in India and complications in Asia: perhaps internal upheaval would also be needed, the empire shattered into little states, and above all the introduction of parliamentary stupidity, together with everyone's obligation to read a newspaper over breakfast. I say this without wishing it to happen. At heart I would prefer the opposite: Russia becoming so much more threatening that Europe would have to resolve to become equally threatening itself. That would mean ACQUIRING ONE WILL through a new caste ruling the Continent, a lasting, dreadful will of its own, capable of setting goals thousands of years ahead. Then the endlessly prolonged comedy of its petty states and its many wills, dynastic as well as democratic, could finally end. The age of petty politics is over; the next century will bring the battle for world dominion—the COMPULSION towards great politics.

209. How far the new warlike age, into which we Europeans have plainly entered, might encourage another, stronger kind of skepticism is something I want to discuss for now only through a parable. Lovers of German history will already understand it. That unscrupulous enthusiast for tall, handsome grenadiers, the troubling, half-crazy father of Frederick the Great, had on one point a genius's instinctive knack and lucky grasp. As King of Prussia he brought into being a military and skeptical genius—and with him, in reality, the new German type that has now emerged triumphantly. He knew what Germany then lacked, something whose absence was a hundred times more alarming and serious than any shortage of culture or social polish. His hostility towards young Frederick sprang from the anxiety of a deep instinct. MEN WERE LACKING, and to his bitter sorrow he suspected that his own son was not man enough. On this point he was wrong; but who in his position would not have been wrong? He saw his son slipping into atheism, ESPRIT, and the agreeable frivolity of clever Frenchmen. Behind them he saw that great bloodsucker, the spider of skepticism. He suspected the incurable misery of a heart no longer hard enough for either good or evil, and of a broken will that could no longer command, was no longer ABLE to command. Yet within his son a new, harder, more dangerous skepticism was growing. Who knows TO WHAT EXTENT his father's hatred and the icy sadness of a will sentenced to solitude actually fostered it? This was the skepticism of daring manliness, closely allied to a genius for war and conquest, which first entered Germany in the person of the great Frederick. It despises yet grasps; it undermines and takes possession; it disbelieves without thereby losing itself. It grants the spirit a dangerous freedom while keeping the heart under strict guard. This is skepticism in its GERMAN form: a continuing Fredericianism raised to the highest spiritual level. For a considerable time it has held Europe under the rule of the German spirit and its critical, historical distrust. The extraordinarily strong, tough masculinity of the great German philologists and historical critics gradually established a NEW conception of the German spirit, despite all the Romanticism in music and philosophy. Properly understood, those men were also all artists of destruction and dissolution. In this new conception, the tendency towards masculine skepticism was unmistakable: a fearless gaze, a dissecting hand both courageous and severe, a determined will to undertake dangerous voyages of discovery, spiritual North Pole expeditions beneath barren, perilous skies. Warm-blooded, superficial humanitarians may have good reasons for crossing themselves before this spirit, this CET ESPRIT FATALISTE, IRONIQUE, MEPHISTOPHELIQUE, as Michelet calls it with a shudder. But to grasp how revealing this fear of the “man” in the German spirit is—the spirit that woke Europe from its “dogmatic slumber”—we should recall the older conception that the new one had to overcome. It was not so long ago that a masculinized woman could presume, with complete abandon, to recommend the Germans to Europe's attention as gentle, good-hearted, weak-willed, poetic fools. Finally, we need only understand Napoleon's astonishment on seeing Goethe deeply enough: it reveals what people had meant by “the German spirit” for centuries. “VOILA UN HOMME!”—in other words, “But this is a MAN! I only expected to see a German!”

210. Suppose, then, that some feature in this picture of the philosophers of the future makes us wonder whether they must be skeptics in the sense just described. That would name something in them, rather than name what they themselves are. They could with equal justice call themselves critics, and certainly they will be experimenters. The name with which I ventured to christen them already placed explicit emphasis on their attempts and their love of attempting. Is this because, as critics in body and soul, they will enjoy employing experiments in a new and perhaps broader, more dangerous sense? Will their passion for knowledge oblige them to venture further into daring and painful trials than the sensitive, pampered taste of a democratic century can approve? Certainly these coming men will be least able to do without the serious, conscientious qualities that separate the critic from the skeptic. I mean confidence in standards of value, deliberate use of a consistent method, cautious courage, the ability to stand alone and accept responsibility for oneself. Indeed, among themselves they will admit a DELIGHT in denial and dissection, and a certain thoughtful cruelty that knows how to wield the knife surely and skilfully even while the heart bleeds. They will be STERNER, perhaps not always towards themselves alone, than humane people would wish. They will not concern themselves with “truth” so that it may “please”, “elevate”, or “inspire” them. Rather, they will put little faith in “TRUTH” bringing such emotional festivities in its wake. These rigorous spirits will smile when someone says before them, “That thought lifts me up; why shouldn't it be true?” or “That work enchants me; why shouldn't it be beautiful?” or “That artist makes me feel larger; why shouldn't he be great?” Perhaps they will feel more than amusement: genuine disgust at everything so rapturous, idealistic, feminine, and hermaphroditic. Anyone able to look into their deepest hearts would find it hard to discover an intention to reconcile “Christian sentiments” with “antique taste”, or even with “modern parliamentarism”. Such reconciliation necessarily occurs even among philosophers in our very uncertain and therefore very conciliatory century. These future philosophers will demand of themselves critical discipline and every habit that encourages clarity and rigour in intellectual matters; they may even display these as their special adornment. Nevertheless, they will not want to be called critics on that account. They will regard it as a considerable insult to philosophy to decree, as people now so gladly do, that “philosophy itself is criticism and critical science—and absolutely nothing else!” This estimate of philosophy may win the approval of every Positivist in France and Germany; perhaps it even pleased KANT's heart and taste—remember the titles of his chief works. Nevertheless our new philosophers will say that critics are the philosopher's instruments, and precisely because they are instruments, they are very far from being philosophers themselves! Even the great Chinaman of Konigsberg was only a great critic.

211. I insist that people finally stop confusing philosophical workers, and scientific men generally, with philosophers. Precisely here we must strictly give “each his own”, rather than give the former far too much and the latter far too little. The genuine philosopher's education may require him to have stood on every step where his servants, the scientific workers of philosophy, stay standing and MUST stay standing. Perhaps he himself must once have been a critic, a dogmatist, a historian, and also a poet, collector, traveller, solver of riddles, moralist, seer, “free spirit”, and almost everything else. Only so can he travel through the whole range of human values and judgments, and BE ABLE, with different eyes and consciences, to look from a height into every distance, from a depth towards every height, from a corner across every open expanse. But these are only preparations for his task. The task itself demands something different: he must CREATE VALUES. Philosophical workers, following the excellent examples of Kant and Hegel, have to establish and formulate some great existing body of valuations. These are earlier DETERMINATIONS OF VALUE, creations of value that have gained acceptance and are called “truths” for a time, whether in the LOGICAL, POLITICAL (moral), or ARTISTIC sphere. Such investigators must make everything that has happened and been valued so far visible, conceivable, intelligible, and manageable. They must shorten everything long, even “time” itself, and SUBJUGATE the entire past. This enormous, wonderful task can surely satisfy every refined pride and every persistent will engaged in carrying it out. GENUINE PHILOSOPHERS, HOWEVER, COMMAND AND LEGISLATE. They declare, “This is how it SHALL be!” They first determine humanity's destination and purpose, and in doing so put aside the previous work of all philosophical workers and all who have subjugated the past. Their creative hand reaches towards the future; everything that exists or has existed becomes their means, their instrument, their hammer. Their “knowing” is CREATING; their creating lays down laws; their will to truth is—WILL TO POWER. Do such philosophers exist today? Have they ever existed? MUST they not exist one day? ...

212. It becomes increasingly clear to me that the philosopher, a man INDISPENSABLE for tomorrow and the day after, has always found himself—and HAS HAD TO find himself—in opposition to his own day. His enemy has always been his age's ideal. Until now, all those extraordinary people who advance humanity and whom we call philosophers have seldom thought of themselves as lovers of wisdom. Rather, they have regarded themselves as disagreeable fools and dangerous questioners. Their mission, their harsh, involuntary, inescapable mission—and ultimately its greatness—has been to serve as their age's bad conscience. By applying the vivisector's knife to the breast of THEIR AGE'S VIRTUES, they have revealed their secret: they acted for the sake of a NEW human greatness, a new, untrodden road to human elevation. Again and again they exposed the hypocrisy, laziness, self-indulgence, self-neglect, and falsehood hidden beneath the most revered forms of contemporary morality. They showed how much virtue had OUTLIVED its time. Always they said, “We must move from here to the place where YOU feel least at home.” Faced with a world of “modern ideas” that wants to shut everyone into a corner, a “specialty”, a philosopher—if philosophers could exist today—would have to locate human greatness, the very concept of “greatness”, precisely in breadth and variety, in all-round development. He would even measure worth and rank by how much and how many different things a person could bear and take upon himself, by how FAR he could extend his responsibility. Today's taste and virtue weaken and thin out the will; nothing suits the spirit of the age better than weakness of will. Consequently the philosopher's ideal must give particular weight, within its conception of “greatness”, to strength of will, severity, and the capacity to sustain a decision. It has as much right to do so as the opposite doctrine, with its ideal of foolish, renouncing, humble, selfless humanity, had in an opposite age—such as the sixteenth century, which suffered from its accumulated energy of will and the wildest torrents and floods of selfishness. In Socrates' day, among men whose instincts were worn out, old conservative Athenians letting themselves go “for the sake of happiness”, as they said, or for pleasure, as their behaviour showed, IRONY may have been necessary for greatness of soul. They constantly mouthed the old pompous words to which their way of life had long since forfeited any right. What was needed was the wicked Socratic assurance of that old physician and plebeian who cut as ruthlessly into his own flesh as into the flesh and heart of the “noble”, with a look that said plainly enough, “Don't pretend with me! Here—we are equals!” Today, by contrast, the herd animal alone receives and distributes honours throughout Europe. “Equality of right” can all too easily become equality in wrongdoing: I mean a general war against everything rare, strange, and privileged, against the higher man, higher soul, higher duty, higher responsibility, and against creative fullness of power and mastery. Today, therefore, “greatness” includes nobility, the desire to stand apart, the ability to be different and alone, the necessity of living on one's own initiative. A philosopher will disclose something of his own ideal when he says, “The greatest shall be the one who can be the most solitary, the most hidden, the most different: the man beyond good and evil, master of his virtues and overflowing with will. This shall be called GREATNESS: to be as various as one can be whole, as wide as one can be full.” And once again the question: is greatness POSSIBLE—today?

213. Learning what a philosopher is presents a difficulty: it cannot be taught. One must “know” it through experience—or possess the pride NOT to know it. Nowadays everyone talks about things they CANNOT have experienced; unfortunately this is especially true of talk about philosophers and philosophical matters. Very few know these things, very few are permitted to know them, and every popular notion about them is false. Take, for example, the genuinely philosophical union of bold, overflowing spirituality moving at a presto pace with dialectical rigour and necessity that never makes a false step. Most thinkers and scholars have no personal experience of this union; consequently, if someone describes it in their presence, they find it unbelievable. Every necessity seems to them a nuisance, a painful compulsory obedience, a condition of constraint. They regard thinking itself as something slow and hesitant, almost a burden, and often as “worthy of the SWEAT of the noble”—certainly not as something easy and divine, closely allied to dancing and exuberance! For them “thinking” and approaching something “seriously”, “laboriously”, are one and the same; that is all their “experience” has taught them. Artists may have a finer intuition here. They know very well that precisely when they cease doing anything “arbitrarily” and everything follows necessity, their sense of freedom, subtlety, and power reaches its height: their sense of creatively determining, arranging, and shaping. In short, necessity and “freedom of will” then become the same thing for them. Finally, states of the soul have an order of rank, and problems have a corresponding order. The highest problems ruthlessly repel anyone who ventures too close without being destined to solve them by the height and power of his spirituality. What good does it do when agile everyday minds, or clumsy, honest mechanics and empiricists, push up close to these problems in their plebeian ambition, almost into this “holy of holies”—as happens so often today! Coarse feet must never step on such carpets: the fundamental law of things ensures that. Those doors stay closed to intruders, however often they batter and break their heads against them. One must always be born to a high station, or, more precisely, BRED for it. A person has a right to philosophy, in the higher sense of the word, only through descent; here too ancestors and “blood” decide. Many generations must prepare the way for a philosopher's arrival. Each of his virtues must separately have been acquired, cultivated, passed down, and embodied. This includes not only the bold, easy, delicate movement and flow of his thoughts, but above all readiness for great responsibilities; the majesty of a ruling gaze and a look of contempt; the feeling of distance from the multitude and its duties and virtues; kindly protection and defence of whatever is misunderstood and slandered, whether God or devil; delight and practice in the highest justice; the art of command; breadth of will; the lingering eye that seldom admires, seldom looks upward, seldom loves....

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Our Virtues
paragraphs: 214. OUR virtues? We probably still have virtues of our own, though naturally they are not those solid, sincere virtues for which we respect our grandfathers and also keep them at a little distance. We Europeans of the day after tomorrow, we first arrivals of the twentieth century—with our dangerous curiosity, our many-sidedness and skill at disguise, our mellow, apparently sweetened cruelty of sense and spirit—will presumably, IF we must have virtues, possess only those that have reached an understanding with our most secret, heartfelt inclinations and our most passionate needs. Very well, let us search for them in our labyrinths! We know how many things lose their way there, how many disappear completely! And what could be finer than SEARCHING for one's own virtues? Isn't that almost BELIEVING in one's own virtues? But this “belief in one's own virtues”—isn't it practically the same as what used to be called one's “good conscience”, that long, respectable pigtail of an idea our grandfathers wore behind their heads, and often enough behind their understanding too? So, however little we think ourselves old-fashioned and grandfatherly respectable in other ways, in one respect we remain our grandfathers' worthy grandchildren. We last Europeans with good consciences still wear their pigtail.—Ah! If only you knew how soon, how very soon, things will change!

215. In the starry sky, two suns sometimes determine a single planet's course. In certain cases, suns of different colours shine around one planet, lighting it now red, now green, then bathing it simultaneously in a mixture of colours. Likewise, because the machinery of our “firmament” is so complicated, we modern people are governed by DIFFERENT moralities. Our actions shine by turns in different colours and seldom have an unambiguous character. Often, too, our actions are themselves MANY-COLOURED.

216. Love our enemies? I think that lesson has been thoroughly learned: it happens thousands of times today, on both large and small scales. Indeed, sometimes something higher and more sublime happens: we learn to DESPISE while loving, precisely when we love most deeply. Yet all this occurs unconsciously, without noise or display, with the modesty and secrecy of goodness, which forbids grand declarations and formulas of virtue. Morality as a pose offends our taste today. This TOO is progress, just as it was progress when our fathers finally found religion as a pose distasteful—including hostility to religion and Voltairean bitterness against it, with everything else that once belonged to the freethinker's pantomime. There is music in our conscience, a dance in our spirit, with which Puritan litanies, moral sermons, and sanctimonious goodness simply will not harmonize.

217. We should handle carefully anyone who sets great store by a reputation for moral tact and fine moral discernment! Once such people have made a mistake IN FRONT OF us, or even ABOUT us, they never forgive us. Inevitably they become our instinctive slanderers and detractors, even while remaining our “friends”. Blessed are the forgetful, for they “get over” even their own blunders.

218. France's psychologists—and where else today are there still psychologists?—have not yet exhausted their bitter, varied enjoyment of betise bourgeoise, as though... In short, they give something away by it. Flaubert, for example, that honest citizen of Rouen, eventually saw, heard, and tasted nothing else. It became his way of tormenting himself, his refined cruelty. Since this is growing tiresome, I would recommend a different pleasure for a change: the unconscious cunning with which good, fat, honest mediocrity always deals with higher spirits and their tasks. This subtle, barbed, Jesuitical cunning is a thousand times subtler than middle-class taste and understanding at their best, subtler even than its victims' understanding. Here is renewed proof that “instinct” is the most intelligent kind of intelligence yet discovered. In short, you psychologists, study the philosophy of the “rule” as it fights the “exception”: there is a spectacle fit for gods and divine malice! Or, to put it plainly, practise vivisection on “good people”, on “homo bonae voluntatis”, ON YOURSELVES!

219. Passing moral judgment and condemnation is the intellectually shallow person's favourite revenge on those who are less shallow. It is also compensation for nature's meagre gifts, and finally a chance to acquire spirit and BECOME subtle: malice makes people spiritual. Deep down they rejoice that a standard exists by which people richly endowed with intellectual gifts and privileges count as their equals. They fight for the “equality of all before God” and almost NEED belief in God for this purpose. Among them we find atheism's most powerful opponents. Tell them, “An elevated spirituality is beyond all comparison with the honesty and respectability of a merely moral person”, and they would fly into a rage; I shall take care not to say it. I would rather flatter them with my theory that elevated spirituality itself exists only as the final product of moral qualities. It combines all the qualities attributed to the “merely moral” person, after these have been acquired one by one through long discipline and practice, perhaps over many generations. Elevated spirituality is precisely justice made spiritual, together with that beneficial severity which knows itself entitled to uphold DEGREES OF RANK in the world, among things as well as among people.

220. Now that praising the “disinterested person” has become so fashionable, we must discover—probably at some risk—WHAT people actually find interesting. What things generally concern ordinary people deeply and fundamentally, including the cultivated, even the learned, and perhaps philosophers too, unless appearances deceive us? This inquiry reveals that most of what interests and enchants higher natures and more refined, demanding tastes seems entirely “uninteresting” to the average person. If he nevertheless notices devotion to such interests, he calls it desinteresse and wonders how anyone can act “disinterestedly”. Some philosophers have given this popular amazement a seductive, mystical expression pointing beyond this world—perhaps because they had no experience of the higher nature themselves? They might instead have stated the bare, honestly reasonable truth: “disinterested” action is extremely interesting and “interested” action, provided that... “And love?”—What! Must even acting for love's sake be “unegoistic”? You fools—! “And the praise of self-sacrifice?”—Anyone who has really sacrificed something knows that he wanted and received something in return. Perhaps he exchanged something in himself for something else in himself, giving something up here to gain more there, perhaps to be more altogether, or even to feel “more”. But a more fastidious spirit dislikes lingering in this territory of questions and answers. Here truth must suppress so many yawns whenever she is forced to answer. And truth, after all, is a woman: one must not use force on her.

221. “Sometimes,” said a moral pedant and dealer in trifles, “I honour and respect an unselfish man. But I do so because I think he has a right to serve another at his own expense, rather than because he is unselfish. In short, everything depends on who HE is and who THE OTHER is. In someone made and destined to command, for instance, self-denial and modest withdrawal would waste virtues instead of being virtues themselves: that is how it seems to me. Every morality of selflessness that treats its claims as unconditional and addresses everyone offends good taste. It also encourages sins of omission, offering a FURTHER temptation under philanthropy's mask—precisely a temptation and an injury to the higher, rarer, more privileged kinds of human being. Moral systems must first be made to bow before DEGREES OF RANK. Their presumption must be brought home to their consciences, until they finally understand that it is IMMORAL to say, ‘What is right for one is right for another.’”—So spoke my moral pedant and bonhomme. Perhaps he deserved laughter for urging moral systems to behave morally in this way? But if one wants the laughers on ONE'S OWN side, one must not be too thoroughly right. Even good taste requires a grain of wrong.

222. Wherever sympathy, suffering with others, is preached today—and, if I understand correctly, no other religion is preached any more—the psychologist should keep his ears open. Through all the vanity and noise natural to these preachers, as to every preacher, he will hear a hoarse, groaning, unmistakable note of SELF-CONTEMPT. It belongs to the darkening and disfiguring of Europe that has increased for a century, IF IT IS NOT ACTUALLY ITS CAUSE! The first symptoms are already documented in a thoughtful letter from Galiani to Madame d'Epinay. The man of “modern ideas”, that conceited ape, is profoundly dissatisfied with himself: this much is certain. He suffers, and his vanity wants him only “to suffer with his fellows”.

223. The mixed European, on the whole a fairly ugly plebeian, absolutely needs a costume. He needs history as a wardrobe. Admittedly, he notices that none of the costumes fits properly, and keeps changing, changing. Consider the nineteenth century's hurried preferences and alterations in its masquerades of style, and also its desperate moments when “nothing suits” us. We dress up in vain as romantic, classical, Christian, Florentine, barocco, or “national”, in moribus et artibus: none of it “clothes us”! Yet the “spirit”, especially the “historical spirit”, profits even from this desperation. Again and again a new specimen of the past or the foreign is tried on, taken off, packed away, and above all studied. Ours is the first studious age in puncto of “costumes”: I mean morals, articles of faith, artistic tastes, and religions. We are prepared as no previous age has been for a carnival on the grand scale, for the most spiritual festival of laughter and arrogance, for the transcendent height of supreme folly and Aristophanic mockery of the world. Perhaps this is where we are still discovering our own field of invention, where even we can still be original: probably as parodists of world history and God's Merry-Andrews. Perhaps, even if nothing else in the present has a future, our laughter itself will have one!

224. The historical sense is the ability to divine quickly the order of rank among the valuations by which a people, community, or individual has lived. It is a “divining instinct” for the relationships between these valuations, and between their authority and that of the forces at work. This historical sense, which we Europeans claim as our special gift, came to us in the wake of the enchanting, mad semi-barbarism into which Europe's democratic mixing of classes and races plunged it. Only the nineteenth century recognized this faculty as its sixth sense. Through that mixture, the past of every form and manner of life, of cultures once closely adjoining and layered over one another, pours into us “modern souls”. Our instincts now reach backward in every direction; we ourselves are a kind of chaos. In the end, as I have said, the spirit discovers its advantage in this. Our semi-barbarism of body and desire gives us secret access everywhere, access no noble age ever possessed. Above all it admits us to the labyrinth of unfinished civilizations and to every kind of semi-barbarism that has existed on earth. Since by far the greater part of human civilization so far has itself been semi-barbarism, the “historical sense” amounts almost to a sense and instinct for everything, a taste and tongue for everything. This immediately shows it to be an IGNOBLE sense. For instance, we enjoy Homer again. Perhaps our happiest acquisition is knowing how to appreciate Homer, whom people of distinguished culture could not and cannot so easily make their own, and scarcely permitted themselves to enjoy. Think of seventeenth-century Frenchmen such as Saint-Evremond, who reproached him for his ESPRIT VASTE, or even Voltaire, that century's last echo. Their palate's decisive Yes and No, their ready disgust, their hesitant reluctance towards anything unfamiliar, their horror of the bad taste even of lively curiosity, and the general unwillingness of every distinguished, self-sufficient culture to admit a new desire, dissatisfaction with its own condition, or admiration for something strange—all this prejudices them even against the world's finest things if those things are not their property or cannot become their prey. No faculty is less intelligible to such people than this historical sense with its servile, plebeian curiosity. Shakespeare presents the same case: that marvellous Spanish-Moorish-Saxon synthesis of taste would have made an ancient Athenian from AEschylus' circle half die of laughter or annoyance. Yet we welcome precisely this wild mixture of colours, this blending of the most delicate, coarse, and artificial, with secret trust and warmth. We enjoy it as an artistic refinement reserved especially for us. We let the repulsive fumes and the closeness of the English populace, in which Shakespeare's art and taste live, trouble us as little as they might on the Chiaja in Naples. There, with every sense awake, we willingly walk on enchanted, despite the smell of drains from the town's lower quarters. We people of the “historical sense” undeniably have our virtues: we are unassuming, unselfish, modest, brave, accustomed to self-control and self-denial, very grateful, patient, and accommodating. Yet for all this we perhaps have little “taste”. Let us finally admit what we find hardest to grasp, feel, taste, and love, what meets our deepest prejudice and almost our hostility: precisely the perfection and final ripeness of every culture and art. It is the essentially noble in works and people, their moment of calm seas and serene self-sufficiency, the golden quality and coolness of everything that has perfected itself. Perhaps our great virtue, the historical sense, necessarily conflicts with GOOD taste, at least with the very bad taste. We can summon up within ourselves only imperfectly, hesitantly, and by force those small, brief, happy gifts and glorifications of human life that shine here and there. I mean those marvellous moments and experiences when a great power voluntarily stops before the limitless and infinite, when an overflowing refined delight is enjoyed through a sudden halt and hardening, through standing firm and planting oneself on still-trembling ground. Let us confess that PROPORTION is foreign to us. What really itches in us is a craving for the infinite, the immeasurable. Like a rider on a horse panting to press forward, we modern people, we semi-barbarians, drop the reins before the infinite. OUR greatest bliss comes only when we—ARE IN THE GREATEST DANGER.

225. Whether called hedonism, pessimism, utilitarianism, or eudaemonism, every way of thinking that measures things' value by PLEASURE and PAIN—that is, by accompanying circumstances and secondary considerations—is a plausible-looking naivety. Anyone conscious of CREATIVE powers and an artist's conscience will look down on these ways of thinking with contempt, though not without sympathy. Sympathy for you! Certainly not sympathy as you understand it: not sympathy for social “distress”, for “society” and its sick and unfortunate, for the hereditarily vicious and defective lying around us on the ground. Still less is it sympathy for the grumbling, angry, revolutionary slave classes striving for power, which they call “freedom”. OUR sympathy is higher and sees further: we see how MAN makes himself smaller, how YOU make him smaller! There are moments when YOUR sympathy fills us with indescribable anguish, when we resist it and find your seriousness more dangerous than any frivolity. You want, if possible—and no “if possible” could be more foolish—TO ABOLISH SUFFERING. And we? It really seems that WE would rather increase suffering and make it worse than ever! Well-being as you understand it is certainly no goal; to us it looks like an END, a condition that immediately makes humanity ridiculous and contemptible, and its destruction DESIRABLE! The discipline of suffering, of GREAT suffering—don't you know that THIS discipline alone has produced every elevation of humanity so far? The soul's tension under misfortune gives it energy; it shudders before ruin, invents and shows courage in undergoing, enduring, interpreting, and using misfortune. Whatever depth, mystery, disguise, spirit, ingenuity, or greatness the soul has received—hasn't it received these through suffering, through the discipline of great suffering? In the human being, CREATURE and CREATOR are joined. There is matter, fragments, excess, clay, mud, folly, and chaos; but there is also the creator, the sculptor, the hammer's hardness, the spectator's divinity, and the seventh day. Do you understand this opposition? Do you understand that YOUR sympathy for the “creature in man” concerns what must be shaped, bruised, forged, stretched, roasted, annealed, and refined—what necessarily must SUFFER and IS INTENDED to suffer? And our sympathy—don't you understand the object of our OPPOSITE sympathy, when it resists yours as the worst kind of pampering and weakening? So it is sympathy AGAINST sympathy! But let me repeat: there are higher problems than pleasure, pain, and sympathy, and every philosophy concerned only with these is naive.

226. WE IMMORALISTS.—The world that concerns US, where we must fear and love, is almost invisible and inaudible: a world of delicate commands and delicate obedience, of “almost” in every respect, exacting, treacherous, sharp, and tender. Yes, it is well protected against clumsy spectators and intrusive curiosity! We are woven into a strong net and garment of duties from which we CANNOT free ourselves. Precisely here, even we are “men of duty”! Sometimes, admittedly, we dance in our “chains” and between our “swords”. More often, however, we grind our teeth in these circumstances and grow impatient with the hidden harshness of our lot. Yet whatever we do, fools and appearances say of us, “These men have NO duties.” Fools and appearances are always against us!

227. Honesty: suppose that is the virtue we free spirits cannot shake off. Well, we will work on it with all our perversity and love, never tiring of “perfecting” ourselves in OUR one remaining virtue. May its gaze one day spread like a golden-blue, mocking twilight over this ageing civilization and its dull, gloomy seriousness! And if our honesty should one day tire, sigh, stretch its limbs, find us too hard, and wish for something more pleasant, easy, and gentle, like an agreeable vice, let us remain HARD, we latest Stoics. Let us send every devilish thing in us to help it: our disgust at clumsiness and vagueness, our “NITIMUR IN VETITUM”, our love of adventure, our sharp and fastidious curiosity, our subtlest, most disguised intellectual Will to Power and universal conquest, greedily roaming through all the territories of the future. Let us bring all our “devils” to the aid of our “God”! People will probably misunderstand and misjudge us for this: what does it matter! They will say, “Their ‘honesty’ is nothing but their devilry!” What does it matter! Even if they were right, haven't all gods so far been devils sanctified and baptized anew? After all, what do we know about ourselves? What do we know about what the spirit guiding us wants TO BE CALLED? It is a question of names. Or about how many spirits we shelter? We free spirits must take care that our honesty does not become our vanity, our ornament and showpiece, our limitation, our stupidity! Every virtue tends towards stupidity, every stupidity towards virtue. “Stupid to the point of sanctity”, they say in Russia. Let us beware of becoming saints and bores out of sheer honesty! Isn't life a hundred times too short for us to bore ourselves? One would have to believe in eternal life in order to...

228. I hope I may be forgiven for discovering that all moral philosophy so far has been tedious and belongs among the aids to sleep. In my view, NOTHING has harmed “virtue” MORE than the TEDIOUSNESS of its advocates. Nevertheless, I would not overlook their general usefulness. It is desirable that as few people as possible should think about morals, and consequently highly desirable that morals should never become interesting! But we needn't worry! Things today remain as they always were. I see nobody in Europe who has, or REVEALS, any idea that philosophizing about morals could be dangerous, tricky, and ensnaring, that it could involve DISASTER. Look, for example, at those tireless, unavoidable English utilitarians: how ponderously and respectably they stalk along—a Homeric image would express it better—in Bentham's footsteps, just as he had stalked after the respectable Helvetius! No, Helvetius was no dangerous man, that CE SENATEUR POCOCURANTE, to borrow Galiani's phrase. There is no new thought, no finer turn or better expression of an old thought, not even a proper history of earlier thinking on the subject. Taken altogether, it is an IMPOSSIBLE literature unless one knows how to season it with mischief. The old English vice called CANT, or MORAL TARTUFFISM, has in fact crept into these moralists too, this time disguised as the scientific spirit. If one MUST read them, one must certainly keep an eye on their motives. Nor do they lack a secret struggle with pangs of conscience, which descendants of Puritans must naturally suffer throughout their scientific tinkering with morals. Isn't a moralist the opposite of a Puritan, after all: a thinker who regards morality as questionable, worthy of interrogation, in short as a problem? Isn't moralizing immoral? Ultimately they all want English morality accepted as authoritative because this would best serve humanity, or “general utility”, or “the happiness of the greatest number”—no! the happiness of ENGLAND. By every means they want to persuade themselves that pursuing English happiness—COMFORT and FASHION, and at the highest level a seat in Parliament—is also the true path of virtue. Indeed, they would have it that all virtue the world has known consisted precisely in that pursuit. None of these ponderous, conscience-stricken herd animals, who advocate egoism as a means to general welfare, wants to know or even suspect that “general welfare” is no ideal, goal, or comprehensible concept, but merely a nostrum. What is fair to one MAY NOT be fair to another; demanding one morality for everyone actually harms higher people. In short, there are DIFFERENCES OF RANK between people, and therefore between moralities. These English utilitarians are an unassuming, fundamentally mediocre breed, and, as I said, insofar as they bore us, their usefulness cannot be valued too highly. We should even ENCOURAGE them, as these verses partly attempt: Hail, you worthy barrow-wheelers, Ever “longer—better” dealers, Stiffer still in head and knee; Never thrilled and never jesting, Mediocrity unending, SANS GENIE ET SANS ESPRIT!

229. These later ages may pride themselves on their humanity, but they retain so much fear, so much SUPERSTITION born of fear, of the “cruel wild beast” whose conquest is their particular boast, that even obvious truths have long gone unspoken, as if centuries had agreed to silence them. Such truths seem to help revive the beast supposedly killed at last. Perhaps I take a risk by letting one escape. Let others catch it again and feed it enough “milk of pious sentiment” [FOOTNOTE: An expression from Schiller's William Tell, Act IV, Scene 3.] to make it lie quietly, forgotten, in its old corner. We must learn about cruelty afresh and open our eyes; we must finally learn impatience, so that such shameless, gross errors as ancient and modern philosophers have fostered about tragedy can no longer parade around virtuously and boldly. Almost everything we call “higher culture” rests on making CRUELTY more spiritual and more intense: that is my thesis. The “wild beast” has not been killed at all; it lives and flourishes, and has merely been transfigured. Cruelty constitutes tragedy's painful pleasure. Whatever pleases us in so-called tragic sympathy, and underlies everything sublime, right up to the highest and most delicate thrills of metaphysics, draws its sweetness solely from the cruelty mixed into it. Think of the Roman in the arena, the Christian in the ecstasies of the cross, the Spaniard watching the fire and stake or a bullfight, today's Japanese spectator pushing his way into a tragedy, the worker in the Paris suburbs yearning for bloody revolutions, the Wagnerienne whose will comes unhinged as she “undergoes” “Tristan and Isolde”. What they all enjoy, what they strive with mysterious passion to drink in, is the love-potion of that great Circe, “cruelty”. Here we must entirely set aside the blundering psychology of earlier times, which could teach only that cruelty originated in seeing OTHERS suffer. There is abundant, overflowing enjoyment in one's own suffering too, and in making oneself suffer. Wherever people have been persuaded to deny themselves in the RELIGIOUS sense, or to mutilate themselves, like the Phoenicians and ascetics, or more generally to strip away sensuality and flesh and practise contrition, Puritan spasms of repentance, vivisection of conscience, or Pascal-like SACRIFIZIA DELL' INTELLETO, cruelty secretly entices and drives them onward. It is the dangerous thrill of cruelty TOWARDS THEMSELVES. Finally, consider that even the seeker of knowledge acts as an artist and glorifier of cruelty, compelling his spirit to perceive AGAINST its own inclination and often against his heart's wishes. He forces it to say No where he would like to affirm, love, and adore. Indeed, every profound, fundamental examination of something violates and deliberately injures the spirit's fundamental will, which instinctively seeks appearances and surfaces. Even every desire for knowledge contains a drop of cruelty.

230. Perhaps my reference to a “fundamental will of the spirit” needs more detail to be understood; allow me a word of explanation. That commanding something popularly called “the spirit” wants to rule both inside and outside itself, and to feel that it rules. It has the will to make simplicity from multiplicity, a binding, taming, commanding will, essentially a will to rule. Its needs and abilities here are the same as those physiologists attribute to everything that lives, grows, and reproduces. The spirit's power to appropriate what is foreign shows itself in a strong tendency to assimilate the new to the old, simplify the manifold, and overlook or reject outright contradictions. In the same way, it arbitrarily underlines, emphasizes, and falsifies particular features and outlines in foreign material, in every piece of the “outside world”. Its aim is to incorporate new “experiences”, to fit new things into old arrangements: in short, growth—or, more precisely, the FEELING of growth, the feeling of increased power. The same will employs an apparently opposite impulse: a sudden preference for ignorance, an arbitrary exclusion, the shutting of windows, an inner refusal of this or that, a prohibition on approach. It takes a defensive attitude towards much that could be known, content with darkness and a confining horizon, accepting and approving ignorance. All this is necessary according to the degree of its power to appropriate, its “digestive power”, metaphorically speaking. In fact, “the spirit” resembles a stomach more than anything else. Here too belongs its occasional inclination to let itself be deceived, perhaps with a sly suspicion that things are NOT as they appear but are merely being allowed to pass that way. It delights in uncertainty and ambiguity, rejoices in arbitrary, eccentric narrowness and mystery, in what is too close, in the foreground, in enlargement, reduction, distortion, and beautification. It enjoys the arbitrariness of all these displays of power. Finally, there is the spirit's conscientious readiness to deceive other spirits and put on a show before them: the constant pressure and striving of a creative, shaping, changeable power. The spirit enjoys its cunning and its many disguises, and the security they give it. Precisely its Protean arts protect and conceal it best! AGAINST this inclination towards appearances, simplification, disguise, covering—in short, towards an outside, since every outside is a covering—works the sublime tendency of the seeker of knowledge. He takes things deeply, from many sides, thoroughly, and INSISTS on doing so. This is a kind of cruelty in intellectual conscience and taste, which every courageous thinker will acknowledge in himself, provided he has, as he should, spent enough time sharpening and hardening his eye for self-examination, and is accustomed to severe discipline and even severe words. He will say, “There is something cruel in the direction my spirit takes.” Let the virtuous and kindly try to convince him otherwise! Admittedly it would sound more agreeable if people spoke, whispered, and sang praises of our “extravagant honesty” instead of our cruelty—we free, VERY free spirits. Perhaps THAT will indeed become our posthumous glory one day! Meanwhile, since there is plenty of time until then, we should be the last to dress ourselves in this flowery, fringed moral language. All our previous work has made us sick of that taste and its lively extravagance. They are lovely, glittering, jingling, festive words: honesty, love of truth, love of wisdom, sacrifice for knowledge, the truthful person's heroism. Something in them swells the heart with pride. Yet we hermits and marmots long ago convinced ourselves, in all the secrecy of a hermit's conscience, that this worthy verbal parade also belongs among the old false decorations, frippery, and gold dust of unconscious human vanity. Beneath these flattering colours and fresh paint, the terrible original text HOMO NATURA must again be recognized. In practice, we must translate humanity back into nature; master all the vain, visionary interpretations and subsidiary meanings scratched and daubed over the eternal original text, HOMO NATURA; and ensure that human beings henceforth face human beings as, hardened by scientific discipline, they now face nature's OTHER forms. With fearless Oedipus-eyes and stopped Ulysses-ears, they must be deaf to the lures of the old metaphysical bird-catchers who have piped far too long, “You are more! You are higher! Your origin is different!” This may be a strange, foolish task, but who can deny that it is a TASK! Why did we choose this foolish task? Or, to ask it differently, “Why knowledge at all?” Everyone will ask us this. Pressed in this way, we who have asked ourselves the question a hundred times have found, and can find, no better answer....

231. Learning changes us. As physiologists know, it does what all nourishment does when it does more than merely “preserve”. Yet at the bottom of our souls, quite “down below”, there is certainly something that cannot be taught: a granite mass of spiritual fate, of predetermined decisions and answers to predetermined, selected questions. In every fundamental problem an unchanging “I am this” speaks. A thinker cannot learn afresh about man and woman, for example; he can only learn completely, following to its end what is already “fixed” about them within him. Occasionally we discover solutions to problems that become strong beliefs for us; perhaps from then on we call them “convictions”. Later we see them merely as steps towards self-knowledge, signposts to the problem we ourselves ARE—or, more precisely, to the great stupidity we embody, our spiritual fate, the UNTEACHABLE in us, quite “down below”. Having just paid myself this generous compliment, perhaps I may more readily be permitted to state some truths about “woman as she is”, provided everyone understands from the outset how literally these are merely—MY truths.

232. Woman wants independence, and therefore begins to enlighten men about “woman as she is”. THIS is one of the worst developments in Europe's general DISFIGUREMENT. What must these clumsy attempts at feminine scientific inquiry and self-exposure bring to light! Woman has so much to be ashamed of. She conceals so much pedantry, superficiality, schoolmasterliness, petty presumption, lack of restraint, and indiscretion—just study her behaviour towards children! Until now, FEAR of man has really kept these things most effectively restrained and governed. Alas, if the “eternally tedious in woman”—of which she has plenty!—is ever allowed out! If she begins, radically and on principle, to unlearn her wisdom and art: charming, playing, frightening sorrow away, relieving burdens and taking things lightly; if she forgets her delicate gift for agreeable desires! Women's voices are already rising which, by Saint Aristophanes! make one afraid. With medical explicitness they threaten us with an account of what woman REQUIRES from man, first and last. Isn't it the very worst taste for woman to set herself up as scientific in this way? Fortunately enlightenment has so far been men's business and men's gift: in it we remained “among ourselves”. Ultimately, considering everything women write about “woman”, we may well doubt whether woman really WANTS enlightenment about herself, or CAN want it. Unless she is seeking a new ORNAMENT for herself—and surely ornament belongs to the eternally feminine?—she wants to make herself feared, perhaps to gain mastery. But she does not want truth: what does woman care about truth? From the outset nothing is more alien, repellent, or hostile to her than truth. Falsehood is her great art, appearance and beauty her chief concern. Let us men admit it: this very art and instinct are what we honour and love in woman. We have the hard task, and gladly relax among beings whose hands, glances, and delicate follies make our seriousness, gravity, and depth seem almost foolish to us. Finally, I ask: has any woman herself ever acknowledged depth in a woman's mind or justice in a woman's heart? Isn't it true that, on the whole, woman herself has so far despised “woman” most, rather than we men? We want woman to stop compromising herself by enlightening us. Likewise, men's care and consideration for woman lay behind the church's decree, mulier taceat in ecclesia. It benefited woman when Napoleon made the excessively eloquent Madame de Stael understand, mulier taceat in politicis! In my opinion, a true friend of woman is whoever calls out to women today, mulier taceat de mulierel.

233. When a woman invokes Madame Roland, Madame de Stael, or Monsieur George Sand as if this proved something in favour of “woman as she is”, she reveals corrupted instincts as well as bad taste. To men, these are the three comical women as they are—nothing more! Indeed, they are the best unintentional arguments against women's emancipation and independence.

234. Stupidity in the kitchen; woman as cook; the appalling thoughtlessness with which the family and master of the house are fed! Woman does not understand what food means, yet insists on doing the cooking! Had woman been a thinking creature, her thousands of years as cook should surely have led her to discover the most important physiological facts and take possession of the art of healing as well! Bad female cooks, the complete absence of reason in the kitchen, have delayed and obstructed humanity's development longer than anything else. Even today things are scarcely better. A word for High School girls.

235. Certain turns and flights of imagination, certain sentences, little handfuls of words, suddenly crystallize a whole culture, a whole society. One is Madame de Lambert's passing remark to her son: “MON AMI, NE VOUS PERMETTEZ JAMAIS QUE DES FOLIES, QUI VOUS FERONT GRAND PLAISIR”. Incidentally, no remark ever addressed to a son was more motherly or more wise.

236. I am certain every noble woman will reject what Dante and Goethe believed about woman: Dante when he sang, “ELLA GUARDAVA SUSO, ED IO IN LEI”, and Goethe when he interpreted it as “the eternally feminine draws us ALOFT”. For THIS is exactly what she believes about the eternally masculine. 237. SEVEN APOPHTHEGMS FOR WOMEN Even endless boredom flees When a man falls to our knees! Age, alas! and sober learning Help weak virtue keep from turning. Dark attire and silence sweet: Every lady's dress—discreet. Who deserves my thanks for bliss? God!—and she who sewed me this! Young, a cave with flowers arrayed; Old, a dragon leaves its shade. Noble title, handsome leg, And a man: for HIM I'd beg! Few words, much sense in their mass—Slippery ground for the she-ass! 237A. Until now men have treated women like birds that have lost their way and flown down among them from above: as delicate, fragile, wild, strange, sweet, and enlivening creatures, but also creatures that must be caged to keep them from flying away.

238. To misunderstand the fundamental problem of “man and woman”, deny its deepest antagonism and the need for an eternally hostile tension, perhaps dream instead of equal rights, equal education, equal claims and obligations, is a TYPICAL sign of a shallow mind. A thinker who proves shallow at this dangerous point—shallow in his instincts!—should generally arouse suspicion. More than that, he has given himself away and been found out. He will probably prove too “short” for every fundamental question of life, present or future, unable to descend into ANY of its depths. A man with depth both in spirit and in desire, however, who also possesses that deep benevolence capable of severity and harshness and easily mistaken for them, can think about woman only as ORIENTALS do. He must regard her as a possession, as property to be confined, as a being destined for service who fulfils her purpose in it.
