On this matter he must take his stand on Asia's immense rationality and superior instinct, as the Greeks once did. Those finest heirs and pupils of Asia, as everyone knows, gradually became STRICTER towards woman—in short, more Oriental—as their culture and power INCREASED from Homer to Pericles. Let us consider for ourselves HOW necessary, HOW logical, even HOW desirable in humane terms this was!

239. Men have never treated the weaker sex with as much respect as they do today. Like disrespect for old age, this belongs to democracy's basic tendency and taste. Is it surprising that this respect is immediately abused? Women want more and learn to make demands; eventually the tribute of respect feels almost irritating. They would prefer a contest over rights, even outright conflict. In a word, woman is losing her modesty. Let us immediately add that she is losing her taste as well. She is unlearning her FEAR of man; but the woman who “unlearns fear” sacrifices her most womanly instincts. It is reasonable and understandable enough that woman should venture forward when man's fear-inspiring quality—or, more precisely, the MAN in man—is no longer wanted or fully developed. Harder to understand is that precisely through this, woman deteriorates. This is happening today: let us not deceive ourselves! Wherever the industrial spirit has defeated the military and aristocratic spirit, woman seeks a clerk's economic and legal independence. “Woman as clerkess” stands above the entrance to the modern society now taking shape. As she claims new rights, aspires to become “master”, and writes woman's “progress” on her flags and banners, the opposite happens with terrible clarity: WOMAN GOES BACKWARD. Since the French Revolution, woman's influence in Europe has DECLINED in proportion to the growth of her rights and demands. Thus “the emancipation of woman”, insofar as women themselves want and demand it, rather than merely shallow-headed men, proves a remarkable symptom of the increasing weakness and deadening of the most womanly instincts. There is STUPIDITY in this movement, an almost masculine stupidity of which a well-brought-up woman—always a sensible woman—might be thoroughly ashamed. She loses her intuition for the ground on which she can most surely win; neglects practice with her own weapons; lets herself go before man, perhaps even “to the book”, where she once kept herself controlled and displayed refined, artful humility. With her virtuous audacity she destroys man's belief in a VEILED, fundamentally different ideal in woman, something eternally, necessarily feminine. Loudly and at length she argues him out of believing that woman must be preserved, cared for, protected, and indulged like a delicate, strangely wild, often agreeable domestic animal. She clumsily and indignantly collects everything resembling servitude and bondage that woman's place in the existing social order has entailed and still entails—as though slavery were a counterargument rather than a condition of every higher culture, every elevation of culture. What does all this signify except the breaking down of womanly instincts, a defeminization? Certainly the learned asses of the male sex include plenty of foolish friends and corrupters of woman. They advise her to strip herself of femininity in this way and imitate all the stupidities afflicting “man” in Europe, European “manliness”. They would lower woman to “general culture”, even to reading newspapers and interfering in politics. Here and there they even want to turn women into free spirits and literary workers, as though a woman without piety would not seem perfectly repulsive or ridiculous to a profound, godless man. Almost everywhere the most morbid and dangerous kind of music, our newest German music, is ruining her nerves, making her more hysterical by the day and less able to perform her first and last function: bearing strong children. They want to “cultivate” her still further in general, intending, as they say, to make the “weaker sex” STRONG through culture. As if history did not teach emphatically that humanity's “cultivation” and weakening—the weakening, dispersal, and languishing of its FORCE OF WILL—have always advanced together. As if the world's most powerful and influential women, and finally Napoleon's mother, owed their power and ascendancy over men to schoolmasters rather than to their strength of will. What inspires respect in woman, and often fear, is her NATURE, more “natural” than man's: her genuinely carnivorous, cunning flexibility, her tiger claws under the glove, her NAIVETE in selfishness, her inability to be trained and her innate wildness, the incomprehensibility, scope, and waywardness of her desires and virtues. What stirs sympathy despite our fear for that dangerous, beautiful cat, “woman”, is her seeming more afflicted, vulnerable, hungry for love, and condemned to disillusionment than any other creature. Fear and sympathy: with these feelings man has so far stood before woman, always with one foot already in tragedy, which tears us apart while delighting us. What? Is all this now to end? Is woman's DISENCHANTMENT under way? Is woman's tediousness slowly emerging? Oh Europe! Europe! We know the horned animal that has always attracted you most, from which danger repeatedly threatens you! Your old fable might become “history” once again: an immense stupidity might once more overpower you and carry you off! And no god hidden underneath it—no! Just an “idea”, a “modern idea”!

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — Peoples and Countries
paragraphs: 240. I HEARD Richard Wagner's overture to the Mastersinger again, as though for the first time. It is a magnificent, sumptuous, heavy work of late art, proud enough to assume that two centuries of music remain alive in its listeners if they are to understand it. It honours the Germans that this pride was justified! What flavours and powers, what seasons and climates mingle here! At one moment it strikes us as ancient, at another as foreign, bitter, and too modern. It is as wilful as it is grandly traditional, often mischievous, more often rough and coarse. It has fire and courage, yet also the loose, brownish skin of fruit that ripens too late. It flows broadly and fully; suddenly an inexplicable hesitation appears, like a gap opening between cause and effect, an oppressive dreaminess, almost a nightmare. Already, though, the old stream of pleasure widens again, pleasure in its many forms, old and new happiness. ESPECIALLY present is the artist's delight in himself, which he refuses to hide: his astonished, happy awareness of mastering the devices he uses here, the new, newly acquired, incompletely tested artistic devices he seems to reveal to us. Yet taken altogether there is no beauty, no South, none of the delicate clarity of southern skies, no grace, no dance, scarcely any desire for logic. There is even a certain clumsiness, deliberately emphasized, as if the artist were saying, “It is part of my intention”. Heavy drapery, something wilfully barbaric and ceremonial, a fluttering of learned, venerable conceits and jokes: something German in the word's best and worst senses, something in the German manner, many-sided, shapeless, inexhaustible. A certain German strength and overflowing fullness of soul is unafraid to conceal itself beneath the RAFFINEMENTS of decadence, and perhaps feels most at home there. It is a true, genuine sign of the German soul, simultaneously young and old, overripe yet still too rich in possibilities for the future. This music best expresses what I think of the Germans: they belong to the day before yesterday and the day after tomorrow—THEY HAVE NO TODAY YET.

241. We “good Europeans” also have hours when we allow ourselves warm-hearted patriotism, a plunge back into old loves and narrow views—I have just supplied an example. We have hours of national excitement, patriotic anguish, and every other old-fashioned flood of feeling. What runs its course in us within hours may take duller spirits a considerable time to finish with: half a year for some, half a lifetime for others, according to the speed and strength of their digestion and “change of material”. Indeed, I can imagine sluggish, hesitant races that, even in our fast-moving Europe, would need half a century to overcome such ancestral attacks of patriotism and attachment to the soil, and return to reason—that is, to “good Europeanism”. While considering this possibility, I happened to overhear two old patriots talking. Evidently both were hard of hearing, and therefore spoke all the louder. “HE possesses about as much philosophy, and knows about as much of it, as a peasant or a corps-student,” said one. “He is still innocent. But what does that matter today! This is the age of the masses: they prostrate themselves before everything massive. The same holds in politicis. They call a statesman ‘great’ if he builds them a new Tower of Babel, some monstrous empire and power. What do they care that we more cautious, conservative people still hold the old belief that only a great thought makes an action or undertaking great? Suppose a statesman forced his people henceforth to practise ‘high politics’, for which nature had poorly equipped and prepared them, so that they had to sacrifice their old, dependable virtues for the love of a new and doubtful mediocrity. Suppose he condemned his people to ‘practise politics’ altogether, when they had previously had better things to do and think about, and had never been able to shake off, deep in their souls, a sensible disgust at the restlessness, emptiness, and noisy quarrels of essentially political nations. Suppose he stirred his people's sleeping passions and greed, made their former reserve and love of standing apart into a disgrace, their exotic character and hidden persistence into an offence, disparaged their deepest inclinations, overturned their consciences, narrowed their minds, and made their tastes ‘national’—what! A statesman who did all this, for which his people would have to do penance throughout their future, if they had a future, would be GREAT, would he?” “Certainly!” the other old patriot answered fiercely. “Otherwise he COULD NOT have done it! Perhaps wanting such a thing was madness! But perhaps everything great began in just that kind of madness!” “Abuse of language!” his companion shouted back. “Strong! Strong! Strong and mad! NOT great!” The old men had plainly grown heated, shouting their “truths” into each other's faces. Happy and apart, I reflected on how soon someone stronger might master the strong, and on the compensation for one nation's intellectual shallowness: the deepening of another.

242. Whether we call what now distinguishes the European “civilization”, “humanization”, or “progress”, or simply use the political formula of Europe's DEMOCRATIC movement without praise or blame, an immense PHYSIOLOGICAL PROCESS goes on behind the moral and political foreground these formulas indicate. Europeans increasingly grow alike; they increasingly detach themselves from the climatic and hereditary conditions in which unified races arise; they increasingly become independent of any particular environment that would impose the same demands on body and soul for centuries. In other words, an essentially SUPER-NATIONAL, nomadic human type slowly emerges, whose typical distinction, physiologically speaking, is the highest degree of skill and power in adaptation. Great setbacks may slow the TEMPO of this process of the EUROPEAN'S EVOLUTION, yet perhaps they will only increase its force and depth. The still-raging storm of “national feeling” belongs among these, as does the anarchism now appearing. This process will probably produce results its naive promoters and enthusiasts, the apostles of “modern ideas”, would least like to anticipate. The new conditions that, on average, level human beings into mediocrity—useful, industrious, clever herd people capable of many services—are also extraordinarily suited to producing exceptional people with the most dangerous and attractive qualities. Adaptability, daily testing changing circumstances and beginning new work with every generation, almost every decade, prevents the type from becoming POWERFUL. The collective impression of these future Europeans will probably be of numerous, talkative, weak-willed, very handy workers who NEED a master and commander as they need their daily bread. Thus Europe's democratization will tend to produce a type prepared for SLAVERY in the subtlest sense. Yet in individual, exceptional cases, the STRONG person will necessarily become stronger and richer than perhaps ever before, because of an unprejudiced education and an immense variety of practice, skills, and disguises. What I meant to say is that Europe's democratization also involuntarily prepares the breeding of TYRANTS—taking that word in every sense, including its most spiritual.

243. I am pleased to hear that our sun is travelling rapidly towards the constellation Hercules, and I hope the people of this earth will follow its example. And we good Europeans should lead the way!

244. Germans were once commonly singled out as “deep”. But now the most successful type of new Germanism hungers for quite different honours, perhaps finding everything deep deficient in “smartness”. It is almost timely and patriotic to wonder whether that old compliment deceived us: whether German depth is really something else and something worse, something we are, thank God, about to shed successfully. Let us therefore learn anew about German depth. All we need is a little vivisection of the German soul. Above all, that soul is multiple, varied in origin, piled up and layered rather than actually built: its ancestry accounts for this. A German bold enough to declare, “Two souls, alas, live in my breast”, would guess the truth badly—or, more precisely, fall far short of the true number of souls. The Germans are a people formed from an extraordinary mixing and mingling of races, perhaps even predominantly pre-Aryan; they are the “people of the centre” in every sense. Consequently they are more elusive, expansive, contradictory, unknown, incalculable, surprising, and even frightening to themselves than other peoples are. They evade DEFINITION, and that alone drives the French to despair. It IS characteristic of Germans that the question “What is German?” never dies among them. Kotzebue certainly knew his Germans well enough: “We are known”, they cried to him triumphantly—but Sand also thought he knew them. Jean Paul knew what he was doing when he expressed outrage at Fichte's dishonest but patriotic flatteries and exaggerations. Yet Goethe probably thought differently about the Germans from Jean Paul, even though he agreed with him about Fichte. What did Goethe really think about the Germans? On many matters around him he never spoke plainly, and throughout his life he knew how to maintain a shrewd silence, probably with good reason. Certainly neither the “Wars of Independence” nor the French Revolution made him look up with greater joy. The event that led him to RECONSTRUCT his “Faust”, and indeed the whole problem of “man”, was Napoleon's appearance. In some remarks Goethe condemns what Germans pride themselves on with impatient severity, as though speaking from abroad. He once defined the famous German cast of mind as “Indulgence towards its own and others' weaknesses”. Was he wrong? One characteristic of Germans is that people are seldom entirely wrong about them. The German soul contains passages, galleries, caves, hiding places, and dungeons. Its disorder has much of mystery's charm; the German knows the side roads to chaos well. Since everything loves its symbol, he loves clouds and everything obscure, developing, twilight-like, damp, and veiled. Whatever is uncertain, unfinished, shifting, and growing seems “deep” to him. The German himself does not EXIST: he is BECOMING, he is “developing himself”. Hence “development” is the specifically German discovery and success among philosophical formulas, a ruling idea that, together with German beer and music, works to Germanize all Europe. Foreigners are astonished and attracted by the riddles posed by the contradictory character at the German soul's base—riddles Hegel systematized and Richard Wagner finally set to music. “Good-natured and spiteful”: this combination, absurd for any other people, is unfortunately justified all too often in Germany. One need only live among Swabians for a while to know it! The German scholar's clumsiness and social unpleasantness fit alarmingly well with his physical tightrope-dancing and nimble daring, which all the gods have learned to fear. Anyone wanting the “German soul” demonstrated ad oculos need only look at German taste, arts, and manners: what boorish indifference to “taste”! How the noblest and commonest sit side by side! How disordered and rich this soul's whole constitution is! The German DRAGS his soul along; he drags everything he experiences. He digests events badly and never gets “finished” with them. German depth often amounts merely to difficult, hesitant “digestion”. Just as all chronic invalids and dyspeptics like convenience, the German loves “frankness” and “honesty”: being frank and honest is so CONVENIENT! This trustfulness, accommodation, and laying of cards on the table, this German HONESTY, is probably the most dangerous and successful disguise the German now knows. It is his particular Mephistophelean art; with it he can “still achieve much”! The German lets himself go and gazes out with faithful, blue, empty German eyes—and other countries immediately mistake him for his dressing gown! What I meant was this: whatever “German depth” may be, and perhaps among ourselves we take the liberty of laughing at it, we would do well to keep honouring its appearance and reputation. We should not trade our old reputation as a profound people too cheaply for Prussian “smartness” and Berlin wit and sand. It is wise for a people to pose, and LET itself be taken, as deep, clumsy, good-natured, honest, and foolish. Doing so might even be—profound! Finally, let us honour our name: we are not called the “TIUSCHE VOLK”, the deceptive people, for nothing....

245. The “good old” age is gone; it sang itself to an end in Mozart. How fortunate WE are that his ROCOCO still speaks to us, that his “good company”, tender enthusiasm, childlike pleasure in Chinese things and their flourishes, courtesy of heart, longing for elegance, love, light steps and tears, and faith in the South can still appeal to SOMETHING REMAINING in us! Ah, one day that too will be over! But who doubts that understanding and taste for Beethoven will disappear even sooner! He was only the last echo of a break and transition in style, NOT, like Mozart, the final echo of a great European taste that had lasted for centuries. Beethoven stands between an old, mellow soul continually breaking down and a future soul, too young, always COMING. His music is covered by the twilight of eternal loss and eternal extravagant hope, the same light that bathed Europe when it dreamed with Rousseau, danced around the Revolution's Tree of Liberty, and finally almost fell down worshipping Napoleon. But how quickly THIS very feeling now fades, how hard it is today even to GRASP it. How strange to our ears is the language of Rousseau, Schiller, Shelley, and Byron, in whom TOGETHER the same European destiny could SPEAK that knew how to SING in Beethoven! All the German music that followed belongs to Romanticism, a movement historically shorter, more fleeting, and more superficial than that great interlude: Europe's transition from Rousseau to Napoleon and the rise of democracy. Weber—but what do WE care today about “Freischutz” and “Oberon”! Or Marschner's “Hans Heiling” and “Vampyre”! Or even Wagner's “Tannhauser”! This music is extinct, though not yet forgotten. Moreover, Romantic music as a whole was neither noble nor musical enough to hold its place anywhere except in the theatre and before the masses. From the beginning it was second-rate music, little esteemed by genuine musicians. Felix Mendelssohn was different, that serene master whose lighter, purer, happier soul won admiration quickly and was forgotten just as quickly: the beautiful EPISODE of German music. But Robert Schumann took things seriously and was taken seriously from the start; he was the last to establish a school. Don't we now feel satisfaction, relief, deliverance, that this very Romanticism of Schumann's has been overcome? Schumann fled into his soul's “Saxon Switzerland”, with a nature half like Werther and half like Jean Paul—certainly not like Beethoven! Certainly not like Byron! His MANFRED music is a mistake and misunderstanding amounting to an injustice. His taste was fundamentally PETTY: a dangerous inclination, doubly dangerous among Germans, towards quiet lyricism and intoxication with feelings. Always withdrawing, timidly retreating into seclusion, this noble weakling revelled only in anonymous joy and sorrow. A sort of girl and NOLI ME TANGERE from the beginning, Schumann was already merely a GERMAN event in music, no longer a European event as Beethoven had been and Mozart still more so. With Schumann, German music faced its greatest danger: LOSING ITS VOICE FOR EUROPE'S SOUL and sinking into a merely national concern.

246. Books written in German are torture for a reader with a THIRD ear! How indignantly he stands beside that slowly revolving swamp of unmusical sounds and rhythms without dance which Germans call a “book”! And consider even the German who READS books! How lazily, reluctantly, badly he reads! How many Germans know, and feel obliged to know, that every good sentence contains ART, art that must be divined to understand the sentence! Misunderstand its TEMPO, for example, and you misunderstand the sentence itself! There must be no uncertainty about the syllables determining its rhythm. A break in over-rigid symmetry should be felt as intentional and delightful. Every STACCATO and RUBATO deserves a sensitive, patient ear. One should divine meaning in the succession of vowels and diphthongs, and hear how delicately and richly their order can colour and recolour them. Which German book-reader is accommodating enough to acknowledge these duties and demands, to listen for so much art and intention in language? After all, one simply “has no ear for it”. Thus the starkest contrasts of style go unheard, and the finest artistry is virtually WASTED on the deaf. These thoughts occurred to me when I noticed how clumsily and without insight two masters of prose had been confused. One lets his words fall hesitantly and coldly, as though from the roof of a damp cave, relying on their dull sound and echo. The other handles language like a flexible sword, feeling from his arm down to his toes the dangerous delight of the trembling, over-sharp blade that longs to bite, hiss, and cut.

247. The fact that even our good musicians write badly shows how little German style concerns itself with harmony and the ear. The German does not read aloud or read for the ear; he reads only with his eyes, putting his ears away in a drawer for the occasion. In antiquity, when a man read—and that happened seldom enough—he read something to himself in a loud voice. Silent reading surprised people, who secretly searched for the reason. A loud voice meant all the swellings, inflections, changes of key, and shifts of TEMPO that delighted the ancient PUBLIC world. Written style then obeyed the same laws as spoken style. These laws depended partly on the extraordinary development and refined demands of ear and larynx, and partly on the strength, endurance, and power of ancient lungs. In the ancient sense, a period is above all a physiological whole, because it fits within one breath. Periods like those of Demosthenes and Cicero, rising twice and falling twice, all in one breath, delighted people of ANTIQUITY. Their own training taught them to appreciate the excellence, rarity, and difficulty of delivering such a period. WE modern people, short of breath in every sense, really have no right to the GREAT period! Those ancients were all amateurs in the art of speaking, and therefore connoisseurs, and therefore critics; in this way they drove their orators to the highest achievement. Similarly, in the last century, when every Italian lady and gentleman knew how to sing, virtuosity in singing, and with it the art of melody, reached its height. Germany, however, properly speaking knew only one kind of public discourse that was EVEN APPROXIMATELY artistic: the sermon. This remained so until very recently, when a kind of platform eloquence began timidly and awkwardly to flutter its young wings. Only the preacher in Germany knew the weight of a syllable or word, how a sentence strikes, leaps, rushes, flows, and closes. He alone possessed a conscience in his ears, often a bad one; there are plenty of reasons why a German so rarely attains skill in oratory, or almost always attains it too late. With good reason, therefore, German prose's masterpiece is the work of its greatest preacher: the BIBLE has so far been the best German book. Beside Luther's Bible, almost everything else is mere “literature”, something that did not grow in Germany and therefore has not taken, and does not take, root in German hearts as the Bible has.

248. There are two kinds of genius: one chiefly begets and wants to beget; the other willingly receives fertilization and gives birth. Among gifted nations, likewise, some have inherited woman's problem of pregnancy and the secret task of shaping, ripening, and perfecting. The Greeks were such a nation, and so are the French. Others must fertilize and originate new ways of life: the Jews, the Romans, and—may one ask in all modesty—the Germans? These nations are tormented and enraptured by unknown fevers, irresistibly driven beyond themselves, amorous and yearning for foreign races, for those that “allow themselves to be fertilized”. At the same time they are imperious, like everything conscious of abundant generative strength and therefore of authority “by the grace of God”. These two kinds of genius seek one another as man and woman do. And, like man and woman, they misunderstand one another as well.
249. Each nation has a “Tartuffery” of its own, which it calls its virtue. We do not know—cannot know—the best in ourselves.

250. What does Europe owe the Jews? Many things, good and bad, and above all one thing combining the best and worst: morality's grand style, the terror and majesty of infinite demands and meanings, all the Romanticism and sublimity of moral questioning. Consequently it owes them precisely the most attractive, ensnaring, exquisite element in life's shimmering colours and temptations, whose afterglow now lights the sky of European culture, its evening sky—perhaps with a dying light. For this, those of us who are artists among spectators and philosophers are—grateful to the Jews.

251. When a people suffers, and WANTS to suffer, from national nervous fever and political ambition, we must accept that clouds and disturbances will pass over its spirit—in short, little attacks of stupidity. Today's Germans, for example, alternate between anti-French folly, anti-Semitic folly, anti-Polish folly, Christian-romantic folly, Wagnerian folly, Teutonic folly, Prussian folly—just look at those poor historians, the Sybels and Treitschkes, with their tightly bandaged heads—and whatever other names these little darkenings of German spirit and conscience go by. Forgive me if I too failed to escape the disease completely during a brief, daring visit to heavily infected ground. Like everyone else, I began thinking about matters that did not concern me, the first symptom of political infection. About the Jews, for instance, listen to this. I have never yet met a German favourably disposed towards the Jews. However firmly all prudent, politically minded men reject actual anti-Semitism, perhaps their prudence and policy oppose only the feeling's dangerous excess, especially its distasteful, disgraceful expression, rather than the feeling itself. We must not deceive ourselves here. Germany has more than ENOUGH Jews; the German stomach, German blood, finds it difficult, and will long find it difficult, to deal with even this quantity of “Jew”, as Italians, Frenchmen, and Englishmen have done through stronger digestion. That is the unmistakable statement and language of a general instinct which must be heard and acted upon. “Let no more Jews enter! Close the doors, especially to the East, Austria included!” Thus commands the instinct of a people whose nature remains weak and uncertain, easily erased or extinguished by a stronger race. The Jews, however, are unquestionably the strongest, toughest, and purest race now living in Europe. They know how to succeed even under the worst conditions, indeed better than under favourable ones, through virtues of a sort people today would like to label vices. Above all, they possess a firm faith with no need to feel ashamed before “modern ideas”. WHEN they change at all, they change as the Russian Empire makes its conquests: like an empire with plenty of time, not born yesterday, following the principle “as slowly as possible”! A thinker concerned for Europe's future will count on the Jews, as on the Russians, in every view of that future, as the most reliable and probable factors in the great interplay and battle of forces. What Europe now calls a “nation” is really more RES FACTA than NATA, sometimes confusingly close to RES FICTA ET PICTA. In every case it is something developing, young, easily shifted, not yet a race, much less a race AERE PERENNUS like the Jews. Such “nations” should most carefully avoid hot-headed rivalry and hostility! Certainly the Jews COULD now gain ascendancy, indeed literal supremacy, over Europe if they wanted it, or were driven to it, as the anti-Semites seem to wish. It is equally certain that they are NOT working or planning towards that end. Instead, they now wish and desire, even somewhat insistently, to be taken into and absorbed by Europe. They long finally to settle somewhere, accepted and respected, ending nomadic life and the “wandering Jew”. We should certainly acknowledge this impulse and tendency and MEET IT HALFWAY; perhaps it signals a moderation of Jewish instincts. For that purpose it might be useful and fair to banish the anti-Semitic loudmouths from the country. We should make these approaches prudently and selectively, much as the English nobility does. Naturally, the stronger, more sharply defined types of new Germanism could enter relations with the Jews with least hesitation: for example, aristocratic officers from the Prussian border. It would be interesting in many ways to see whether a genius for money and patience, and especially some intellect and intellectuality, sadly lacking there, could be added and cultivated alongside the hereditary art of commanding and obeying, both of which already give that region a classic reputation. But here I should interrupt my festive speech and lively Teutonomania, for I have reached my SERIOUS SUBJECT: the “European problem” as I understand it, breeding a new ruling caste for Europe.

252. The English are no philosophical race. Bacon represents an ATTACK on the philosophical spirit generally; Hobbes, Hume, and Locke represent a lowering and devaluation of the idea of a “philosopher” lasting more than a century. Kant rose up and raised himself AGAINST Hume; Schelling RIGHTLY said of Locke, “JE MEPRISE LOCKE”. In opposing the English mechanical reduction of the world to stupidity, Hegel and Schopenhauer agreed, as did Goethe. Those two hostile brother-geniuses of philosophy pushed in different directions towards opposite poles of German thought, wronging each other as only brothers can. What England lacks and has always lacked was well known to Carlyle, that half-actor and rhetorician, that absurd muddlehead. His passionate grimaces tried to conceal what he knew about himself: what Carlyle LACKED—real intellectual POWER, real DEPTH of understanding, in short, philosophy. Such an unphilosophical race characteristically clings to Christianity: it NEEDS Christianity's discipline to “moralize” and humanize it. The Englishman is gloomier, more sensual, headstrong, and brutal than the German; precisely as the baser of the two, he is also the more pious. His NEED for Christianity is that much GREATER. To sensitive nostrils, English Christianity itself still carries a distinctively English smell of spleen and alcoholic excess, against which it is, for good reasons, used as an antidote: the finer poison neutralizing the coarser. For coarse-mannered people, a finer poisoning really is progress, a step towards spirituality. Christian pantomime, prayer, and psalm-singing still disguise English coarseness and rustic primness most satisfactorily—or, more accurately, explain and express them differently. As for the herd of drunkards and rakes who once learned moral grunting under Methodism, and more recently as the “Salvation Army”, a fit of repentance may indeed be the relatively highest expression of “humanity” to which they can rise. We may reasonably concede that much. Yet even the most humane Englishman offends by his lack of music, figuratively and literally. His body's and soul's movements possess neither rhythm nor dance, not even a desire for rhythm, dance, “music”. Listen to his speech; watch the most beautiful Englishwoman WALKING—nowhere on earth are there lovelier doves and swans—and finally listen to them sing! But I ask too much...

253. Some truths are best recognized by mediocre minds, being best suited to them; some truths have charm and seductive power only for mediocre spirits. We are driven to this probably unwelcome conclusion as respectable but mediocre Englishmen—Darwin, John Stuart Mill, and Herbert Spencer come to mind—begin to dominate the middle-class region of European taste. Indeed, who could doubt that it is useful for SUCH minds to prevail for a time? It would be mistaken to think highly developed, independently soaring minds especially suited to establishing and collecting many small, ordinary facts and drawing conclusions from them. As exceptions, they stand from the outset at something of a disadvantage towards those who are “the rules”. After all, they have more to do than perceive: they must BE something new, MEAN something new, REPRESENT new values! The gap between knowledge and ability may be larger, and more mysterious, than we suppose. The capable person on the grand scale, the creator, may have to be ignorant. Scientific discoveries like Darwin's, on the other hand, may benefit from a certain narrowness, dryness, and hardworking carefulness—in short, something English. Finally, remember that the English, with their profound mediocrity, once before brought about a general decline in European intelligence. What people call “modern ideas”, “the ideas of the eighteenth century”, or “French ideas”—against which the GERMAN spirit rose in profound disgust—is indisputably English in origin. The French merely aped and acted out these ideas; they were their best soldiers and, alas! their first and deepest VICTIMS. Through the devilish Anglomania of “modern ideas”, the AME FRANCAIS has finally grown so thin and wasted that we now recall its sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, its deep, passionate strength and outstanding inventiveness, almost in disbelief. Yet we must firmly uphold this historically just verdict against present prejudices and appearances: European NOBLESSE, in feeling, taste, and manners, in every elevated meaning of the word, is FRANCE'S work and invention. European ignobility, the plebeianism of modern ideas, is ENGLAND'S work and invention.

254. Even today France remains the home of Europe's most intellectual, refined culture, its advanced school of taste. But one must know how to find this “France of taste”. Those who belong to it stay well hidden. Perhaps only a few embody and sustain it, and perhaps they do not stand on very strong legs: some are fatalists, hypochondriacs, invalids; others overindulged, overrefined people whose AMBITION is to conceal themselves. All share one trait: they close their ears to the democratic BOURGEOIS's delirious folly and noisy outpourings. For a stupefied, brutalized France now sprawls in the foreground. At Victor Hugo's funeral it recently celebrated a genuine orgy of bad taste and self-admiration. These hidden people share something else: a desire to resist intellectual Germanization—and an even greater inability to do so! In this intellectual France, also a pessimistic France, Schopenhauer has perhaps become more at home and more native than he ever was in Germany. Not to mention Heinrich Heine, long since reincarnated in Paris's more refined and demanding lyric poets; or Hegel, who now exercises an almost tyrannical influence in the form of Taine, the FOREMOST living historian. As for Richard Wagner, the more French music learns to adapt to the actual needs of the AME MODERNE, the more it will “Wagnerite”. We can safely predict that: it is already happening enough! Nevertheless, despite every willing or unwilling Germanization and vulgarization of taste, the French can still proudly claim three things as their inheritance and possession, indelible signs of their old intellectual superiority in Europe. FIRST, their capacity for artistic feeling and devotion to “form”, for which L'ART POUR L'ART and many other expressions were invented. France has possessed this capacity for three centuries. Its respect for the “small number” has repeatedly made possible a kind of chamber music of literature, sought in vain elsewhere in Europe. SECOND, the French can claim superiority through their old, many-sided MORALISTIC culture. Thanks to it, even minor newspaper ROMANCIERS and random BOULEVARDIERS DE PARIS generally display a psychological sensitivity and curiosity of which Germany, for example, has no conception, let alone the thing itself! Germans lack a couple of centuries of the necessary moralistic work which, as I said, France has willingly undertaken. Calling Germans “naive” on that account praises a deficiency. Set against German inexperience and innocence IN VOLUPTATE PSYCHOLOGICA, which is not unconnected with the tedium of German company, stands Henri Beyle. He is the most successful expression of genuine French curiosity and inventiveness in this realm of delicate thrills: that remarkable man who anticipated and ran ahead, traversing HIS Europe with a Napoleonic TEMPO, surveying and discovering, in effect, several centuries of the European soul. It took two generations to CATCH UP with him in one way or another, to divine long afterwards some of the riddles that troubled and enchanted this strange Epicurean and questioner, France's last great psychologist. There is a THIRD claim to superiority: French character successfully combines North and South halfway between them. This makes the French understand many things and imposes other things on them that an Englishman can never comprehend. Their temperament turns alternately towards and away from the South, with Provencal and Ligurian blood occasionally bubbling over. It protects them from the dreadful northern grey-on-grey, from sunless spectral abstractions and impoverished blood, that GERMAN sickness of taste. Its current prevalence has prompted the firm prescription of blood and iron, meaning “high politics”, according to a dangerous healing art that makes me wait and wait, but not yet hope. France also retains an instinctive understanding and ready welcome for rarer, seldom-satisfied people too comprehensive to find contentment in any patriotism. They know how to love the South in the North and the North in the South: born Midlanders, “good Europeans”. BIZET made music for them, this latest genius who saw a new beauty and seduction, who discovered a piece of the SOUTH IN MUSIC.

255. I believe we should take many precautions against German music. Suppose someone loves the South as I do: as a great school of recovery from the most spiritual and the most sensual illnesses, an endless abundance and radiance of sunlight spread over a sovereign existence that believes in itself. Such a person will learn to be somewhat wary of German music, because by damaging his taste again it will also damage his health again. If this Southerner, Southern by BELIEF rather than birth, dreams of music's future, he must also dream of freeing it from Northern influence. He must hear the prelude to a deeper, mightier, perhaps more perverse and mysterious music, a music beyond Germany which does not fade, pale, and die, as all German music does, before the blue, exuberant sea and the clear Mediterranean sky. It would be music beyond Europe, holding its own even against the desert's brown sunsets, its soul akin to the palm tree, at home roaming with great, beautiful, solitary beasts of prey... I can imagine music whose rarest charm would be that it knew nothing any longer of good and evil. Only here and there, perhaps, a sailor's homesickness, golden shadows, and tender weaknesses might brush lightly across it. From far away this art would see the colours of a sinking, almost incomprehensible MORAL world fleeing towards it, and would be hospitable and deep enough to receive these late-arriving fugitives.

256. The nationalistic craze has caused, and still causes, a sickly estrangement among Europe's nations. Shortsighted, hasty politicians now hold power with its help, never suspecting how necessarily temporary their policy of disintegration must be. Because of all this, and much else that cannot presently be mentioned, people now overlook the clearest signs that EUROPE WANTS TO BE ONE, or wilfully misinterpret them. Among this century's deeper, broader-minded men, the true general direction of their souls' mysterious work was to prepare that new SYNTHESIS and tentatively anticipate the future European. Only in their poses, or their weaker moments, perhaps in old age, did they belong to the “fatherlands”. When they became “patriots”, they were merely resting from themselves. I mean such men as Napoleon, Goethe, Beethoven, Stendhal, Heinrich Heine, and Schopenhauer. Do not take it amiss if I include Richard Wagner. We must not let his own misunderstandings deceive us about him—geniuses like him seldom have the right to understand themselves—still less the unseemly noise of present French resistance and opposition to him. The fact remains that Richard Wagner and the LATER FRENCH ROMANTICISM of the forties are intimately, closely related. Their kinship is fundamental, in every height and depth of their demands. In their varied, tumultuous art, it is Europe, ONE Europe, whose soul urgently and longingly presses outward and upward—where? Into a new light? Towards a new sun? But who would try to state precisely what all these masters of new languages could not express distinctly? Certainly the same storm and stress tormented them; these last great seekers SOUGHT in the same way! All were steeped in literature up to their eyes and ears, the first artists of universal literary culture. Most were themselves writers and poets, mediators and mixers of arts and senses: Wagner as musician belongs among painters, as poet among musicians, as artist generally among actors. All were fanatics for EXPRESSION “at any cost”—I especially name Delacroix, Wagner's closest relative. All made great discoveries in the sublime, and also in the disgusting and terrifying; greater still were their discoveries in effect, display, and the art of the show-shop. Their talent exceeded even their genius; they were VIRTUOSI through and through, with mysterious access to everything that seduces, attracts, compels, and overturns. Born enemies of logic and the straight line, they craved the strange, exotic, monstrous, crooked, and contradictory. As people, they were Tantaluses of the will, plebeian upstarts who knew themselves incapable of a noble TEMPO or LENTO in life and action—think of Balzac, for instance. Unrestrained workers, they nearly destroyed themselves through work; rebels against laws and conventions of conduct, ambitious and insatiable, without balance or enjoyment. All finally shattered and sank before the Christian cross, with reason and justice: which of them was deep and original enough for an ANTI-CHRISTIAN philosophy? Taken together, they were a boldly daring, magnificently overbearing class of higher men, soaring and dragging others upward, who first had to teach their century—and it was the century of the MASSES—the concept “higher man”... Let Richard Wagner's German friends discuss whether anything in his art is purely German, or whether its distinction lies precisely in sources and impulses BEYOND GERMANY. In this connection, do not underestimate how indispensable Paris was to the development of his type. At the decisive moment, the force of his instincts made him long to visit it; the entire style of his activity, of his self-appointed apostolate, could perfect itself only in sight of the French socialist original. A subtler comparison may find, to the credit of Wagner's German nature, that he acted in everything with greater strength, daring, severity, and elevation than a nineteenth-century Frenchman could have done, because we Germans are still closer to barbarism than the French. Perhaps Wagner's most remarkable creation is inaccessible, incomprehensible, and inimitable to the entire late Latin race, not just now but forever: Siegfried, that VERY FREE man, probably far too free, hard, cheerful, healthy, and ANTI-CATHOLIC for the taste of old, mellow civilizations. This anti-Latin Siegfried may even have sinned against Romanticism. Well, Wagner amply atoned for that sin in his sad old age. Anticipating a taste that has since entered politics, he began, with his characteristic religious fervour, at least to preach THE ROAD TO ROME, if not to walk it. To prevent misunderstanding of those last words, I call on a few forceful rhymes. They will reveal even to less sensitive ears what I mean, what I mean AGAINST the “last Wagner” and his Parsifal music: Is this our way? From German hearts, this tortured wailing? From German flesh, this self-assailing? These priestly hands spread wide in prayer, This incense rising through the air? This faltering, falling, stumbling motion, This wavering ding-dong of devotion? These sly looks at nuns, these Ave bells ringing, This utterly false, ecstatic heavenward springing? Is this our way? Think hard! You still await admission: What you hear is ROME—ROME'S FAITH BY INTUITION!

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — What Is Noble?
paragraphs: 257. Every elevation of the type "man" has so far been the work of an aristocratic society — and so it will always be. Such a society believes in a long ladder of rank and worth among human beings, and it requires slavery in some form. Without the pathos of distance — the distance that grows from an embodied difference of classes, from the ruling caste's habit of looking out and down upon its subordinates and instruments, from its constant practice of obeying and commanding, of holding down and holding apart — that other, more mysterious pathos could never have arisen: the longing for an ever-greater widening of distance within the soul itself, the formation of ever higher, rarer, further, more extended, more comprehensive states — in short, the elevation of the type "man," the continued self-overcoming of man, to use a moral formula in a supermoral sense. One must not indulge any humanitarian illusions about the origin of an aristocratic society — that is, the precondition for the elevation of the type "man." The truth is hard. Let us acknowledge without prejudice how every higher civilization has hitherto originated! Men with a still natural nature, barbarians in every terrible sense of the word, men of prey, still possessed of unbroken strength of will and lust for power, flung themselves upon weaker, more moral, more peaceful races (perhaps trading or cattle-rearing communities), or upon old mellow civilizations in which the final vital force was flickering out in brilliant fireworks of wit and depravity. At the start, the noble caste was always the barbarian caste: their superiority lay not first of all in their physical but in their psychical power — they were more complete men (which at every point also means: more complete beasts).

258. Corruption — the sign that anarchy threatens to break out among the instincts, and that the foundation of the emotions, called "life," is convulsed — is something radically different depending on the organization in which it shows itself. When, for instance, an aristocracy like that of France at the beginning of the Revolution threw away its privileges with sublime disgust and sacrificed itself to an excess of its own moral sentiments, that was corruption. It was really only the closing act of a corruption that had existed for centuries: that aristocracy had been surrendering its lordly prerogatives step by step, lowering itself into a function of the monarchy (and at the end into its decoration and parade-dress). The essential thing in a good and healthy aristocracy is that it regards itself not as a function of the monarchy or the commonwealth but as the significance and highest justification of them — that it therefore accepts with a good conscience the sacrifice of countless individuals who, for its sake, must be suppressed and reduced to imperfect men, to slaves and instruments. Its fundamental belief must be precisely that society is not allowed to exist for its own sake but only as a foundation and scaffolding by which a select class of beings can raise themselves to their higher duties and to a higher existence — like those sun-seeking climbing plants in Java, called Sipo Matador, that wrap their arms around an oak so long and so often until at last, high above it but supported by it, they can unfold their crowns in the open light and display their happiness.

259. To refrain mutually from injury, violence, and exploitation, and to put one's will on a par with that of others — this can, in a certain rough sense, make for good conduct among individuals, provided the necessary conditions are present (that the individuals are actually similar in force and worth, and co-related within one organization). The moment one wishes to take this principle more generally, and possibly even as the fundamental principle of society, it at once reveals what it really is: a will to the denial of life, a principle of dissolution and decay. One must think here profoundly, to the very roots, and resist all sentimental weakness. Life itself is essentially appropriation, injury, conquest of the strange and weak, suppression, severity, the imposition of one's own forms, incorporation — at the very least and mildest: exploitation. But why should one forever use precisely these words, on which disparaging intent has long been stamped? Even that organization within which, as was previously supposed, individuals treat each other as equal — as happens in every healthy aristocracy — must itself, if it is a living and not a dying organization, do toward other bodies all that its members refrain from doing to one another. It will have to be an embodied will to power; it will seek to grow, to gain ground, to attract to itself and win ascendancy — not out of any morality or immorality, but because it lives, and because life is precisely will to power. On no point is the ordinary consciousness of Europeans more unwilling to be corrected than on this. People rave everywhere, even under the banner of science, about future conditions of society in which "the exploiting character" will be absent. To my ears that sounds as if they promised to invent a mode of life that dispensed with all organic functions. Exploitation does not belong to a depraved or primitive society; it belongs to the nature of the living being as a primary organic function. It is a consequence of the intrinsic will to power, which is precisely the will to life. As a theory this may be a novelty — as a reality it is the fundamental fact of all history. Let us be at least this honest with ourselves!

260. On a journey through the many finer and coarser moralities that have prevailed or still prevail on earth, I found certain traits recurring together and linked with one another, until at last two primary types emerged and a fundamental distinction came to light. There is master-morality and slave-morality. I should add at once that in all higher and mixed civilizations there are also attempts at reconciling the two — more often still their confusion and mutual misunderstanding, and sometimes their close juxtaposition, even within the same man, within one soul. The distinctions of moral values have originated either in a ruling caste, pleasantly conscious of being different from those it ruled, or among the ruled — the slaves and dependents of every kind. In the first case, when it is the rulers who determine the concept "good," it is the exalted, proud states of soul that are felt to be what distinguishes and determines rank. The noble type of man separates from himself those in whom the opposite of such states shows itself; he despises them. It should be noted that in this first kind of morality the opposition "good" and "bad" means practically the same as "noble" and "despicable." The opposition "good" and "evil" has a different origin. The cowardly, the timid, the petty, those who think only of narrow utility are despised; so too the distrustful with their constrained glances, the self-abasing, the dog-like men who let themselves be mistreated, the mendicant flatterers, and above all the liars. It is a fundamental belief of all aristocrats that the common people are untruthful. "We truthful ones" — so the nobility called itself in ancient Greece. It is obvious that moral designations were first applied to men and only derivatively, at a later period, to actions. Historians of morals therefore make a gross mistake when they start with questions like "Why have sympathetic actions been praised?" The noble type of man feels himself to be the determiner of values. He does not require approval; he passes judgment: "What harms me is harmful in itself." He knows that it is he alone who confers honor on things; he is a creator of values. He honors whatever he recognizes in himself: such morality is self-glorification. In the foreground is the feeling of fullness, of power that seeks to overflow, the happiness of high tension, the consciousness of a wealth that would gladly give and bestow. The noble man also helps the unfortunate, but not — or scarcely — out of pity; rather from an impulse generated by the superabundance of power. The noble man honors in himself the powerful one, the man who has power over himself, who knows how to speak and how to keep silent, who takes pleasure in subjecting himself to severity and hardness, and who has reverence for all that is severe and hard. "Wotan placed a hard heart in my breast," an old Scandinavian saga says — rightly expressed from the soul of a proud Viking. Such a man is even proud of not being made for sympathy, and so the saga hero adds a warning: "He who has not a hard heart when young will never have one." The noble and brave who think in this way are the furthest removed from a morality that sees the characteristic of the moral precisely in sympathy, in acting for others, in désintéressement. Faith in oneself, pride in oneself, a fundamental enmity and irony toward "selflessness" — these belong as surely to noble morality as do a careless scorn and caution in the presence of sympathy and the "warm heart." It is the powerful who know how to honor; it is their art, their realm of invention. Profound reverence for age and tradition — all law rests on this double reverence — the belief and prejudice in favor of ancestors and against newcomers, is typical of the morality of the powerful. If, conversely, men of "modern ideas" believe almost instinctively in "progress" and "the future," and show less and less respect for age, the ignoble origin of these "ideas" has complacently betrayed itself. A morality of the ruling class is, however, most foreign and irritating to present-day taste in the sternness of its principle that one has duties only to one's equals; that toward beings of lower rank, toward all that is foreign, one may act as one pleases, or "as the heart desires," and in any case "beyond good and evil" — here sympathy and similar sentiments can find their place. The ability and duty to exercise prolonged gratitude and prolonged revenge — both only within the circle of equals — artfulness in retaliation, raffinement of the idea of friendship, a certain need for enemies (as outlets for the emotions of envy, quarrelsomeness, arrogance — in order, in fact, to be a good friend): all these are typical features of noble morality. As noted, it is not the morality of "modern ideas," and is therefore hard to realize today, and also hard to unearth and uncover. It is otherwise with the second type of morality, slave-morality. Suppose that the abused, the oppressed, the suffering, the unfree, the weary, and those uncertain of themselves moralize — what will be the common element in their moral estimates? A pessimistic suspicion about the entire human situation will probably find expression, perhaps a condemnation of man together with his situation. The slave has an unfavorable eye for the virtues of the powerful; he has a skepticism and distrust, a refinement of distrust for everything "good" that is honored there — he would like to persuade himself that even their happiness is not genuine. On the other hand, those qualities that serve to ease the existence of sufferers are brought forward and bathed in light: here sympathy, the kind and helping hand, the warm heart, patience, diligence, humility, and friendliness come to honor, for here these are the most useful qualities and almost the only means of bearing the burden of existence. Slave-morality is essentially a morality of utility. Here is the origin of the famous opposition "good" and "evil": power and dangerousness are assumed to reside in the evil — a certain dreadfulness, subtlety, and strength that do not allow themselves to be despised. According to slave-morality, then, the "evil" man arouses fear; according to master-morality, it is precisely the "good" man who arouses and wishes to arouse fear, while the "bad" man is thought of as the despicable being. The contrast reaches its peak when, in consistency with slave-morality, a shade of disparagement — it may be slight and well-meaning — attaches itself at last to the "good" man of this morality. On the servile mode of thought, the good man must in any case be the safe man: good-natured, easily deceived, perhaps a little stupid, un bonhomme. Wherever slave-morality gains ascendancy, language shows a tendency to approximate the meanings of the words "good" and "stupid." One last fundamental difference: the desire for freedom, the instinct for happiness, and the refinements of the feeling of liberty belong as necessarily to slave-morality as artifice and enthusiasm in reverence and devotion are the regular symptoms of an aristocratic mode of thinking and valuing. From this it is easy to see why love as a passion — our European speciality — must be of noble origin; its invention, as is well known, is owed to the Provençal knight-poets, those brilliant, ingenious men of the gai saber, to whom Europe owes so much, and almost owes itself.

261. Vanity is one of the things hardest for a noble man to understand: he will be tempted to deny it where another kind of man thinks he sees it self-evidently. The problem for him is to picture to himself beings who seek to arouse a good opinion of themselves that they do not actually possess — and so do not "deserve" — and who yet afterward believe in this good opinion. This strikes him as so tasteless and self-disrespecting on the one hand, and on the other so grotesquely unreasonable, that he would like to consider vanity an exception and is doubtful about it in most cases where it is spoken of. He will say, for instance: "I may be mistaken about my value, but I may nevertheless insist that others acknowledge my value exactly as I rate it. That, however, is not vanity — it is self-conceit, or in most cases what is called 'humility' or 'modesty.'" Or he will even say: "For many reasons I can delight in the good opinion of others — perhaps because I love and honor them and rejoice in their joys, perhaps because their good opinion endorses and strengthens my belief in my own value, perhaps because their good opinion, even where I do not share it, is useful to me or promises to be so — but none of this is vanity." The noble man must force himself, with the help of history above all, to recognize that from time immemorial, in all the strata of society that were in any way dependent, the ordinary man was only what he passed for. Unaccustomed to fixing values, he did not assign to himself any other value than that which his master assigned him (for creating values is the peculiar right of masters). It may be regarded as the result of an extraordinary atavism that the ordinary man today is still always waiting for an opinion about himself and then instinctively submitting to it — and not only to a "good" opinion, but also to a bad and unjust one. (Think, for instance, of the greater part of the self-valuations and self-depreciations that believing women learn from their confessors, and that the believing Christian in general learns from his Church.) In fact, with the slow rise of the democratic social order (and its cause, the blending of the blood of masters and slaves), the originally noble and rare impulse of masters to assign a value to themselves and to think well of themselves will be more and more encouraged and extended. But it has at every time an older, ampler, more deeply rooted tendency opposed to it — and in the phenomenon of vanity this older tendency masters the younger. The vain person takes pleasure in every good opinion of himself (quite apart from its usefulness and regardless of its truth or falsehood), just as he suffers from every bad one: for he submits himself to both, he feels himself subjected to both, by that oldest instinct of submission which breaks forth in him. It is "the slave" in the vain man's blood, the remnant of the slave's craftiness — and how much of "the slave" is still left in woman, for instance! — that seeks to seduce others into good opinions of it; it is the slave, too, who immediately afterward falls prostrate before these opinions, as if he had not called them forth. To repeat: vanity is an atavism.

262. A species originates, and a type becomes established and strong, through the long struggle with essentially constant unfavorable conditions. On the other hand, breeders know by experience that species receiving superabundant nourishment, and in general a surplus of protection and care, immediately tend to develop variations strongly marked, and become fertile in prodigies and monstrosities (including monstrous vices). Now look at an aristocratic commonwealth — say, an ancient Greek polis or Venice — as a voluntary or involuntary arrangement for the rearing of human beings. There are men side by side, thrown on their own resources, who want to make their kind prevail, chiefly because they must prevail — or else face the terrible danger of extermination. The favor, the superabundance, the protection under which variations are fostered are lacking; the species needs itself as species, as something that, precisely through its hardness, its uniformity, and simplicity of structure, can prevail and make itself permanent in constant struggle with neighbors or with rebellious or rebellion-threatening vassals. The most varied experience teaches it what qualities have allowed it to exist despite all gods and men and have so far made it victorious: these qualities it calls virtues, and these alone it cultivates to maturity. It does so with severity — indeed it desires severity. Every aristocratic morality is intolerant in the education of youth, in the control of women, in marriage customs, in the relations of old and young, in penal laws (which have an eye only for the degenerate); it even counts intolerance among the virtues, under the name of "justice." A type with few but strongly marked features, a species of severe, warlike, shrewdly silent, reserved, and reticent men (who, precisely as such, have the most delicate sensibility for the charm and nuances of society), is thus established, unaffected by the vicissitudes of generations. The constant struggle with uniformly unfavorable conditions is, as noted, the cause of a type becoming stable and hard. Finally, however, a happy state comes: the enormous tension relaxes; perhaps there are no more enemies among neighboring peoples, and the means of life — even of the enjoyment of life — are present in superabundance. At one stroke the bond and constraint of the old discipline is severed: it is no longer felt necessary, no longer a condition of existence — if it is to continue, it can only do so as a form of luxury, as an archaizing taste. Variations, whether they be deviations (into the higher, finer, and rarer) or deteriorations and monstrosities, now appear suddenly on the scene in the greatest exuberance and splendor. The individual dares to be individual and to detach himself. At this turning point of history there appear, side by side and often mixed and entangled together, a magnificent, virgin-forest-like upward growth and upward striving, a kind of tropical tempo in the rivalry of growth, and an extraordinary decay and self-destruction, owing to the savagely opposing and seemingly exploding egoisms that strive against one another "for sun and light" and can no longer assign themselves any limit, restraint, or forbearance through the existing morality. It was this morality itself that piled up the strength so enormously, that bent the bow in so threatening a manner; it is now "out of date," it is getting "out of date." The dangerous and disquieting point has been reached when the greater, more manifold, more comprehensive life is lived beyond the old morality. The "individual" stands out and is obliged to have recourse to his own lawgiving, his own arts and artifices, for self-preservation, self-elevation, and self-deliverance. Nothing but new "Whys," nothing but new "Hows," no common formulas any longer; misunderstanding and disregard leagued together; decay, deterioration, and the loftiest desires frightfully entangled; the genius of the race overflowing from all the cornucopias of good and bad; a portentous simultaneity of spring and autumn, full of new charms and mysteries peculiar to the fresh, still inexhausted, still unwearied corruption. Danger is again present — the mother of morality — great danger, this time shifted into the individual, into neighbor and friend, into the street, into one's own child, into one's own heart, into all the most personal and secret recesses of desire and will. What will the moral philosophers of this time have to preach? They discover, these sharp observers and loafers, that the end is quickly approaching, that everything around them decays and produces decay, that nothing will last until the day after tomorrow — except one species of man, the incurably mediocre. The mediocre alone have a prospect of continuing and propagating themselves; they will be the men of the future, the sole survivors. "Be like them! Become mediocre!" is now the only morality that still has significance, that still gets a hearing. But it is difficult to preach this morality of mediocrity! It can never admit what it is and what it wants! It has to speak of moderation and dignity and duty and brotherly love — it will have trouble concealing its irony!

263. There is an instinct for rank which, more than anything else, is already the sign of a high rank; there is a delight in the nuances of reverence that leads one to infer noble origin and habits. The refinement, goodness, and loftiness of a soul are put to a perilous test when something of the highest rank passes by that is not yet protected by the awe of authority from obtrusive touches and incivilities: something that goes its way like a living touchstone, undistinguished, undiscovered, tentative, perhaps voluntarily veiled and disguised. He whose task and practice it is to investigate souls will make use of many varieties of this art to determine the ultimate value of a soul, the unalterable, innate order of rank to which it belongs: he will test it by its instinct for reverence. Différence engendre haine: the vulgarity of many a nature suddenly spurts up like dirty water when any holy vessel, any jewel from closed shrines, any book bearing the marks of great destiny, is brought before it. On the other hand, there is an involuntary silence, a hesitation of the eye, a cessation of all gestures, by which it is signaled that a soul feels the nearness of what is most worthy of respect. The way in which reverence for the Bible has on the whole been maintained in Europe is perhaps the best example of the discipline and refinement of manners that Europe owes to Christianity: books of such depth and supreme significance require for their protection an external tyranny of authority, in order to win the thousands of years necessary to exhaust and decipher them. Much has been achieved when the feeling is finally instilled into the masses (the shallow-pates and boobies of every kind) that they are not allowed to touch everything, that there are holy experiences before which they must take off their shoes and keep away the unclean hand — it is almost their highest advance toward humanity. By contrast, among the so-called cultured classes, the believers in "modern ideas," nothing is perhaps so repulsive as their shamelessness, the easy insolence of eye and hand with which they touch, taste, and finger everything. It is possible that even now there is more relative nobility of taste, more tact for reverence, among the people — among the lower classes of the people, especially among peasants — than among the newspaper-reading demimonde of intellect, the cultured class.

264. It cannot be effaced from a man's soul what his ancestors most preferably and constantly did: whether they were perhaps diligent economizers attached to a desk and a cash-box, modest and citizen-like in their desires and in their virtues; or whether they were accustomed to commanding from morning till night, fond of rough pleasures and probably of rougher duties and responsibilities; or whether, finally, at some time they sacrificed old privileges of birth and possession in order to live wholly for their faith — for their "God" — as men of an inexorable and sensitive conscience that blushes at every compromise. It is quite impossible for a man not to have the qualities and predilections of his parents and ancestors in his constitution, whatever appearances may suggest to the contrary. This is the problem of race. Given that one knows something of the parents, one may draw a conclusion about the child: any kind of offensive incontinence, any kind of sordid envy, any kind of clumsy self-vaunting — the three things which together have constituted the genuine plebeian type in all times — must pass to the child as surely as bad blood; and with the help of the best education and culture one will only succeed in deceiving about such heredity. And what else does education and culture try to do nowadays? In our very democratic — or rather, very plebeian — age, "education" and "culture" must be essentially the art of deceiving: deceiving about origin, about the inherited plebeianism in body and soul. An educator who today preached truthfulness above everything else and constantly called out to his pupils, "Be true! Be natural! Show yourselves as you are!" — even such a virtuous and sincere ass would soon learn to resort to Horace's furca — naturam expellere — and with what results? Plebeianism usque recurret.

265. At the risk of displeasing innocent ears, I submit that egoism belongs to the essence of a noble soul — I mean the unalterable belief that to a being such as "we," other beings must naturally be in subjection and must sacrifice themselves. The noble soul accepts the fact of his egoism without question, and also without any feeling of harshness, constraint, or arbitrariness, but rather as something that may have its basis in the primary law of things. If he sought a name for it, he would say: "It is justice itself." He acknowledges under certain circumstances, though they made him hesitate at first, that there are other equally privileged ones. As soon as he has settled this question of rank, he moves among these equals with the same assurance of modesty and delicate respect as he enjoys in dealing with himself — in accordance with an innate heavenly mechanism that all the stars understand. This artfulness and self-limitation in intercourse with his equals is another instance of his egoism: every star is a similar egoist. He honors himself in them, and in the rights he concedes to them; he has no doubt that the exchange of honors and rights, as the essence of all intercourse, belongs also to the natural condition of things. The noble soul gives as he takes, prompted by the passionate and sensitive instinct of requital that is at the root of his nature. The notion of "favor," inter pares, has neither significance nor good repute; there may be a sublime way of letting gifts, as it were, light upon one from above, and of drinking them thirstily like dew-drops, but the noble soul has no aptitude for those arts and displays. His egoism prevents it: in general he looks "aloft" unwillingly — he looks either forward, horizontally and deliberately, or downward: he knows that he is on a height.
266. "One can only truly esteem him who does not look out for himself." — Goethe to Rath Schlosser.

267. The Chinese have a proverb that mothers even teach their children: "siao-sin" ("make thy heart small"). This is the essentially fundamental tendency of latter-day civilizations. I have no doubt that an ancient Greek would first of all remark the self-dwarfing in us Europeans of today — in this respect alone we should immediately be "distasteful" to him.

268. What, after all, is ignobleness? Words are vocal symbols for ideas; ideas, however, are more or less definite mental symbols for frequently returning and concurring sensations, for groups of sensations. It is not enough to use the same words in order to understand one another: we must use the same words for the same kind of inner experiences; in the end we must have experiences in common. For this reason the people of one nation understand one another better than those of different nations, even when using the same language — or rather, when people have lived long together under similar conditions (of climate, soil, danger, need, toil), an entity arises that "understands itself": a nation. In all souls a like number of frequently recurring experiences have gained the upper hand over those occurring more rarely; about these matters people understand one another rapidly, and always more rapidly — the history of language is the history of a process of abbreviation. On the basis of this quick comprehension people always unite more closely. The greater the danger, the greater the need to agree quickly and readily about what is necessary; not to misunderstand one another in danger is indispensable in human intercourse. In all loves and friendships too one has the experience that nothing of the kind continues once the discovery has been made that, in using the same words, one of the two parties has feelings, thoughts, intuitions, wishes, or fears different from those of the other. (The fear of the "eternal misunderstanding" is the good genius which so often keeps persons of different sexes from too hasty attachments to which sense and heart prompt them — and not some Schopenhauerian "genius of the species"!) Whichever groups of sensations within a soul awaken most readily, begin to speak, and give the word of command — these decide the general order of rank of its values and ultimately determine its list of desirable things. A man's estimates of value betray something of the structure of his soul, of where it sees its conditions of life, its intrinsic needs. Suppose now that necessity has from time immemorial drawn together only those men who could express similar requirements and similar experiences through similar symbols. It follows on the whole that the easy communicability of need — which ultimately implies the undergoing only of average and common experiences — must have been the most potent of all the forces that have hitherto operated on mankind. The more similar, the more ordinary people, have always had and still have the advantage; the more select, more refined, more unique, more difficult to comprehend are liable to stand alone, succumb to accidents in their isolation, and seldom propagate themselves. One must appeal to immense opposing forces to thwart this natural, all-too-natural progressus in simile — the evolution of man to the similar, the ordinary, the average, the gregarious, the ignoble!

269. The more a psychologist — a born, an unavoidable psychologist and soul-diviner — turns his attention to the more select cases and individuals, the greater is his danger of being suffocated by sympathy. He needs sternness and cheerfulness more than any other man. For the corruption and ruination of higher men, of the more unusually constituted souls, is in fact the rule: it is dreadful to have such a rule always before one's eyes. The manifold torment of the psychologist who has discovered this ruination, who discovers it once and then discovers it almost repeatedly throughout all history — this universal inner "desperateness" of higher men, this eternal "too late!" in every sense — may perhaps one day cause him to turn with bitterness against his own lot and to attempt self-destruction: to "go to ruin" himself. In almost every psychologist one may perceive a telltale inclination for delightful intercourse with commonplace and well-ordered men; the fact is thereby disclosed that he always requires healing, that he needs a sort of flight and forgetfulness, away from what his insight and incisiveness — his "business" — has laid upon his conscience. The fear of his memory is peculiar to him. He is easily silenced by the judgment of others; he hears with unmoved countenance how people honor, admire, love, and glorify where he has perceived, or he even conceals his silence by expressly assenting to some plausible opinion. Perhaps the paradox of his situation becomes so dreadful that precisely where he has learned great sympathy together with great contempt, the multitude, the educated, and the visionaries have on their part learned great reverence — reverence for "great men" and marvelous animals for whose sake one blesses and honors the fatherland, the earth, the dignity of mankind, and oneself, to whom one points the young, and in view of whom one educates them. And who knows but in all great instances hitherto the same happened: that the multitude worshipped a god, and that the "god" was only a poor sacrificial animal!
